items.stem: Where g = 9.81 m s⁻², a light 2.4 m cord holds angle 38° to the vertical as its 1.4 kg bob circles steadily in a horizontal plane.
items.workedSolution: (a) Resolving vertically, T cos 38° = (1.4)(9.81) gives T = 17.4 N. (b) Horizontal radius r = 2.4 sin 38° = 1.48 m; horizontal dynamics T sin θ = mv²/r yields v = 3.37 m s⁻¹. (c) Period P = 2πr / v = 2.76 s.

markScheme.criterion: Equates vertical component T cos θ to weight mg.
Obtains tension 17.4 N.
Uses r = L sin θ and equates T sin θ (or mg tan θ) to m v² / r.
Obtains speed 3.37 m s⁻¹.
Applies P = 2π r / v or P = 2π√(L cos θ / g).
Obtains period 2.76 s.

items.stem: An exoplanet of radius 8.00 × 10⁷ m orbits a star of radius 6.40 × 10⁸ m. Its orbital period is 4.50 days, as shown in the transit light curve.
items.workedSolution: (a) Dip $= 1.56\%$. (b) $T = 3.89 × 10⁵ s$. (c) orbital plane must align closely with the line of sight from Earth.

markScheme.criterion: Applies $(r_p / R_s)^2 \times 100$.
Correct dip 1.56%.
Multiplies 4.50 days by $24 \times 3600$.
Correct period 3.89 × 10⁵ s.
States orbital plane must lie almost along our line of sight.
Notes very small transit dip or long wait to confirm periodicity.

Convert the orbital period of 4.50 days into seconds.
State one major observational limitation of the transit method for discovering Earth-sized planets in wide orbits.
parts.expectedAnswer: The orbital plane must align closely with the line of sight from Earth, and a small rocky planet creates a tiny brightness dip that repeats infrequently.
workingSteps: State strict alignment along Earth's line of sight.
Note tiny fractional dip and long intervals between repeat transits.

items.stem: Star X plotted in the red giant region of the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram has luminosity $L = 100\,L_{\odot}$ ($3.83 \times 10^{28}\text{ W}$) and surface temperature $T = 2900\text{ K}$. Given the Sun has radius $R_{\odot} = 6.96 \times 10^8\text{ m}$, what is the radius of Star X expressed in solar radii?
items.workedSolution: From $L = 4\pi R^2 \sigma T^4$, $R = \sqrt{\frac{3.83 \times 10^{28}}{4\pi (5.67 \times 10^{-8})(2900)^4}} = 2.76 × 10¹⁰ m$. Dividing by $R_{\odot} = 6.96 \times 10^8\text{ m}$ gives 39.6 R⊙.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 39.6 R⊙.

items.stem: A newly formed neutron star has a mass of $1.50 M_{\odot}$ ($M_{\odot} = 1.99 \times 10^{30}\text{ kg}$) compressed into a sphere of radius $12.0\text{ km}$. Calculate its mean density.
items.workedSolution: $M = 1.50 \times 1.99 \times 10^{30} = 2.99 \times 10^{30}\text{ kg}$, $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi (1.20 \times 10^4)^3 = 7.24 \times 10^{12}\text{ m}^3$. Thus $\rho = M / V = 4.12 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³$, comparable to nuclear density.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 4.12 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.

items.stem: Two exoplanets orbit a Sun-like star in circular orbits: exoplanet X orbits at $1.50\text{ AU}$ with period $1.84\text{ yr}$, and exoplanet Y orbits at $6.00\text{ AU}$. The diagram compares the outer radial gravitational field of a uniform planet with its near-surface field.
items.workedSolution: (a) Outside its surface, a uniform spherical body acts gravitationally as if all its mass were at its centre. (b) Close to a planet's surface, gravitational field lines are parallel, equally spaced, and directed vertically downwards. This represents a uniform field. (c) $T_{\text{Y}} = 1.84 \times 8 = 14.7 yr$.

markScheme.criterion: Specifies spherical symmetry / uniform density distribution.
States that outside its surface, a uniform spherical body acts as if all its mass were at its centre.
States field lines are vertical and directed downwards towards the surface.
States lines are parallel and equally spaced.
Links parallel, equally spaced downward field lines close to the surface to a uniform gravitational field strength g.
Identifies radius ratio r₂/r₁ = 4.00.
Applies T₂ = T₁ (r₂/r₁)^(3/2).
Obtains T_Y = 14.7 yr.

items.stem: A smooth vertical circular track of radius 0.875 m has a small 1.85 kg ball entering at 7.2 m s⁻¹ with no friction or air drag. Calculate the minimum entry speed to stay in contact at the top (g = 9.8 m s⁻²).
items.workedSolution: For zero contact loss at the peak, v_top ≥ √(gR). Conservation of energy from bottom to top (Δh = 2R) gives ½m v_bot,min² = ½m(gR) + mg(2R) => v_bot,min = √(5gR) = √(5 × 9.8 × 0.875) = 6.55 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates v_bot,min = √(5gR) = 6.55 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: At 5930 K, a spherical black-body star (radius 1.51 × 10¹⁰ m) shines from 5.23 × 10¹⁶ m away from Earth. Given b = 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K, determine its peak emission wavelength in nm.
items.workedSolution: Applying Wien's displacement law gives λ_max = b / T = 2.90 × 10⁻³ / 5930 = 4.89 × 10⁻⁷ m = 489 nm.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates λ_max = 2.90 × 10⁻³ / 5930 = 489 nm.

items.stem: One parsec (1 pc) is the distance where 1 AU yields a 1 arcsecond shift, giving d / pc = 1 / (p / arcsec). Convert with 1 pc = 3.26 ly to find how far in light-years a 2.21 × 10²⁹ W star lies if its Earth 1 AU parallax is 0.571 arcsec.
items.workedSolution: Distance in parsecs d = 1 / p = 1 / 0.571 = 1.75 pc. Converting to light-years gives d = 1.75 × 3.26 = 5.71 ly.

items.stem: Astronomers combine Wien's law, Stefan's law ($P = \sigma A T^4$), and the inverse-square law ($I = P / (4\pi d^2)$) to calculate a star's radius from Earth. What key physical assumptions are made?
items.workedSolution: Combining Stefan's law with the inverse-square law assumes the star acts as a black body radiating equally in all directions, with negligible interstellar absorption.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that the star acts as a black body radiating equally in all directions, with negligible interstellar absorption.

options.label: A
options.text: They assume the star radiates only monochromatic visible light along a narrow beam directed at Earth.
options.distractorRationale: Stars emit continuous broad black-body spectra isotropically in all directions.

options.label: B
options.text: They assume interstellar dust amplifies apparent brightness while stars behave as perfect reflectors.
options.distractorRationale: Interstellar dust absorbs/scatters starlight, and stars are modelled as black-body emitters.

options.label: C
options.text: They assume Stefan's law applies only to stars on the main sequence and fails for red giants.
options.distractorRationale: Stefan's law applies to all spherical black-body emitters including giants and dwarfs.

options.label: D
options.text: They assume the star acts as a black body with isotropic emission and negligible interstellar absorption between the star and Earth.

items.stem: Passing the peak of a smooth vertical loop (radius 1.6 m) at steady speed 6.26 m s⁻¹, a small ball of mass 0.9 kg presses on the track. Find the normal force (g = 9.8 m s⁻²).
items.workedSolution: At the peak, both normal contact force and weight mg act downward toward the centre: F_top + mg = m v² / R, so F_top = m(v²/R − g) = 0.9 × ((6.26)² / 1.6 − 9.8) = 13.2 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies radial force equation at apex to obtain 13.2 N.

items.stem: A student measures a conical pendulum with a light 1.8 m cord at 20° to the vertical and a 0.6 kg bob in steady horizontal motion. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Resolving vertically, T cos 20° = (0.6)(9.8) gives T = 6.26 N. (b) Horizontal radius r = 1.8 sin 20° = 0.616 m; horizontal dynamics T sin θ = mv²/r yields v = 1.48 m s⁻¹. (c) Period P = 2πr / v = 2.61 s.

markScheme.criterion: Equates vertical component T cos θ to weight mg.
Obtains tension 6.26 N.
Uses r = L sin θ and equates T sin θ (or mg tan θ) to m v² / r.
Obtains speed 1.48 m s⁻¹.
Applies P = 2π r / v or P = 2π√(L cos θ / g).
Obtains period 2.61 s.

items.stem: From an inner circular orbit of radius r₁ = 7.57 × 10⁶ m, a 320 kg satellite is lifted to an outer orbit at r₂ = 1.21 × 10⁷ m. The planet has mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 5.41 × 10⁶ m (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²).
items.workedSolution: (a) Initial bound energy E_tot(r₁) = −GMm/(2r₁) = -8.42 × 10⁹ J. (b) Final bound energy E_tot(r₂) = -5.27 × 10⁹ J, so ΔE_tot = 3.15 × 10⁹ J. (c) Outer orbital period T₂ = 2π√(r₂³/GM) = 1.33 × 10⁴ s.

markScheme.criterion: Applies E_tot = −GMm / (2r₁).
Obtains -8.42 × 10⁹ J.
Evaluates E_tot(r₂) − E_tot(r₁) = ½GMm(1/r₁ − 1/r₂).
Obtains 3.15 × 10⁹ J.
Applies Kepler's third law at outer radius r₂.
Obtains 1.33 × 10⁴ s.

items.stem: Use g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air drag. A small ball of mass 1.85 kg on a light string traces a vertical circle of radius 4.32 m, passing the bottom at 16.9 m s⁻¹. Calculate its speed at the top.
items.workedSolution: Climbing one diameter raises height by Δh = 2R. By conservation of energy, ½m v_top² + mg(2R) = ½m v_bot², so v_top = √(v_bot² − 4gR) = √((16.9)² − 4 × 9.81 × 4.32) = 10.8 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses Δh = 2R in v_top = √(v_bot² − 4gR) to obtain 10.8 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A gap of 5.57 × 10⁸ m separates the centres of airless spheres Major Moon (radius 6.37 × 10⁶ m, mass 1.04 × 10²⁵ kg) and Minor Moon (radius 1.57 × 10⁶ m, mass 2.12 × 10²³ kg). Set V_g = 0 at infinity and G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Balance of fields gives x₀ = d√M₁/(√M₁ + √M₂) = 4.87 × 10⁸ m. (b) Combined scalar potential V(x₀) = -1.63 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. (c) Potential barrier from x = R₁ to x₀ is ΔV = 1.07 × 10⁸ J kg⁻¹, giving v_min = √(2ΔV) = 1.46 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies x₀ = d√M₁ / (√M₁ + √M₂).

Sums both negative scalar potentials −GM₁/x₀ − GM₂/(d − x₀).
Obtains V(x₀) = -1.63 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹.
Equates ½v_min² to potential barrier V(x₀) − V(R₁).
Obtains v_min = 1.46 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A spherical planet of uniform density has mass 2.21 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 1.08 × 10⁷ m. A probe of mass 508 kg is lowered into a narrow shaft inside the planet to a distance of 2.7 × 10⁶ m from the centre. Taking G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², calculate the gravitational field strength at this point.
items.workedSolution: Inside a uniform sphere (r < R), enclosed mass M_enc = M(r/R)³, so g(r) = G M r / R³ = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 2.21 × 10²⁴ × 2.7 × 10⁶) / (1.08 × 10⁷)³ = 0.316 N kg⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates gravitational field strength at r = 2.7 × 10⁶ m to obtain 0.316 N kg⁻¹.

items.stem: Consider a 952 kg probe moving along the line joining Host World and Icy Moon as it passes 1.68 × 10⁸ m from Host World's centre. Their centres are 3.05 × 10⁸ m apart, with mass 5.36 × 10²⁴ kg (radius 7.33 × 10⁶ m) for Host World and mass 7.54 × 10²³ kg (radius 2.09 × 10⁶ m) for Icy Moon. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Equating GM₁/x₀² = GM₂/(d − x₀)² yields x₀ = d√M₁/(√M₁ + √M₂) = 2.22 × 10⁸ m. (b) At x = 1.68 × 10⁸ m, |g| = |GM₁/x² − GM₂/(d − x)²| = 0.00999 N kg⁻¹. (c) Net force F = m|g| = 9.51 N.

markScheme.criterion: Equates opposing inverse-square field strengths GM₁/x₀² = GM₂/(d − x₀)².
Takes square root correctly to form x₀ = d√M₁ / (√M₁ + √M₂).
Obtains x₀ = 2.22 × 10⁸ m.
Subtracts opposing field magnitudes at x and (d − x).
Obtains |g| = 0.00999 N kg⁻¹.
Multiplies by spacecraft mass to obtain 9.51 N.

parts.prompt: Calculate the distance from the centre of Host World to the point between them where the resultant gravitational field strength is zero.
workingSteps: At the null point, G M₁ / x₀² = G M₂ / (d − x₀)².
Taking square roots gives x₀ = [√M₁ / (√M₁ + √M₂)] d = 2.22 × 10⁸ m.

parts.prompt: Calculate the magnitude of the resultant gravitational field strength when the probe is 1.68 × 10⁸ m from the centre of Host World.
workingSteps: |g| = |G M₁ / x² − G M₂ / (d − x)²| = 0.00999 N kg⁻¹.

parts.prompt: State the magnitude of the resultant gravitational force on the 952 kg probe at this point.

items.stem: In the figure, a 320 kg trolley circles horizontally around a smooth 25° banked track of radius 72 m. Sideways friction is zero, and g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Zero vertical acceleration gives N cos 25° = mg gives N = 3.46 × 10³ N. (b) Horizontal component F_c = N sin 25° = 1.46 × 10³ N. (c) Setting m v² / r = F_c yields v_ideal = 18.1 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses N cos θ = mg (zero vertical acceleration).
Obtains N = 3.46 × 10³ N.
Evaluates F_c = N sin θ or mg tan θ.
Obtains F_c = 1.46 × 10³ N.
Equates m v² / r to F_c and solves for v.
Obtains v_ideal = 18.1 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the magnitude of the normal contact force on the trolley.
workingSteps: Vertical equilibrium gives N cos θ = mg.

parts.prompt: Determine the horizontal centripetal force acting toward the centre of the circle.
workingSteps: Horizontal component of normal reaction provides the centripetal force: F_c = N sin θ = mg tan θ.

parts.prompt: Hence calculate the ideal frictionless speed of the trolley.
workingSteps: From m v² / r = F_c, v = √(F_c r / m) = √(g r tan θ) = 18.1 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses v ≈ (Δλ / λ₀) c to obtain 1.92 × 10⁴ km s⁻¹.

items.stem: How do astronomers combine measurements of Type Ia supernovae and galaxy spectra to evaluate the Hubble constant?
items.workedSolution: Plotting $v$ against $d$ gives gradient $H$ because distance modulus from type Ia peak absolute magnitude and recession velocity from spectral redshift determine the Hubble constant.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that distance modulus from type Ia peak absolute magnitude and recession velocity from spectral redshift determine the Hubble constant.

items.stem: A satellite of mass 1150 kg orbits a spherical planet in a circular path at altitude h = 1.37 × 10⁷ m above the surface. The planet has mass 1.73 × 10²⁵ kg and radius 5.25 × 10⁶ m, with G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) With orbital radius r = 1.895 × 10⁷ m, g = GM/r² = 3.21 N kg⁻¹. (b) Orbital speed v = √(GM/r) = 7.80 × 10³ m s⁻¹. (c) Period T = 2πr/v = 1.53 × 10⁴ s.

markScheme.criterion: Uses centre-to-centre orbital radius r in g = GM / r².
Obtains g = 3.21 N kg⁻¹.
Equates v²/r to g (or GM/r²).
Obtains v = 7.80 × 10³ m s⁻¹.
Applies T = 2πr / v or Kepler's third law.
Obtains T = 1.53 × 10⁴ s.

items.stem: Refer to the energy graph for a 1350 kg spacecraft at radius 3.3 × 10⁷ m about a planet (2.99 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 7.86 × 10⁶ m). Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻² and zero potential energy at infinity. Determine its total mechanical energy.
items.workedSolution: For a circular orbit, E_k = +GMm/(2r) and E_p = −GMm/r, so E_tot = E_k + E_p = −GMm/(2r) = −(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 2.99 × 10²⁴ × 1350) / (2 × 3.3 × 10⁷) = -4.08 × 10⁹ J.

markScheme.criterion: Applies E_tot = −GMm / (2r) with negative sign to obtain -4.08 × 10⁹ J.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 1/2 in E_tot = −GMm/(2r), quoting gravitational potential energy −GMm/r instead.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits the negative bound-state sign, reporting +GMm/(2r) instead of −GMm/(2r).

options.label: D

items.stem: A car of mass 1480 kg moves at a constant speed of 8.79 m s⁻¹ around a flat circular track of radius 65 m. Between the tyres and the surface, μ_s = 0.36, and g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) a_c = v² / r = (8.79)² / 65 = 1.19 m s⁻². (b) Below the slipping limit, f_s = m a_c = 1480 × 1.19 = 1.76 × 10³ N. (c) Maximum speed without slipping v_max = √(μ_s g r) = 15.2 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies a_c = v² / r.
Obtains 1.19 m s⁻².
Multiplies mass by centripetal acceleration (rather than using limiting μ_s mg).
Obtains 1.76 × 10³ N.
Equates m v_max² / r to μ_s mg.
Obtains 15.2 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A monochromatic 70.0 keV diagnostic X-ray beam passes through a 3.50 cm layer of tissue with iodine contrast medium. Take $Z = 53$ and $\mu = 0.420\text{ cm}^{-1}$ for the medium, and effective $Z = 7$ for unstained soft tissue.
items.workedSolution: (a) I/I₀ = 0.230. (b) (53/7)³ = 434. (c) In diagnostic X-ray imaging, photoelectric absorption dominates with attenuation proportional to atomic number cubed. This gives strong contrast between bone and soft tissue. (d) Above a threshold energy of 1.02 MeV, an X-ray photon near a nucleus converts into an electron-positron pair.

markScheme.criterion: Applies I/I₀ = exp(−μx) with consistent cm units.
Obtains transmitted fraction 0.230.
Raises ratio 53/7 to the third power.
Obtains ratio 434.
States photon is completely absorbed with μ ∝ Z³.
Links strong Z³ dependence to sharp contrast between bone or contrast media and soft tissue.
States pair production requires photon energy ≥ 2m_e c² = 1.02 MeV.
Notes that 70.0 keV is far below the 1.02 MeV threshold needed to produce an electron-positron pair.

parts.prompt: Derive and calculate the orbital radius r_GEO of a geostationary satellite measured from Earth's centre.
workingSteps: Equate gravitational force and centripetal force: GMm/r² = m(4π²r/T²)

parts.prompt: State the altitude of the geostationary orbit above Earth's surface.
Calculate the minimum change in total orbital energy needed to transfer the spacecraft from its circular low-Earth orbit to the geostationary orbit.
State all three orbital conditions required for the satellite to remain fixed above one location on Earth's surface.
parts.expectedAnswer: The satellite must have a twenty-four hour orbital period matching Earth rotation, directly above the equator, and orbiting west-to-east.
workingSteps: Required conditions: twenty-four hour orbital period matching Earth rotation, directly above the equator, and orbiting west-to-east.

items.stem: A space agency must choose orbits for two missions. Mission Alpha provides continuous television signals to fixed household dishes across Europe. Mission Beta monitors daily polar ice-sheet retreat worldwide.
items.workedSolution: Mission Alpha needs a geostationary orbit with a twenty-four hour period matching Earth's rotation, directly above the equator, moving west-to-east. This keeps the satellite stationary in the sky for fixed household dishes. Mission Beta needs a polar low-Earth orbit passing over both poles at low altitude (~200–1200 km). As Earth rotates beneath it, the satellite scans the whole surface with higher image resolution and lower signal delay. By Kepler's third law (T² ∝ r³) and v = √(GM/r), Mission Beta orbits much closer to Earth at higher speed. It has a much shorter period (~100 min) and needs less launch energy than Mission Alpha (~36 000 km altitude).

markScheme.criterion: L1a: Assigns geostationary orbit to Mission Alpha for fixed-dish continuity and polar LEO to Mission Beta for polar coverage.
L1b: Lists all three geostationary conditions: T = 24 h, directly above the equator, orbiting west-to-east.
L2a: Explains how polar LEO sweeps every part of Earth's surface (including poles) as Earth rotates underneath.
L2b: Compares altitudes and periods quantitatively/qualitatively (GEO ~36 000 km, 24 h vs LEO ~200–1200 km, ~90–110 min).
L3a: Compares orbital speeds using v = √(GM/r): polar LEO travels much faster than geostationary satellites.
L3b: Contrasts operational trade-offs: polar LEO gives higher image resolution, lower latency, and cheaper launch. However, it needs tracking dishes and gives intermittent passes.

parts.prompt: Recommend and justify the required orbit for each mission. State the exact conditions for Mission Alpha's orbit, and compare orbital radius, speed, energy, coverage, and signal properties between the two missions.
parts.expectedAnswer: polar low-Earth orbit sweeps the entire Earth surface as Earth rotates beneath giving higher image resolution and lower signal latency. Mission Alpha requires a geostationary orbit with a twenty-four hour period matching Earth's rotation, directly in the equatorial plane, moving west-to-east, so the satellite stays stationary in the sky for fixed household antennas. Mission Beta requires a polar low-Earth orbit: passing over both poles at low altitude (~200–1200 km), a polar low-Earth orbit sweeps the entire Earth surface as Earth rotates beneath giving higher image resolution and lower signal latency, ideal for polar ice-sheet monitoring. By Kepler's third law (T² ∝ r³) and v = √(GM/r), Mission Beta orbits much closer to Earth at significantly higher speed with a much shorter period (~100 min) and lower launch energy requirement than Mission Alpha (~36 000 km altitude).
workingSteps: Assign geostationary orbit to Mission Alpha with all three required conditions.
Assign polar LEO to Mission Beta explaining global/polar ground-track scanning.
Compare orbital radius, orbital speed, period, image resolution, and signal latency.

items.stem: For a steady horizontal orbit on a light 1.1 m string angled 42° from vertical, the ball has mass 1.2 kg. Calculate its speed using g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: Orbit radius r = L sin θ = 1.1 sin 42° = 0.736 m. Since T sin θ = mv²/r and T cos θ = mg, v = √(g r tan θ) = √(9.81 × 0.736 × tan 42°) = 2.55 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses r = L sin θ and v = √(g L sin θ tan θ) to obtain 2.55 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: What physical observation allows astronomers to detect an unseen exoplanet via the radial-velocity (wobble) method?
items.workedSolution: The radial-velocity method relies on detecting the periodic Doppler shift of stellar absorption lines caused by orbit around the common centre of mass.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that periodic Doppler shift of stellar absorption lines caused by orbit around the common centre of mass.

options.text: Direct photography of reflected starlight from the planet's surface at all orbital phases.
options.distractorRationale: Direct imaging is distinct from radial-velocity spectroscopy and suffers severe glare.

options.label: B
options.text: Periodic changes in the host star's absolute magnitude caused by nuclear fusion cycles.
options.distractorRationale: Radial-velocity detection tracks spectral wavelength shifts, not fusion-driven brightness changes.

options.label: C
options.text: Measuring the periodic Doppler shift of stellar absorption lines caused by orbit around the common centre of mass.

options.label: D
options.text: Permanent redshift of the star's spectrum caused by cosmic expansion alone.
options.distractorRationale: An orbiting planet creates a periodic oscillation between redshift and blueshift.

items.stem: Star X on the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram has luminosity $L = 400\,L_{\odot}$ and surface temperature $T = 3600\text{ K}$. Take $L_{\odot} = 3.83 \times 10^{26}\text{ W}$ and $R_{\odot} = 6.96 \times 10^8\text{ m}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $L = 400 \times 3.83 \times 10^{26} = 1.53 × 10²⁹ W$. (b) $R = \sqrt{\frac{1.53 × 10²⁹ W}{4\pi(5.67 \times 10^{-8})(3600)^4}} = 3.58 × 10¹⁰ m$. (c) $R / R_{\odot} = 51.4 R⊙$. (d) Star X lies in the red giant region (cool surface, high luminosity, and very large radius in the upper-right). Since $L \propto T^4$ for fixed $R$ and $T$ decreases rightward, constant-radius lines slope down toward the bottom-right.

markScheme.criterion: Correct luminosity 1.53 × 10²⁹ W.
Rearranges $L = 4\pi R^2 \sigma T^4$ for $R$.
Correct radius 3.58 × 10¹⁰ m.
Divides $R$ by $R_{\odot} = 6.96 \times 10^8\text{ m}$.
Correct ratio 51.4 R⊙.
Identifies red giant region with cool surface temperature high luminosity and very large stellar radius in the upper-right region.
Explains constant $R$ gives $L \propto T^4$, so luminosity drops as $T$ decreases to the right.

items.stem: A spectroscopic binary system is viewed in the plane of its circular orbit. For the brighter star, the $\text{H}\alpha$ line (rest wavelength $656.3\text{ nm}$) oscillates between $656.00\text{ nm}$ and $656.60\text{ nm}$ (maximum shift $0.300\text{ nm}$) with an orbital period of $8.00\text{ days}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) spectroscopic binary viewed in its orbital plane produces periodic alternating blue and red Doppler shifts. (b) $v = 3.00 \times 10^8 \times (0.300 / 656.3) = 137 km s⁻¹$. (c) $r = vT/(2\pi) = 1.51 × 10¹⁰ m$.

markScheme.criterion: Explains spectroscopic binary viewed in its orbital plane produces periodic alternating blue and red Doppler shifts.
Correctly links approach to blue-shift and recession to red-shift.
Substitutes into $\Delta\lambda / \lambda = v / c$.
Correct orbital speed 137 km s⁻¹.
Converts $8.00\text{ days}$ to seconds and applies $r = vT/(2\pi)$.
Correct orbital radius 1.51 × 10¹⁰ m.

Connect approaching motion to shorter wavelength and receding motion to longer wavelength.

items.stem: A rocket launches a scientific satellite from rest on the surface of a non-rotating airless planet into a circular orbit of radius $r$. Which statement accurately describes the minimum mechanical energy required?
items.workedSolution: ΔE = E_orbit − E_surface = (−GMm/(2r)) − (−GMm/R) = ΔE_p + E_k,orbit. Launching from rest on a non-rotating planet into circular orbit therefore requires supplying both the gain in gravitational potential energy and the orbital kinetic energy.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct explanation: launching from rest into circular orbit supplies both the gain in gravitational potential energy and the orbital kinetic energy.

options.label: A
options.text: Launching from rest on a non-rotating planet surface into circular orbit requires supplying both the gain in gravitational potential energy and the orbital kinetic energy.

options.label: B
options.text: The minimum energy equals only the increase in gravitational potential energy because orbital motion requires zero kinetic energy.
options.distractorRationale: A circular orbit requires kinetic energy E_k = +GMm/(2r) in addition to the potential energy gain.

options.label: C
options.text: The minimum energy equals the full escape energy GMm/R regardless of the target orbital radius.
options.distractorRationale: Escape energy brings total energy to zero at infinity; a bound orbit has negative total energy −GMm/(2r).

options.label: D
options.text: The minimum energy is zero because gravitational force does all the work needed to lift the satellite into orbit.
options.distractorRationale: Gravity acts radially inwards, so work must be done against gravity plus kinetic energy supplied for orbital speed.

items.stem: Attached to a light string, a small ball of mass 0.2 kg traces a vertical circle of radius 0.6 m. Passing the lowest point at 5.96 m s⁻¹, it faces no air resistance, with g = 9.8 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) By energy conservation, ½mv_bot² = ½mv_top² + mg(2R), v_top = √(v_bot² − 4gR) = 3.46 m s⁻¹. (b) Downward radial balance F_top + mg = mv_top²/R gives F_top = 2.04 N. (c) Setting F_top = 0 gives v_top = √(gR) and v_bot,min = √(5gR) = 5.42 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies energy conservation with vertical rise Δh = 2R.
Obtains v_top = 3.46 m s⁻¹.
Uses F_top = m(v_top²/R − g) at the apex.
Obtains F_top = 2.04 N.
Combines v_top,min² = gR with v_bot,min² = v_top,min² + 4gR.
Obtains v_bot,min = 5.42 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the speed of the ball as it passes the highest point of the circle.
workingSteps: Conservation of mechanical energy with Δh = 2R gives v_top² = v_bot² − 4gR.

parts.prompt: Determine the magnitude of the string tension acting on the ball at the highest point.
workingSteps: At the apex, F_top + mg = m v_top² / R.

workingSteps: At threshold contact, v_top = √(gR), so v_bot,min = √(gR + 4gR) = √(5gR).

items.stem: Recall that d / pc = 1 / (p / arcsec), because a 1 AU baseline giving 1 arcsecond defines 1 pc. Using 1 pc = 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m, astronomers track a 4.6 × 10²⁹ W star across Earth's 1 AU orbit with parallax 0.18 arcsec.
items.workedSolution: (a) Distance in parsecs is d = 1 / 0.18 = 5.56 pc. (b) In SI units, d = 1.71 × 10¹⁷ m. (c) Apparent brightness b = L / (4π d²) = 1.25 × 10⁻⁶ W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Applies d(pc) = 1 / p(arcsec).
Obtains 5.56 pc.
Multiplies distance in parsecs by 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m pc⁻¹.
Obtains 1.71 × 10¹⁷ m.
Applies inverse-square law b = L / (4π d²).
Obtains 1.25 × 10⁻⁶ W m⁻².

items.workedSolution: (a) 290 nm. (b) 580 nm. (c) higher temperature shifts peak to shorter wavelength and raises intensity at all wavelengths, and total radiated power per unit area grows by $16\times$.

Correct peak wavelength 580 nm.

items.stem: Moving steadily at 4.29 m s⁻¹, a 3.6 kg test mass circles the inside of a smooth vertical track (radius 1.11 m). Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Minimum top speed v_min = √(gR) = 3.30 m s⁻¹. (b) At the top, F_top = m(v²/R − g) = 24.4 N. (c) At the bottom, F_bot = m(v²/R + g) = 95.0 N.

markScheme.criterion: Sets support force to zero at apex so mg = m v_min² / R.
Obtains 3.30 m s⁻¹.
Subtracts mg from m v² / R at the top.
Obtains 24.4 N.
Adds mg to m v² / R at the bottom.
Obtains 95.0 N.

items.stem: Find the time for one complete revolution of a 1.2 kg sphere swinging steadily in a horizontal circle. Its light string is 1.65 m long and stays at 24° to the vertical. Use g = 9.8 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: By vertical and radial balance, T cos θ = mg and T sin θ = m ω² (L sin θ), ω = √(g / (L cos θ)). Thus the period is P = 2π√(L cos θ / g) = 2π√((1.65 cos 24°) / 9.8) = 2.46 s.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates 2π√(L cos 24° / g) to obtain 2.46 s.

items.stem: To reach outer orbit r₂ = 2.52 × 10⁷ m from inner orbit r₁ = 1.26 × 10⁷ m on a Hohmann ellipse, how long does a 463 kg satellite travel? Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², planet mass 1.1 × 10²⁵ kg, and radius 5.72 × 10⁶ m.
items.workedSolution: For the transfer ellipse, semi-major axis a = ½(r₁ + r₂) = 1.89 × 10⁷ m. Moving from the inner orbit to the outer orbit takes half an orbital period: t_H = π√(a³ / GM) = 9.53 × 10³ s.

markScheme.criterion: Uses a = ½(r₁ + r₂) and t_H = π√(a³ / GM) to obtain 9.53 × 10³ s.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Takes half the outer circular period using r₂ instead of the transfer ellipse semi-major axis (r₁ + r₂)/2.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the full elliptical period 2π√(a³ / GM) instead of the half-orbit Hohmann coast time π√(a³ / GM).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses major axis (r₁ + r₂) instead of semi-major axis a = (r₁ + r₂)/2 in Kepler's third law.

items.stem: Take gravitational field strength g = 9.81 m s⁻². Moving steadily at 5.56 m s⁻¹, a 0.75 kg mass traces a vertical circle (radius 1.4 m) on a light string.
items.workedSolution: (a) Minimum top speed v_min = √(gR) = 3.71 m s⁻¹. (b) At the top, F_top = m(v²/R − g) = 9.20 N. (c) At the bottom, F_bot = m(v²/R + g) = 23.9 N.

markScheme.criterion: Sets support force to zero at apex so mg = m v_min² / R.
Obtains 3.71 m s⁻¹.
Subtracts mg from m v² / R at the top.
Obtains 9.20 N.
Adds mg to m v² / R at the bottom.
Obtains 23.9 N.

items.stem: Suppose a 45 kg trolley sweeps into the base of a smooth vertical loop of radius 2.5 m at 15.9 m s⁻¹. Neglect drag and friction, with g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Energy conservation gives ½mv_bot² = ½mv_top² + mg(2R), v_top = √(v_bot² − 4gR) = 12.4 m s⁻¹. (b) Downward radial balance F_top + mg = mv_top²/R gives F_top = 2.34 × 10³ N. (c) Setting F_top = 0 gives v_top = √(gR) and v_bot,min = √(5gR) = 11.1 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies energy conservation with vertical rise Δh = 2R.
Obtains v_top = 12.4 m s⁻¹.
Uses F_top = m(v_top²/R − g) at the apex.
Obtains F_top = 2.34 × 10³ N.
Combines v_top,min² = gR with v_bot,min² = v_top,min² + 4gR.
Obtains v_bot,min = 11.1 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Two airless spherical bodies stand 5.89 × 10⁸ m apart (centre to centre), namely Major Moon (mass 4.42 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 7.33 × 10⁶ m) and Minor Moon (mass 1.77 × 10²³ kg, radius 1.57 × 10⁶ m). Set zero potential at infinity (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²). What is the net potential at the null point?
items.workedSolution: At the zero-field point x₀ = d√M₁/(√M₁ + √M₂) = 4.91 × 10⁸ m, scalar potentials add negatively: V_g(x₀) = −GM₁/x₀ − GM₂/(d − x₀) = −(G/d)(√M₁ + √M₂)² = -7.21 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Sums both negative scalar potentials at x₀ to obtain -7.21 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹.

items.stem: A spherical planet of uniform density has mass 2.69 × 10²⁵ kg and radius 4.92 × 10⁶ m. A small probe of mass 123 kg is lowered into a narrow shaft inside the planet to r = 3.2 × 10⁶ m from the centre, with G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Surface field g₀ = GM/R² = 74.1 N kg⁻¹. (b) At r = 3.2 × 10⁶ m, uniform-sphere interior scaling g = g₀(r/R) gives 48.2 N kg⁻¹. (c) Force on probe F = mg = 5.93 × 10³ N.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes M and R into g₀ = GM / R².
Obtains g₀ = 74.1 N kg⁻¹.
Applies linear interior field law g(r) = GMr/R³.
Obtains g = 48.2 N kg⁻¹.
Multiplies probe mass by field strength at r.
Obtains F = 5.93 × 10³ N.

workingSteps: For a uniform sphere with r < R, g(r) = g₀ (r / R) = G M r / R³.

parts.prompt: Calculate the magnitude of the gravitational force on the 123 kg probe at this position.

items.stem: Without spin or atmosphere, a 6.95 × 10²⁴ kg spherical planet (radius 8.76 × 10⁶ m) has a 952 kg probe located 3.94 × 10⁷ m from its centre. Take zero potential at infinity (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²).
items.workedSolution: (a) Radial potential at R gives V_surface = −GM/R = -5.29 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹. (b) Escape speed v_esc = √(−2 V_surface) = √(2GM/R) = 1.03 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹. (c) At r = 3.94 × 10⁷ m, E_p = −GMm/r = -1.12 × 10¹⁰ J.

markScheme.criterion: Applies V_g = −GM / R with negative sign.
Obtains -5.29 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹.
Uses v_esc = √(2GM / R) or √(−2 V_surface).
Obtains 1.03 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.
Applies E_p = −GMm / r at probe radius.
Obtains -1.12 × 10¹⁰ J.

items.stem: Two bodies, Major Moon (mass 5.07 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 6.37 × 10⁶ m) and Minor Moon (mass 3.17 × 10²³ kg, radius 1.74 × 10⁶ m), have centres 3.46 × 10⁸ m apart. How far from the centre of Major Moon is the net gravitational field zero?
items.workedSolution: Setting the two opposing field strengths equal: G M₁ / x₀² = G M₂ / (d − x₀)² gives (d − x₀)/x₀ = √(M₂/M₁), so x₀ = [√M₁ / (√M₁ + √M₂)] d = 2.77 × 10⁸ m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses x₀ = d √M₁ / (√M₁ + √M₂) to obtain 2.77 × 10⁸ m.

items.stem: Banked at 28° with no sideways friction, a smooth road curves with radius 145 m. A 640 kg car follows a horizontal circle around it. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² to calculate the normal contact force.
items.workedSolution: Since vertical acceleration is zero, N cos θ = mg, so N = (640 × 9.81) / cos 28° = 7.11 × 10³ N.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves vertically N cos 28° = mg to obtain N = 7.11 × 10³ N.

items.stem: Astronomers observe an oxygen emission line in the spectrum of a distant galaxy. Its wavelength shifts from rest wavelength λ₀ = 500.7 nm to λ_obs = 510.06 nm, with c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and H₀ = 66 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) z = (λ_obs − λ₀)/λ₀ = 0.0187. (b) Recession speed v ≈ zc = 5.61 × 10³ km s⁻¹. (c) Hubble distance d = v/H₀ = 85.0 Mpc.

markScheme.criterion: Applies z = Δλ / λ₀.
Obtains z = 0.0187.
Multiplies z by c and converts to km s⁻¹.
Obtains v = 5.61 × 10³ km s⁻¹.
Applies d = v / H₀.
Obtains d = 85.0 Mpc.

items.stem: Two Type Ia supernovae, SN-Alpha and SN-Beta, are recorded with peak apparent magnitudes of 13.2 and 15.7 respectively. Take the peak absolute magnitude of a Type Ia supernova to be -19.3.
items.workedSolution: (a) $d = 31.6 Mpc$. (b) $I_1/I_2 = 2.51^{2.5} = 9.98$. (c) consistent peak absolute magnitude because white dwarfs explode at the same Chandrasekhar mass limit.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates $d = 10 \times 10^{6.50}$ pc correctly.
Correct distance 31.6 Mpc.
Correct intensity ratio 9.98.
Explains white dwarf accretion reaches the fixed Chandrasekhar mass limit.
Links fixed critical mass to consistent peak absolute magnitude.

parts.prompt: Calculate the distance to SN-Alpha in megaparsecs.
Calculate how many times greater the peak intensity received on Earth is from SN-Alpha than from SN-Beta.
Explain why Type Ia supernovae have a predictable peak absolute magnitude.
parts.expectedAnswer: They produce a consistent peak absolute magnitude because white dwarfs explode at the same Chandrasekhar mass limit.
workingSteps: A white dwarf accretes mass from a binary companion until reaching the Chandrasekhar limit.
Because the exploding mass is fixed, the peak energy output and absolute magnitude are nearly identical.

items.stem: A satellite of mass 1180 kg orbits a spherical planet in a circular path at an altitude of 1.4 × 10⁷ m above the surface. The planet has mass 1.78 × 10²⁵ kg and radius 5.4 × 10⁶ m. Taking G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², calculate the circular orbital speed of the satellite.
items.workedSolution: Orbital radius from planet centre r = R_p + h = 5.4 × 10⁶ + 1.4 × 10⁷ = 1.94 × 10⁷ m. Equating GMm / r² = mv² / r gives v = √(GM / r) = √(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 1.78 × 10²⁵ / 1.94 × 10⁷) = 7.82 × 10³ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses r = 1.94 × 10⁷ m to obtain 7.82 × 10³ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Consider a 2.15 × 10²⁵ kg spherical planet of radius 5.33 × 10⁶ m. A 931 kg satellite moves around it in a circular orbit (radius 2.24 × 10⁷ m). Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², with potential energy zero at infinity.
items.workedSolution: (a) Orbital kinetic energy: E_k = GMm/(2r) = 2.98 × 10¹⁰ J. (b) E_p = −GMm/r = -5.96 × 10¹⁰ J. (c) Total mechanical energy E_tot = E_k + E_p = −GMm/(2r) = -2.98 × 10¹⁰ J.

markScheme.criterion: Applies E_k = GMm / (2r).
Obtains E_k = 2.98 × 10¹⁰ J.
Applies E_p = −GMm / r including negative sign.
Obtains E_p = -5.96 × 10¹⁰ J.
Sums E_k + E_p or applies E_tot = −GMm / (2r).
Obtains E_tot = -2.98 × 10¹⁰ J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the kinetic energy of the satellite in this circular orbit.
workingSteps: From m v² / r = G M m / r², E_k = ½ m v² = G M m / (2r).

parts.prompt: Calculate the gravitational potential energy of the satellite.
Determine the total mechanical energy of the satellite.
workingSteps: E_tot = E_k + E_p = −G M m / (2r) = -2.98 × 10¹⁰ J.

items.stem: A Hertzsprung–Russell diagram shows four stars with region names removed, including Star Eta at surface temperature 18500 K and luminosity 0.008 L☉. Use solar values L☉ = 3.83 × 10²⁶ W, R☉ = 6.96 × 10⁸ m, and σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.
items.workedSolution: (a) Star Eta lies in the white-dwarf region. (b) L = 0.008 × 3.83 × 10²⁶ = 3.06 × 10²⁴ W. (c) R = √[L/(4πσT⁴)] = 6.06 × 10⁶ m = 0.00871 R☉.

markScheme.criterion: States white-dwarf.
Multiplies L / L☉ by 3.83 × 10²⁶ W.
Obtains L = 3.06 × 10²⁴ W.
Applies R = √[L / (4π σ T⁴)] and divides by R☉.
Obtains 0.00871 R☉.

items.stem: A car of mass 760 kg travels at a constant speed of 13.5 m s⁻¹ around a flat circular track of radius 90 m. Taking g = 9.81 m s⁻², calculate the minimum coefficient of static friction needed so the car does not slip.
items.workedSolution: Cornering without slipping requires μ_s m g ≥ m v² / r, so μ_min = v² / (g r) = (13.5)² / (9.81 × 90) = 0.206.

markScheme.criterion: Computes μ_min = v² / (g r) = 0.206.

items.stem: A 1000 kg satellite in circular low-Earth orbit at altitude 500 km is transferred to a circular geostationary orbit (T = 86400 s, R_E = 6.37 × 10⁶ m, M_E = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg, G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²). Calculate the minimum energy required to change its total orbital energy.
items.workedSolution: Total circular orbital energy E = −GMm / (2r). ΔE = (GMm / 2)(1/r_LEO − 1/r_GEO) = 2.43 × 10¹⁰ J.

markScheme.criterion: Uses ΔE = (GMm/2)(1/r₁ − 1/r₂) to find 2.43 × 10¹⁰ J.

items.stem: A car of mass 1150 kg travels at a constant speed of 11.7 m s⁻¹ around a flat circular track of radius 28 m. Taking g = 9.8 m s⁻², calculate the minimum coefficient of static friction needed so the car does not slip.
items.workedSolution: Cornering without slipping requires μ_s m g ≥ m v² / r, so μ_min = v² / (g r) = (11.7)² / (9.8 × 28) = 0.499.

markScheme.criterion: Computes μ_min = v² / (g r) = 0.499.

items.stem: At diagnostic X-ray photon energies (~50 keV), photoelectric attenuation scales approximately as $Z^3$. Comparing barium contrast medium ($Z = 56$) with surrounding soft tissue (effective $Z = 7$), estimate the ratio of photoelectric absorption probability per atom $(Z_{\text{Ba}} / Z_{\text{tissue}})^3$.
items.workedSolution: (Z_Ba / Z_tissue)³ = (56 / 7)³ = 8³ = 512.

markScheme.criterion: Applies cubic scaling (56/7)³ = 512.

items.stem: Astrophysics bridges precision orbital mechanics inside the Solar System with large-scale models of the entire universe.
items.workedSolution: Kepler's elliptical equal-area orbits conserve r v between perihelion and aphelion. The Cosmological Principle states that the universe is homogeneous and isotropic on large scales. Kepler's first law states planets move in elliptical orbits with the Sun at one focus. Kepler's second law states that the radius vector from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times. Because gravity acts radially (zero torque about the Sun), angular momentum L = mrv is conserved at apsides, giving r₁v₁ = r₂v₂. Gravitational potential energy converts to kinetic energy as the planet nears perihelion (fastest) and back at aphelion (slowest). The Cosmological Principle states that on large scales (> 100 Mpc) the universe is homogeneous (uniform average density) and isotropic (same in all directions). The same physical laws apply everywhere, while locally planets, stars, and galaxies are clumped and non-uniform.

markScheme.criterion: L1: States Kepler's 1st law: planets follow elliptical orbits with the Sun at one focus.
L1: States Kepler's 2nd law: line joining planet and Sun sweeps equal areas in equal times.
L2: Explains radial gravitational force conserves angular momentum (r₁v₁ = r₂v₂) so speed is maximum at perihelion and minimum at aphelion.
L2: Explains GPE decreases and KE increases as the planet approaches perihelion (constant total orbital energy).
L3: Defines Cosmological Principle: universe is homogeneous (uniform average density) and isotropic (looks the same in all directions) with universal laws.
L3: Explains why the principle holds only on vast intergalactic scales rather than locally where stars/galaxies clump.

parts.prompt: State Kepler's first and second laws of planetary motion, and use energy and angular momentum (including r₁v₁ = r₂v₂) to explain why a planet's speed varies. Define the Cosmological Principle and explain why it applies only on very large scales. [6 marks]
parts.expectedAnswer: Kepler elliptical equal-area orbits conserve r v between perihelion and aphelion while the Cosmological Principle asserts a large-scale homogeneous and isotropic universe. Kepler's first law states planets move in elliptical orbits with the Sun at one focus; Kepler's second law states the radius vector from Sun to planet sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time. Because gravitational force acts purely radially (zero torque about the Sun), angular momentum L = mrv is conserved at apsides giving r₁v₁ = r₂v₂, while total mechanical energy converts from gravitational potential to kinetic energy as the planet falls towards perihelion (fastest) and back at aphelion (slowest). The Cosmological Principle asserts that on large cosmological scales (> 100 Mpc) the universe is homogeneous (uniform average density everywhere) and isotropic (same in all directions) with universal laws of physics; locally, planets, stars, and galaxies are visibly clumped and non-uniform.
workingSteps: State Kepler's 1st law (ellipses with Sun at one focus) and 2nd law (equal areas in equal times).
Connect speed variation to radial gravity (r₁v₁ = r₂v₂) and GPE ↔ KE exchange between perihelion and aphelion.
Define homogeneity, isotropy, and universal physical laws, noting the large-scale averaging requirement.

items.stem: The diagram contrasts a high-altitude geostationary equatorial orbit with a low-Earth polar orbit around the rotating Earth.
items.workedSolution: A geostationary satellite must have a twenty-four hour orbital period matching Earth's rotation. It must also orbit directly above the equator, moving west-to-east. Its circular orbit must lie in the equatorial plane because gravity always acts toward Earth's centre. Any inclined orbit crosses the equator twice per orbit and cannot stay fixed above one surface point. Geostationary satellites orbit at a fixed high altitude (~3.6 × 10⁷ m), giving continuous 24-hour links to fixed ground dishes. However, signals suffer greater delay and weakening and miss the polar caps. By contrast, polar low-Earth satellites orbit much lower (hundreds of km) at higher speed with ~90–100 min periods. As Earth rotates beneath them, they scan the entire surface for weather forecasting, Earth observation, and high-resolution imaging with lower delay.

L1b: States orbit must lie directly above the equator AND move west-to-east (same sense as Earth's rotation).
L2a: Explains that gravity acts toward Earth's centre, so the orbital plane must pass through Earth's centre. It cannot stay fixed above non-zero latitude.
L2b: States a geostationary use (continuous TV or communications with fixed dishes). Notes that high altitude (~36 000 km) causes longer signal delay.
L3a: Explains that a polar LEO orbits at low altitude with high speed and a short ~90–105 min period. It scans the entire surface as Earth rotates beneath it.
L3b: Links polar LEO to weather monitoring, environmental mapping, or Earth observation. Notes higher image resolution and lower signal latency.

Its circular orbit must lie in the equatorial plane because gravity acts toward Earth's centre, so any inclined orbit crosses the equator twice per orbit and cannot stay fixed above one point. Geostationary satellites orbit at a fixed high altitude (~3.6 × 10⁷ m), allowing continuous 24-hour broadcast links with fixed ground dishes, though signals suffer greater delay and miss the polar caps. By contrast, polar low-Earth satellites orbit much lower (hundreds of km) at higher speed with ~90–100 min periods; as Earth rotates beneath them, they scan the entire surface for weather forecasting, Earth observation, and high-resolution imaging with lower latency.

items.stem: Hanging from a fixed point by a light 2.75 m string, a 0.6 kg ball circles horizontally at constant speed with angle 42° to the vertical (g = 9.81 m s⁻²).
items.workedSolution: (a) From zero vertical acceleration, T cos 42° = (0.6)(9.81) gives T = 7.92 N. (b) Horizontal radius r = 2.75 sin 42° = 1.84 m; horizontal dynamics T sin θ = mv²/r yields v = 4.03 m s⁻¹. (c) Period P = 2πr / v = 2.87 s.

markScheme.criterion: Equates vertical component T cos θ to weight mg.
Obtains tension 7.92 N.
Uses r = L sin θ and equates T sin θ (or mg tan θ) to m v² / r.
Obtains speed 4.03 m s⁻¹.
Applies P = 2π r / v or P = 2π√(L cos θ / g).
Obtains period 2.87 s.

items.stem: Earth orbits the Sun at mean radius $1.00\text{ AU}$ with period $1.00\text{ yr}$, while Jupiter orbits at mean radius $5.20\text{ AU}$. In the same solar system, a comet follows an ellipse of eccentricity $e = 0.400$ with $r_{\text{a}}/r_{\text{p}} = (1 + e)/(1 - e)$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $T_{\text{J}} = 11.9 yr$. (b) The line joining a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times. Therefore orbital speed is greatest at perihelion and smallest at aphelion. (c) $v_{\text{p}}/v_{\text{a}} = 2.33$.

markScheme.criterion: Applies T² ∝ r³ ⇒ T₂ = T₁(r₂/r₁)^(3/2).
Obtains orbital period 11.9 yr.
States equal areas are swept in equal time intervals.
Concludes greatest speed at perihelion: equal areas in equal times mean the comet moves fastest at perihelion and slowest at aphelion.
Applies r_p v_p = r_a v_a = (1+e)/(1−e).
Obtains speed ratio 2.33.

parts.expectedAnswer: Kepler's second law states that the line joining a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times so orbital speed is greatest at perihelion and smallest at aphelion.

items.stem: A light string holds a 370 kg object in a vertical circle of radius 2.57 m. At the bottom its speed is 15.1 m s⁻¹, with no air drag. Work out its speed at the peak (g = 9.8 m s⁻²).
items.workedSolution: Rising from bottom to top increases height by Δh = 2R. By conservation of energy, ½m v_top² + mg(2R) = ½m v_bot², so v_top = √(v_bot² − 4gR) = √((15.1)² − 4 × 9.8 × 2.57) = 11.3 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses Δh = 2R in v_top = √(v_bot² − 4gR) to obtain 11.3 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Lying 1.56 × 10¹⁶ m from Earth, a spherical black-body star has radius 1.55 × 10¹⁰ m and temperature 18400 K. With b = 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K, what is its peak wavelength in nm?
items.workedSolution: Applying Wien's displacement law gives λ_max = b / T = 2.90 × 10⁻³ / 18400 = 1.58 × 10⁻⁷ m = 158 nm.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates λ_max = 2.90 × 10⁻³ / 18400 = 158 nm.

items.stem: Two black-body radiation curves are plotted on the same intensity-against-wavelength axes for a hotter star and a cooler star. How does the curve of the hotter star differ?
items.workedSolution: By Wien's and Stefan's laws, higher temperature shifts peak to shorter wavelength and raises intensity at all wavelengths, with total area proportional to $T^4$.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that higher temperature shifts peak to shorter wavelength and raises intensity at all wavelengths.

options.label: A
options.text: Higher temperature shifts the peak to longer red wavelengths while keeping the total area under the curve constant.
options.distractorRationale: Wien's law gives $\lambda_{\max} \propto 1/T$ (shorter wavelength) and area scales as $T^4$.

options.label: B
options.text: The hotter curve peaks at shorter wavelength but crosses below the cooler curve in the infrared.
options.distractorRationale: A hotter black body radiates greater intensity at EVERY wavelength; black-body curves never cross.

options.label: C
options.text: A higher temperature shifts peak to shorter wavelength and raises intensity at all wavelengths so the hotter curve lies strictly above the cooler curve everywhere.

options.label: D
options.text: Both curves peak at the same visible wavelength, with only the peak height changing.
options.distractorRationale: The peak wavelength shifts inversely with absolute temperature.

items.stem: Where g = 9.8 m s⁻², calculate the top normal contact force on a small ball of mass 0.9 kg running at steady speed 5.19 m s⁻¹ inside a smooth vertical loop (radius 1.1 m).
items.workedSolution: At the top of the circle, both normal contact force and weight mg act downward toward the centre: F_top + mg = m v² / R, so F_top = m(v²/R − g) = 0.9 × ((5.19)² / 1.1 − 9.8) = 13.2 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies radial force equation at apex to obtain 13.2 N.

items.stem: A conical pendulum uses a 1.2 kg ball on a light 0.95 m cord. During steady horizontal circular motion, the angle to the vertical is 24° (g = 9.8 m s⁻²).
items.workedSolution: (a) Resolving vertically, T cos 24° = (1.2)(9.8) gives T = 12.9 N. (b) Horizontal radius r = 0.95 sin 24° = 0.386 m; horizontal dynamics T sin θ = mv²/r yields v = 1.30 m s⁻¹. (c) Period P = 2πr / v = 1.87 s.

markScheme.criterion: Equates vertical component T cos θ to weight mg.
Obtains tension 12.9 N.
Uses r = L sin θ and equates T sin θ (or mg tan θ) to m v² / r.
Obtains speed 1.30 m s⁻¹.
Applies P = 2π r / v or P = 2π√(L cos θ / g).
Obtains period 1.87 s.

parts.prompt: Calculate the tension in the cord supporting the ball.
workingSteps: Vertical force balance gives T cos θ = mg.

parts.prompt: Determine the linear speed of the ball along its horizontal circular path.
workingSteps: Horizontal radius r = L sin θ = 0.95 sin 24° = 0.386 m.
From T sin θ = m v² / r, v = √(g r tan θ) = 1.30 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the time period for one complete revolution of the ball.

items.stem: Two circular orbits around a 1.91 × 10²⁵ kg planet (radius 8.52 × 10⁶ m) have radii r₁ = 1.19 × 10⁷ m and r₂ = 4.28 × 10⁷ m. A 1200 kg spacecraft transfers between them. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) At the inner orbit, E_tot(r₁) = −GMm/(2r₁) = -6.42 × 10¹⁰ J. (b) Final bound energy E_tot(r₂) = -1.79 × 10¹⁰ J, so ΔE_tot = 4.64 × 10¹⁰ J. (c) Outer orbital period T₂ = 2π√(r₂³/GM) = 4.93 × 10⁴ s.

markScheme.criterion: Applies E_tot = −GMm / (2r₁).
Obtains -6.42 × 10¹⁰ J.
Evaluates E_tot(r₂) − E_tot(r₁) = ½GMm(1/r₁ − 1/r₂).
Obtains 4.64 × 10¹⁰ J.
Applies Kepler's third law at outer radius r₂.
Obtains 4.93 × 10⁴ s.

items.stem: What minimum speed at the highest point keeps a light 0.65 m string taut for a 0.75 kg ball circling vertically at 3.69 m s⁻¹? Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: At the top limit, tension = 0 so weight alone provides centripetal force: mg = m v_min² / R => v_min = √(g R) = √(9.81 × 0.65) = 2.53 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Sets top support force to zero to obtain v_min = √(gR) = 2.53 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Entering the base of a smooth vertical loop (radius 1.6 m) at 10.3 m s⁻¹, a small 0.5 kg ball climbs to the highest point. Neglect friction and drag. Using g = 9.81 m s⁻², work out the normal contact force at the top.
items.workedSolution: At the highest point, v_top² = v_bot² − 4gR = (10.3)² − 4(9.81)(1.6) = 43.3 m² s⁻². Radial force balance F_top + mg = m v_top² / R gives F_top = 0.5(43.3 / 1.6 − 9.81) = 8.63 N.

markScheme.criterion: Combines v_top² = v_bot² − 4gR with F_top = m(v_top²/R − g) to obtain 8.63 N.

items.stem: In the diagram, Body Beta (mass 1.38 × 10²³ kg, radius 1.83 × 10⁶ m) stands 4.17 × 10⁸ m centre-to-centre from Body Alpha (mass 8.84 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 7.33 × 10⁶ m). Both spheres have no atmosphere. Take zero potential at infinity (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²).
items.workedSolution: (a) Balance of fields gives x₀ = d√M₁/(√M₁ + √M₂) = 3.71 × 10⁸ m. (b) Combined scalar potential V(x₀) = -1.79 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. (c) Potential barrier from x = R₁ to x₀ is ΔV = 7.87 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹, giving v_min = √(2ΔV) = 1.25 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies x₀ = d√M₁ / (√M₁ + √M₂).
Obtains x₀ = 3.71 × 10⁸ m.
Sums both negative scalar potentials −GM₁/x₀ − GM₂/(d − x₀).
Obtains V(x₀) = -1.79 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹.
Equates ½v_min² to potential barrier V(x₀) − V(R₁).
Obtains v_min = 1.25 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

workingSteps: Equating field magnitudes gives x₀ = [√M₁ / (√M₁ + √M₂)] d = 3.71 × 10⁸ m.

parts.prompt: Calculate the total gravitational potential at this null point.
workingSteps: V(x₀) = −G M₁ / x₀ − G M₂ / (d − x₀) = -1.79 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹.

parts.prompt: A spacecraft is launched from the surface of Body Alpha directly toward Body Beta. Determine the minimum launch speed needed for it to reach Body Beta.
workingSteps: ΔV = V(x₀) − V(R₁) = 7.87 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹; v_min = √(2ΔV) = 1.25 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A spherical planet of uniform density has mass 3.38 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 5.9 × 10⁶ m. A probe of mass 370 kg is lowered into a narrow shaft inside the planet to a distance of 2.36 × 10⁶ m from the centre. Taking G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², calculate the gravitational field strength at this point.
items.workedSolution: Inside a uniform sphere (r < R), enclosed mass M_enc = M(r/R)³, so g(r) = G M r / R³ = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 3.38 × 10²⁴ × 2.36 × 10⁶) / (5.9 × 10⁶)³ = 2.59 N kg⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates gravitational field strength at r = 2.36 × 10⁶ m to obtain 2.59 N kg⁻¹.

items.stem: Measured from the centre of an 8.95 × 10²⁴ kg planet (radius 4.46 × 10⁶ m), a 460 kg spacecraft is at 1.16 × 10⁷ m. Take potential as zero at infinity (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²). What is the gravitational potential V_g at the spacecraft?

items.stem: For the two-body pair shown (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²), Primary Asteroid has mass 6.32 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 6.37 × 10⁶ m, and Secondary Moonlet has mass 7.02 × 10²³ kg and radius 1.74 × 10⁶ m. Their centres sit 4.26 × 10⁸ m apart, and a 1690 kg spacecraft moving between them passes 1.49 × 10⁸ m from Primary Asteroid's centre.
items.workedSolution: (a) Setting GM₁/x₀² = GM₂/(d − x₀)² yields x₀ = d√M₁/(√M₁ + √M₂) = 3.20 × 10⁸ m. (b) At x = 1.49 × 10⁸ m, |g| = |GM₁/x² − GM₂/(d − x)²| = 0.0184 N kg⁻¹. (c) Net force F = m|g| = 31.1 N.

markScheme.criterion: Equates opposing inverse-square field strengths GM₁/x₀² = GM₂/(d − x₀)².
Takes square root correctly to form x₀ = d√M₁ / (√M₁ + √M₂).
Obtains x₀ = 3.20 × 10⁸ m.
Subtracts opposing field magnitudes at x and (d − x).
Obtains |g| = 0.0184 N kg⁻¹.
Multiplies by spacecraft mass to obtain 31.1 N.

items.stem: Rounding a frictionless road of radius 58 m banked at 28°, a 1750 kg car stays in a horizontal circle. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Zero vertical acceleration gives N cos 28° = mg gives N = 1.94 × 10⁴ N. (b) Horizontal component F_c = N sin 28° = 9.13 × 10³ N. (c) Setting m v² / r = F_c yields v_ideal = 17.4 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses N cos θ = mg (zero vertical acceleration).
Obtains N = 1.94 × 10⁴ N.
Evaluates F_c = N sin θ or mg tan θ.
Obtains F_c = 9.13 × 10³ N.
Equates m v² / r to F_c and solves for v.
Obtains v_ideal = 17.4 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the magnitude of the normal contact force on the car.
workingSteps: Vertical equilibrium gives N cos θ = mg.

parts.prompt: Determine the horizontal centripetal force acting toward the centre of the circle.
workingSteps: Horizontal component of normal reaction provides the centripetal force: F_c = N sin θ = mg tan θ.

parts.prompt: Hence calculate the ideal frictionless speed of the car.
workingSteps: From m v² / r = F_c, v = √(F_c r / m) = √(g r tan θ) = 17.4 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: In the spectrum of a distant galaxy, a calcium absorption line (rest wavelength 396.8 nm) is observed at 404.22 nm. Taking c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and H₀ = 69.5 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹, calculate the distance to the galaxy in Mpc.
items.workedSolution: Redshift z = (λ_obs − λ₀) / λ₀ = (404.22 − 396.8) / 396.8 = 0.0187. Recession speed v ≈ z c = 5.61 × 10³ km s⁻¹. From Hubble's law v = H₀ d, d = v / H₀ = 5.61 × 10³ / 69.5 = 80.7 Mpc.

markScheme.criterion: Finds z = 0.0187, v = 5.61 × 10³ km s⁻¹, and d = v / H₀ = 80.7 Mpc.

items.stem: Why are Type Ia supernovae especially valuable as extragalactic standard candles for measuring cosmological distances?
items.workedSolution: Type Ia supernovae are reliable standard candles because they have a consistent peak absolute magnitude. This happens because white dwarfs explode at the same Chandrasekhar mass limit.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that consistent peak absolute magnitude because white dwarfs explode at the same Chandrasekhar mass limit.

options.text: They occur only in nearby galaxies where trigonometric parallax is straightforward.
options.distractorRationale: Type Ia supernovae are extraordinarily luminous and used far beyond parallax limits.

options.label: B
options.text: They reach a consistent peak absolute magnitude because white dwarfs explode at the same Chandrasekhar mass limit.

options.label: C
options.text: Their peak apparent magnitude is identical regardless of how far away the galaxy lies.
options.distractorRationale: Peak absolute magnitude M is consistent, whereas apparent magnitude m increases with distance.

options.label: D
options.text: They result from core collapse of red supergiants whose masses vary widely.
options.distractorRationale: Core collapse of massive stars produces Type II supernovae with variable luminosities, not Type Ia.

items.stem: A satellite of mass 233 kg orbits a spherical planet in a circular path at altitude h = 1.89 × 10⁶ m above the surface. The planet has mass 5.36 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 5.4 × 10⁶ m, with G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) With orbital radius r = 7.29 × 10⁶ m, g = GM/r² = 6.73 N kg⁻¹. (b) Orbital speed v = √(GM/r) = 7.00 × 10³ m s⁻¹. (c) Period T = 2πr/v = 6.54 × 10³ s.

markScheme.criterion: Uses centre-to-centre orbital radius r in g = GM / r².
Obtains g = 6.73 N kg⁻¹.
Equates v²/r to g (or GM/r²).
Obtains v = 7.00 × 10³ m s⁻¹.
Applies T = 2πr / v or Kepler's third law.
Obtains T = 6.54 × 10³ s.

Determine the circular orbital speed of the satellite.
workingSteps: Setting centripetal acceleration v² / r = g gives v = √(g r) = √(G M / r).

parts.prompt: Calculate the orbital period of the satellite.

items.stem: What kinetic energy does a 1130 kg satellite have in a circular orbit of radius 4.11 × 10⁷ m? Its planet has mass 2.09 × 10²⁵ kg and radius 9.78 × 10⁶ m, and G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: Equating centripetal and gravity forces (m v² / r = G M m / r²) gives E_k = ½ m v² = G M m / (2r) = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 2.09 × 10²⁵ × 1130) / (2 × 4.11 × 10⁷) = 1.92 × 10¹⁰ J.

markScheme.criterion: Computes E_k = GMm / (2r) = 1.92 × 10¹⁰ J.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Assigns a negative sign to kinetic energy by confusing E_k with total orbital energy E_tot.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses surface altitude (r − R_p) instead of orbital radius r.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 1/2 in E_k = ½mv² = GMm/(2r), computing GMm/r instead.

items.stem: On a Hertzsprung–Russell diagram, Star Alpha has surface temperature 3800 K and luminosity 180 L☉. Taking L☉ = 3.83 × 10²⁶ W, R☉ = 6.96 × 10⁸ m, and σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴, calculate the radius of the star as a multiple of R☉.
items.workedSolution: Luminosity L = 180 × 3.83 × 10²⁶ = 6.89 × 10²⁸ W. From L = 4π R² σ T⁴, R = √[L / (4π σ T⁴)] = 2.15 × 10¹⁰ m, so R / R☉ = R / (6.96 × 10⁸) = 31.0 R☉.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Stefan-Boltzmann scaling to obtain 31.0 R☉.

items.stem: A car of mass 1150 kg moves at a constant speed of 24.7 m s⁻¹ around a flat circular track of radius 105 m. The coefficient of static friction between the tyres and the track is 0.88, and g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) a_c = v² / r = (24.7)² / 105 = 5.81 m s⁻². (b) Below the slipping limit, f_s = m a_c = 1150 × 5.81 = 6.68 × 10³ N. (c) Maximum speed without slipping v_max = √(μ_s g r) = 30.1 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies a_c = v² / r.
Obtains 5.81 m s⁻².
Multiplies mass by centripetal acceleration (rather than using limiting μ_s mg).
Obtains 6.68 × 10³ N.
Equates m v_max² / r to μ_s mg.
Obtains 30.1 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Domestic satellite television dishes remain bolted in one fixed orientation on house walls. Which set of orbital parameters of the transmitting satellite makes this possible?
items.workedSolution: Fixed ground dishes require a twenty-four hour orbital period matching Earth rotation, directly above the equator, and orbiting west-to-east. Therefore the correct statement is: The transmitting satellite follows a twenty-four hour orbital period matching Earth rotation, directly above the equator, and orbiting west-to-east

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: twenty-four hour orbital period matching Earth rotation, directly above the equator, and orbiting west-to-east.

items.stem: Medical physicists choose X-ray tube voltages carefully. Different energies are needed for diagnostic radiographs and high-energy radiotherapy.
items.workedSolution: X-ray attenuation shifts from simple scatter and Z-cubed photoelectric absorption to Compton scattering and 1.02 MeV pair production as energy rises. Below ~20 keV, simple (elastic) scatter deflects low-energy photons off electrons without energy loss. Between ~20 keV and ~100 keV, the photoelectric effect dominates: the whole photon is absorbed to eject an inner-shell electron, with attenuation scaling as Z³. Between ~0.1 MeV and ~5 MeV, Compton scattering dominates: photons scatter off outer electrons, ejecting an electron and leaving with lower energy (longer wavelength), which blurs images. Above the 1.02 MeV threshold (2m_e c²), pair production occurs near nuclei, turning the photon into an e⁻/e⁺ pair. Diagnostic X-rays (~30–100 keV) use the Z³ photoelectric effect for sharp contrast between bone (calcium) and soft tissue, aided by barium (Z = 56) or iodine (Z = 53).

markScheme.criterion: L1: Describes simple scatter (< 20 keV): elastic deflection of X-ray photon with no energy loss.
L1: Describes photoelectric effect (~20–100 keV): complete photon absorption ejecting an electron.
L2: Describes Compton scattering (~0.1–5 MeV): photon ejects outer electron and leaves with lower energy/longer wavelength.
L2: Describes pair production (threshold ≥ 1.02 MeV = 2m_e c²): photon converts near nucleus into electron-positron pair.
L3: Links diagnostic contrast to photoelectric μ ∝ Z³, separating high-Z bone from low-Z soft tissue.
L3: Explains use of high-Z barium or iodine contrast media to outline soft-tissue organs sharply.

parts.prompt: Describe the four ways X-ray photons are attenuated in matter as photon energy rises from below 20 keV to above 2 MeV. Explain why photoelectric absorption and contrast media are vital for diagnostic imaging. [6 marks]
parts.expectedAnswer: X-ray attenuation shifts from simple scatter and Z-cubed photoelectric absorption to Compton scattering and 1.02 MeV pair production as photon energy increases. Below ~20 keV, simple (elastic) scatter deflects low-energy photons off electrons without energy loss. Between ~20 keV and ~100 keV, the photoelectric effect dominates: the entire X-ray photon is absorbed to eject an inner-shell electron, with attenuation coefficient scaling strongly as Z³. Between ~0.1 MeV and ~5 MeV, Compton scattering becomes dominant: photons scatter inelastically off outer electrons, ejecting an electron and emerging at lower energy (longer wavelength), which blurs images. Above the 1.02 MeV threshold (2m_e c²), pair production occurs near nuclei converting the photon into an e⁻/e⁺ pair. Diagnostic X-rays (~30–100 keV) use the Z³ photoelectric effect to produce sharp contrast between bone (high-Z calcium) and soft tissue, enhanced further by swallowing barium (Z = 56) or injecting iodine (Z = 53).
workingSteps: Describe simple scatter (< 20 keV) and photoelectric effect (20–100 keV, complete absorption, μ ∝ Z³).
Describe Compton scattering (0.1–5 MeV, lower-energy scattered photon + recoil electron) and pair production (≥ 1.02 MeV, γ → e⁻ + e⁺).
Link Z³ photoelectric scaling to bone/soft-tissue image contrast and barium/iodine contrast media.

items.stem: An asteroid orbits the Sun in an ellipse with perihelion distance $r_1 = 1.50\text{ AU}$ and aphelion distance $r_2 = 3.50\text{ AU}$. Its orbital speed at perihelion is $v_1 = 42.0\text{ km s}^{-1}$. Using Kepler's second law ($r_1 v_1 = r_2 v_2$), calculate its orbital speed $v_2$ at aphelion.
items.workedSolution: r₁v₁ = r₂v₂ ⇒ v₂ = v₁ (r₁ / r₂) = 42.0 × (1.50 / 3.50) = 18.0 km s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies r₁v₁ = r₂v₂ to obtain v₂ = 18.0 km s⁻¹.

items.workedSolution: (a) By Kepler's law, r_GEO = 4.22 × 10⁷ m. (b) Height above surface h_GEO = 3.59 × 10⁷ m. (c) Transfer energy ΔE = 3.70 × 10¹⁰ J. (d) twenty-four hour orbital period matching Earth rotation, directly above the equator, and orbiting west-to-east.

items.stem: Supported by a light 3.2 m cord at 42° to the vertical, a 0.75 kg ball traces a steady horizontal path. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² to find its centripetal acceleration.
items.workedSolution: Taking the ratio of radial force T sin θ = m a_c by vertical equilibrium T cos θ = mg gives a_c = g tan θ = 9.81 × tan 42° = 8.83 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Applies a_c = g tan 42° to obtain 8.83 m s⁻².

items.stem: Why does the transit photometry method fail to detect the majority of exoplanets orbiting nearby stars?
items.workedSolution: The transit method is geometrically selective because the orbital plane must align closely with the line of sight from Earth.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that orbital plane must align closely with the line of sight from Earth.

items.stem: A massive hot star ($M > 10\,M_{\odot}$) has surface temperature $2.00 \times 10^4\text{ K}$, luminosity $2.50 \times 10^{4}\,L_{\odot}$ ($9.58 \times 10^{30}\text{ W}$), and annual parallax $p = 0.0125\text{ arc-second}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $d = 1/0.0125 = 80.0 pc = 261 ly$. (b) $R/R_{\odot} = 13.2 R⊙$. (c) Fusion needs very high temperature to overcome electrostatic repulsion and high density for frequent collisions. Outward radiation pressure balances inward gravity. (d) This massive star evolves from the main sequence to a red supergiant, crossing the instability strip at high luminosity. It ends in a supernova leaving a neutron star or black hole, whereas the Sun ends as a white dwarf.

items.workedSolution: (a) $\rho = 6.42 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³$. (b) $R_{\text{s}} = 5.31 km < 11.0\text{ km}$, so it is not a black hole. (c) Infrared telescopes need cooling to very low temperatures, while X-ray telescopes use grazing-incidence mirrors in space.

Correct mean density 6.42 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.
Correct Schwarzschild radius 5.31 km.
Notes physical radius $11.0\text{ km} > R_{\text{s}}$, so escape velocity $< c$.
States that infrared telescopes need cooling to very low temperatures, while X-ray telescopes use grazing-incidence mirrors in space.
Notes atmospheric absorption of X-rays and water-vapour absorption/thermal noise for I-R.

parts.prompt: Explain why X-ray and infrared telescopes require specialist optics and siting compared with optical telescopes.
parts.expectedAnswer: Infrared telescopes need cooling to very low temperatures, while X-ray telescopes use grazing-incidence mirrors in space because X-rays penetrate normal-incidence mirrors and are absorbed by Earth's atmosphere.
workingSteps: State that infrared telescopes need cooling to very low temperatures, while X-ray telescopes use grazing-incidence mirrors in space.

items.stem: A comet follows the elliptical orbit around the Sun illustrated in the figure, where the two shaded sectors have equal area. What does Kepler's second law tell us about the comet's motion?
items.workedSolution: Equal areas swept in equal times require a larger arc length per second at smaller r (perihelion) than at larger r (aphelion). By Kepler's second law, the line joining the comet to the Sun sweeps equal areas in equal times. Its orbital speed is therefore greatest at perihelion and smallest at aphelion.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct explanation: equal areas are swept in equal times, so orbital speed is greatest at perihelion and smallest at aphelion.

options.label: A
options.text: The comet travels at constant linear speed around the entire ellipse so it spends equal times at perihelion and aphelion.
options.distractorRationale: At smaller radius (perihelion) a longer arc is needed to sweep the same area, so speed must be greater.

options.label: B
options.text: The comet moves slowest at perihelion where solar gravity is strongest and fastest at aphelion.
options.distractorRationale: Reverses the speed relationship: closer to the Sun, gravitational PE is lower and kinetic energy / speed is greatest.

options.label: C
options.text: The line joining a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times so orbital speed is greatest at perihelion and smallest at aphelion.

options.label: D
options.text: The Sun lies at the geometric centre of the ellipse rather than at one of the two foci.
options.distractorRationale: By Kepler's first law, the Sun sits at one focus of the elliptical orbit.

items.stem: Passing the bottom at 26 m s⁻¹, a trolley of mass 46.3 kg runs around the inside of a smooth vertical loop (radius 9.26 m). Friction and drag are negligible; take g = 9.8 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Equating total energy gives ½mv_bot² = ½mv_top² + mg(2R), v_top = √(v_bot² − 4gR) = 17.7 m s⁻¹. (b) Downward radial balance F_top + mg = mv_top²/R gives F_top = 1.11 × 10³ N. (c) Setting F_top = 0 gives v_top = √(gR) and v_bot,min = √(5gR) = 21.3 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies energy conservation with vertical rise Δh = 2R.
Obtains v_top = 17.7 m s⁻¹.
Uses F_top = m(v_top²/R − g) at the apex.
Obtains F_top = 1.11 × 10³ N.
Combines v_top,min² = gR with v_bot,min² = v_top,min² + 4gR.
Obtains v_bot,min = 21.3 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the speed of the trolley as it passes the highest point of the circle.
workingSteps: Conservation of mechanical energy with Δh = 2R gives v_top² = v_bot² − 4gR.

parts.prompt: Determine the magnitude of the normal contact force acting on the trolley at the highest point.
workingSteps: At the apex, F_top + mg = m v_top² / R.

parts.prompt: Calculate the minimum speed at the lowest point needed to complete the loop without losing contact at the top.
workingSteps: At threshold contact, v_top = √(gR), so v_bot,min = √(gR + 4gR) = √(5gR).

items.stem: Take b = 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K and σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴ for a spherical black-body star (1.46 × 10¹⁰ m radius, 14500 K) lying 2.96 × 10¹⁶ m from Earth.
items.workedSolution: (a) From Wien's displacement law, λ_max = b/T = 200 nm. (b) L = 4πR²σT⁴ = 6.71 × 10³⁰ W. (c) Apparent brightness b_app = L/(4πd²) = 6.10 × 10⁻⁴ W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses λ_max = 2.90 × 10⁻³ / T.
Obtains 200 nm.
Applies L = 4π R² σ T⁴.
Obtains 6.71 × 10³⁰ W.
Applies b_app = L / (4π d²).
Obtains 6.10 × 10⁻⁴ W m⁻².

parts.prompt: Calculate the peak emission wavelength, in nm, of the star's spectrum.
Calculate the total luminosity of the star.
Determine the apparent brightness received at Earth.

items.stem: Tracking a 4.89 × 10²⁸ W star from Earth's 1 AU orbit yields annual parallax 0.13 arcsec. Take 1 pc = 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m. Because 1 AU gives 1 arcsecond at 1 pc, d / pc = 1 / (p / arcsec).
items.workedSolution: (a) By parallax, d = 1 / 0.13 = 7.69 pc. (b) In SI units, d = 2.37 × 10¹⁷ m. (c) Apparent brightness b = L / (4π d²) = 6.91 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Applies d(pc) = 1 / p(arcsec).
Obtains 7.69 pc.
Multiplies distance in parsecs by 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m pc⁻¹.
Obtains 2.37 × 10¹⁷ m.
Applies inverse-square law b = L / (4π d²).
Obtains 6.91 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻².

items.stem: In the vertical-track figure, a 3.5 kg test mass moves at constant speed 4.13 m s⁻¹ inside a smooth circular track of radius 0.772 m. Use g = 9.8 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) At the top limit, v_min = √(gR) = 2.75 m s⁻¹. (b) At the top, F_top = m(v²/R − g) = 43.0 N. (c) At the bottom, F_bot = m(v²/R + g) = 112 N.

markScheme.criterion: Sets support force to zero at apex so mg = m v_min² / R.
Obtains 2.75 m s⁻¹.
Subtracts mg from m v² / R at the top.
Obtains 43.0 N.
Adds mg to m v² / R at the bottom.
Obtains 112 N.

items.stem: A light 0.95 m string stays at 24° to the vertical while supporting a 1.8 kg sphere in a steady horizontal circle. Use g = 9.8 m s⁻² to calculate the string tension.
items.workedSolution: Vertical equilibrium requires T cos θ = mg, so T = (1.8 × 9.8) / cos 24° = 19.3 N.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves T cos 24° = mg to obtain T = 19.3 N.

items.stem: Swinging at steady speed 7.37 m s⁻¹ in a vertical circle (radius 3.28 m), a 1.32 kg mass hangs from a light string. Use g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Critical top speed v_min = √(gR) = 5.67 m s⁻¹. (b) At the top, F_top = m(v²/R − g) = 8.91 N. (c) At the bottom, F_bot = m(v²/R + g) = 34.8 N.

markScheme.criterion: Sets support force to zero at apex so mg = m v_min² / R.
Obtains 5.67 m s⁻¹.
Subtracts mg from m v² / R at the top.
Obtains 8.91 N.
Adds mg to m v² / R at the bottom.
Obtains 34.8 N.

parts.prompt: Calculate the minimum speed at the highest point needed for the string to remain taut.
workingSteps: Setting support force at the top to zero gives m v_min² / R = mg.

parts.prompt: Calculate the tension in the string when the mass passes the highest point at 7.37 m s⁻¹.
workingSteps: At the top, F_top + mg = m v² / R.

parts.prompt: Determine the tension in the string when the mass passes the lowest point at 7.37 m s⁻¹.
workingSteps: At the bottom, F_bot − mg = m v² / R.

items.stem: Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect friction and air drag. A small 1.8 kg ball enters the lowest point of a smooth vertical circular track (radius 4.2 m) at 20.7 m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) Using ½mv_bot² = ½mv_top² + mg(2R), v_top = √(v_bot² − 4gR) = 16.2 m s⁻¹. (b) Downward radial balance F_top + mg = mv_top²/R gives F_top = 95.3 N. (c) Setting F_top = 0 gives v_top = √(gR) and v_bot,min = √(5gR) = 14.4 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies energy conservation with vertical rise Δh = 2R.
Obtains v_top = 16.2 m s⁻¹.
Uses F_top = m(v_top²/R − g) at the apex.
Obtains F_top = 95.3 N.
Combines v_top,min² = gR with v_bot,min² = v_top,min² + 4gR.
Obtains v_bot,min = 14.4 m s⁻¹.

workingSteps: Conservation of mechanical energy with Δh = 2R gives v_top² = v_bot² − 4gR.

parts.prompt: Determine the magnitude of the normal contact force acting on the ball at the highest point.
workingSteps: At the apex, F_top + mg = m v_top² / R.

items.stem: To cross the gravity barrier from Primary Planet's surface to Companion Moon, a probe needs a minimum launch speed. Both airless bodies sit 2.77 × 10⁸ m apart (centre to centre), with mass 1.25 × 10²⁵ kg (radius 7.33 × 10⁶ m) for Primary Planet and mass 1.95 × 10²³ kg (radius 1.83 × 10⁶ m) for Companion Moon. Work out this speed using G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: At launch (x = R₁), the potential is V(R₁) = −GM₁/R₁ − GM₂/(d − R₁) = -1.14 × 10⁸ J kg⁻¹. Null-point potential at x₀ = 2.46 × 10⁸ m is V(x₀) = -3.81 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. Potential barrier ΔV = V(x₀) − V(R₁) = 1.10 × 10⁸ J kg⁻¹, so v_min = √(2ΔV) = 1.48 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ΔV = V(x₀) − V(R₁) and v_min = √(2ΔV) = 1.48 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A spherical planet of uniform density has mass 1.25 × 10²⁵ kg and radius 3.5 × 10⁶ m. A probe of mass 650 kg is lowered into a narrow shaft inside the planet to a distance of 8.75 × 10⁵ m from the centre, with G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Surface field g₀ = GM/R² = 68.1 N kg⁻¹. (b) At r = 8.75 × 10⁵ m, uniform-sphere interior scaling g = g₀(r/R) gives 17.0 N kg⁻¹. (c) Force on probe F = mg = 1.11 × 10⁴ N.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes M and R into g₀ = GM / R².
Obtains g₀ = 68.1 N kg⁻¹.
Applies linear interior field law g(r) = GMr/R³.
Obtains g = 17.0 N kg⁻¹.
Multiplies probe mass by field strength at r.
Obtains F = 1.11 × 10⁴ N.

items.stem: Study a non-rotating, airless sphere of radius 3.19 × 10⁶ m and mass 1.31 × 10²⁵ kg. Set potential to zero at infinity, with G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². Positioned 1.21 × 10⁷ m from its centre is a 780 kg spacecraft.
items.workedSolution: (a) From the surface radius, V_surface = −GM/R = -2.74 × 10⁸ J kg⁻¹. (b) Escape speed v_esc = √(−2 V_surface) = √(2GM/R) = 2.34 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹. (c) At r = 1.21 × 10⁷ m, E_p = −GMm/r = -5.63 × 10¹⁰ J.

markScheme.criterion: Applies V_g = −GM / R with negative sign.
Obtains -2.74 × 10⁸ J kg⁻¹.
Uses v_esc = √(2GM / R) or √(−2 V_surface).
Obtains 2.34 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.
Applies E_p = −GMm / r at probe radius.
Obtains -5.63 × 10¹⁰ J.

items.stem: In the figure, Icy Moon (mass 2.97 × 10²³ kg, radius 1.74 × 10⁶ m) lies 5.38 × 10⁸ m centre-to-centre from Host World (mass 1.07 × 10²⁵ kg, radius 6.37 × 10⁶ m). Calculate the distance from Host World's centre where the resultant field strength is zero.
items.workedSolution: For zero net field, equate the opposing pulls: G M₁ / x₀² = G M₂ / (d − x₀)² gives (d − x₀)/x₀ = √(M₂/M₁), so x₀ = [√M₁ / (√M₁ + √M₂)] d = 4.61 × 10⁸ m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses x₀ = d √M₁ / (√M₁ + √M₂) to obtain 4.61 × 10⁸ m.

items.stem: Find the normal reaction force on an 880 kg car rounding a smooth banked road in a horizontal circle. The radius is 45 m and bank angle is 28° with no sideways friction. Use g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: Because the circular path lies in a horizontal plane, vertical acceleration is zero: N cos θ = mg, so N = (880 × 9.81) / cos 28° = 9.78 × 10³ N.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves vertically N cos 28° = mg to obtain N = 9.78 × 10³ N.

items.stem: Astronomers observe an oxygen emission line in the spectrum of a distant galaxy, where its rest wavelength of 372.7 nm is shifted to 379.67 nm. Take the speed of light as c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and the Hubble constant as H₀ = 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) z = (λ_obs − λ₀)/λ₀ = 0.0187. (b) Recession speed v ≈ zc = 5.61 × 10³ km s⁻¹. (c) Hubble distance d = v/H₀ = 80.1 Mpc.

markScheme.criterion: Applies z = Δλ / λ₀.
Obtains z = 0.0187.
Multiplies z by c and converts to km s⁻¹.
Obtains v = 5.61 × 10³ km s⁻¹.
Applies d = v / H₀.
Obtains d = 80.1 Mpc.
