items.stem: A Type Ia supernova in a galaxy cluster peaks at apparent magnitude $m = 18.2$ (with standard peak absolute magnitude $M = -19.3$). Spectroscopy of the host galaxy shows a redshift magnitude $|z| = 0.0680$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $d = 316 Mpc$. (b) $v = 2.04 × 10⁴ km s⁻¹$. (c) distant type Ia supernovae are dimmer than predicted indicating accelerating expansion driven by dark energy.

markScheme.criterion: Correct distance 316 Mpc.
Computes $v = 0.0680 \times 3.00 \times 10^5\text{ km s}^{-1}$.
Correct speed 2.04 × 10⁴ km s⁻¹.

items.stem: A spacecraft of mass 794 kg orbits a spherical planet in a circular path at an altitude of 8.31 × 10⁶ m above the surface. The planet has mass 1.39 × 10²⁵ kg and radius 5.54 × 10⁶ m. Taking G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², calculate the circular orbital speed of the spacecraft.
items.workedSolution: Orbital radius from planet centre r = R_p + h = 5.54 × 10⁶ + 8.31 × 10⁶ = 1.385 × 10⁷ m. Equating GMm / r² = mv² / r gives v = √(GM / r) = √(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 1.39 × 10²⁵ / 1.385 × 10⁷) = 8.18 × 10³ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses r = 1.385 × 10⁷ m to obtain 8.18 × 10³ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Study the orbit and energy diagram for a 444 kg satellite circling at radius 1.62 × 10⁷ m. The host planet has radius 6.23 × 10⁶ m and mass 8.84 × 10²⁴ kg. Set E_p = 0 at infinity and G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Kinetic energy E_k = GMm/(2r) = 8.08 × 10⁹ J. (b) E_p = −GMm/r = -1.62 × 10¹⁰ J. (c) Total mechanical energy E_tot = E_k + E_p = −GMm/(2r) = -8.08 × 10⁹ J.

markScheme.criterion: Applies E_k = GMm / (2r).
Obtains E_k = 8.08 × 10⁹ J.
Applies E_p = −GMm / r including negative sign.
Obtains E_p = -1.62 × 10¹⁰ J.
Sums E_k + E_p or applies E_tot = −GMm / (2r).
Obtains E_tot = -8.08 × 10⁹ J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the kinetic energy of the satellite in this circular orbit.
workingSteps: From m v² / r = G M m / r², E_k = ½ m v² = G M m / (2r).

parts.prompt: Calculate the gravitational potential energy of the satellite.
Determine the total mechanical energy of the satellite.
workingSteps: E_tot = E_k + E_p = −G M m / (2r) = -8.08 × 10⁹ J.

items.stem: A Hertzsprung–Russell diagram shows four stars with region names removed, including Star Epsilon-2 at surface temperature 6690 K and luminosity 4.7 L☉. Use solar values L☉ = 3.83 × 10²⁶ W, R☉ = 6.96 × 10⁸ m, and σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.
items.workedSolution: (a) Star Epsilon-2 lies in the main-sequence region. (b) L = 4.7 × 3.83 × 10²⁶ = 1.80 × 10²⁷ W. (c) R = √[L/(4πσT⁴)] = 1.12 × 10⁹ m = 1.61 R☉.

markScheme.criterion: States main-sequence.
Multiplies L / L☉ by 3.83 × 10²⁶ W.
Obtains L = 1.80 × 10²⁷ W.
Applies R = √[L / (4π σ T⁴)] and divides by R☉.
Obtains 1.61 R☉.

items.stem: A cart of mass 220 kg travels at a constant speed of 14.8 m s⁻¹ around a flat circular track of radius 90 m without slipping. The coefficient of static friction between the tyres and the track is 0.74, and g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the sideways static frictional force acting on the tyres.
items.workedSolution: Because 14.8 m s⁻¹ is below the slipping limit v_max = √(μ_s g r) = 25.6 m s⁻¹, static friction self-adjusts to match the required centripetal force: f_s = m v² / r = 220 × (14.8)² / 90 = 535 N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses f_s = m v² / r (not μ_s mg) to obtain 535 N.

items.stem: Why is it physically impossible to place a geostationary satellite permanently directly overhead above London (latitude 51.5° N)?
items.workedSolution: The orbital plane must pass through Earth's centre of mass. To stay fixed above one surface point, the satellite needs a twenty-four hour period matching Earth's rotation, directly above the equator, moving west-to-east. Because gravitational attraction acts toward Earth's centre, a geostationary orbit must lie above the equator with a twenty-four hour west-to-east period.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: twenty-four hour orbital period matching Earth rotation, directly above the equator, and orbiting west-to-east.

options.text: Because Earth's magnetic poles deflect all non-equatorial satellites into escape trajectories.

items.stem: A car of mass 1320 kg travels at 11.1 m s⁻¹ around a flat circular track of radius 35 m. Taking μ_s = 0.88 and g = 9.8 m s⁻², calculate the maximum speed of the car before it starts to slip.
items.workedSolution: Just before slipping, m v_max² / r = μ_s m g, independent of mass: v_max = √(μ_s g r) = √(0.88 × 9.8 × 35) = 17.4 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates v_max = √(μ_s g r) = 17.4 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A minor planet orbits the Sun with semi-major axis $a = 3.20\text{ AU}$, perihelion distance $r_1 = 2.00\text{ AU}$, aphelion distance $r_2 = 4.40\text{ AU}$, and perihelion speed $v_1 = 44.0\text{ km s}^{-1}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) v₂ = 20.0 km s⁻¹. (b) T = 5.72 yr. (c) The line joining a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time. (d) On large scales, the universe is homogeneous (uniform average density everywhere) and isotropic (looks the same in all directions), with universal physical laws.

markScheme.criterion: Applies r₁v₁ = r₂v₂ from Kepler's second law.
Obtains v₂ = 20.0 km s⁻¹.
Applies T² = a³ with a = 3.20 AU.
Obtains T = 5.72 yr.
States the line joining a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time.
Defines homogeneous (uniform average density on large scales).
Defines isotropic (looks the same in all directions) and homogeneous (uniform average density) on large scales with universal physical laws.

items.stem: Swinging steadily around a horizontal circle, a 2.2 kg sphere is supported by a light 2.4 m cord angled at 42° from vertical. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Balancing weight vertically, T cos 42° = (2.2)(9.81) gives T = 29.0 N. (b) Horizontal radius r = 2.4 sin 42° = 1.61 m; horizontal dynamics T sin θ = mv²/r yields v = 3.77 m s⁻¹. (c) Period P = 2πr / v = 2.68 s.

markScheme.criterion: Equates vertical component T cos θ to weight mg.
Obtains tension 29.0 N.
Uses r = L sin θ and equates T sin θ (or mg tan θ) to m v² / r.
Obtains speed 3.77 m s⁻¹.
Applies P = 2π r / v or P = 2π√(L cos θ / g).
Obtains period 2.68 s.

items.stem: A distant quasar is powered by a supermassive black hole of mass $5.00 \times 10^8\,M_\odot$ ($M_\odot = 1.99 \times 10^{30}\text{ kg}$) and has cosmological redshift $z = 1.60$. Take $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\text{ N m}^2\text{ kg}^{-2}$, $c = 3.00 \times 10^8\text{ m s}^{-1}$, and $1\text{ AU} = 1.50 \times 10^{11}\text{ m}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $R_s = 9.83 AU$. (b) $\lambda_{\text{obs}} = 1.26 × 10³ nm$ (shifted into the near-infrared).

Divides $R_s$ in metres by $1.50 \times 10^{11}\text{ m AU}^{-1}$.
Correct Schwarzschild radius 9.83 AU.
Applies $\lambda_{\text{obs}} = 486 \times (1 + 1.60)$.
Correct redshifted wavelength 1.26 × 10³ nm.

items.stem: A nearby main-sequence star has an annual stellar parallax angle of $p = 0.250\text{ arc-second}$. Using $d\,(\text{pc}) = \frac{1}{p\,(\text{arc-second})}$ and $1\text{ pc} = 3.26\text{ ly}$, calculate the distance to the star in light-years.
items.workedSolution: Distance in parsecs is $d = \frac{1}{0.250} = 4.00\text{ pc}$. Converting to light-years: $d = 4.00 \times 3.26 = 13.0 ly$.

items.stem: One star in an edge-on circular spectroscopic binary orbits with period $6.00\text{ days}$ ($1\text{ day} = 86\,400\text{ s}$). Its $\text{H}\beta$ line at $486.1\text{ nm}$ shows a maximum Doppler shift of $0.180\text{ nm}$. Calculate its orbital radius about the common centre of mass.
items.workedSolution: Orbital speed $v = \frac{0.180}{486.1} \times 3.00 \times 10^8 = 1.11 \times 10^{5}\text{ m s}^{-1}$. Then $r = \frac{vT}{2\pi} = \frac{1.11 \times 10^{5} \times 6.00 \times 86\,400}{2\pi} = 9.17 × 10⁹ m$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 9.17 × 10⁹ m.

items.stem: A $1200\text{ kg}$ Earth observation satellite ($M_{\text{E}} = 5.97 \times 10^{24}\text{ kg}$, $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\text{ N m}^2\text{ kg}^{-2}$) loses orbital altitude under weak atmospheric drag, descending from circular radius $r_1 = 7200\text{ km}$ to $r_2 = 6700\text{ km}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $v_1 = 7.44 × 10³ m s⁻¹$, $v_2 = 7.71 × 10³ m s⁻¹$. (b) Thermal energy dissipated $= 2.48 GJ$. (c) Atmospheric viscous drag reduces total mechanical energy. The satellite drops to a lower orbital height, where its orbital speed increases.

markScheme.criterion: Applies v = √(GM/r) to obtain v₁ = 7.44 × 10³ m s⁻¹.
Obtains higher final speed v₂ = 7.71 × 10³ m s⁻¹.
Applies ΔE_tot = −(GMm/2)(1/r₂ − 1/r₁).
Obtains thermal energy dissipated 2.48 GJ.
States drag does negative work, making total energy E_tot = −GMm/(2r) more negative.
Deduces orbital radius r decreases and gravitational PE drops by twice |ΔE_tot|.
Concludes that half of the released potential energy increases kinetic energy. Drag reduces total energy, lowering height while raising orbital speed.

parts.prompt: Calculate the circular orbital speed at $r_1 = 7200\text{ km}$ and at $r_2 = 6700\text{ km}$.
parts.expectedAnswer: At r₁, v₁ = 7.44 × 10³ m s⁻¹; at r₂, v₂ = 7.71 × 10³ m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the total mechanical energy dissipated as thermal energy during this orbital decay in $\text{GJ}$.
Explain qualitatively why atmospheric viscous drag causes the satellite's height to decrease while its orbital speed increases.
parts.expectedAnswer: This seemingly paradoxical speed-up happens because atmospheric viscous drag reduces total mechanical energy so the satellite drops to a lower orbital height where its orbital speed increases.
workingSteps: Atmospheric viscous drag reduces total mechanical energy. The satellite therefore drops to a lower orbit where its orbital speed increases.

items.stem: In the sketch, a small 0.212 kg ball enters a smooth vertical loop (radius 0.635 m) at 8.48 m s⁻¹ with no drag or friction. State the minimum bottom speed needed to stay on the track at the top (g = 9.8 m s⁻²).
items.workedSolution: Just keeping contact at the top requires v_top ≥ √(gR). Conservation of energy from bottom to top (Δh = 2R) gives ½m v_bot,min² = ½m(gR) + mg(2R) => v_bot,min = √(5gR) = √(5 × 9.8 × 0.635) = 5.58 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates v_bot,min = √(5gR) = 5.58 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A spherical star radiates as a black body with radius 3.83 × 10⁹ m and surface temperature 6250 K at 4.38 × 10¹⁶ m from Earth. Using σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴, state the apparent brightness b = L / (4πd²) at Earth.
items.workedSolution: Luminosity L = 4π R² σ T⁴ = 4π(3.83 × 10⁹)²(5.67 × 10⁻⁸)(6250)⁴ = 1.59 × 10²⁸ W. Apparent brightness b = L / (4π d²) = σ T⁴ (R / d)² = 6.62 × 10⁻⁷ W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses L = 4πR²σT⁴ and b = L / (4πd²) to obtain 6.62 × 10⁻⁷ W m⁻².

items.stem: Parallax angle 0.693 arcsec is recorded across Earth's 1 AU radius for a 7.1 × 10²⁹ W star. With 1 pc = 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m and d / pc = 1 / (p / arcsec) (a 1 AU base gives 1 arcsecond at 1 pc), what apparent brightness reaches Earth?
items.workedSolution: First compute distance d = (1 / 0.693) pc = 1.44 pc = 4.45 × 10¹⁶ m. Apparent brightness b = L / (4π d²) = 7.1 × 10²⁹ / (4π × (4.45 × 10¹⁶)²) = 2.85 × 10⁻⁵ W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Converts d = (1/p) pc to metres and evaluates b = L/(4πd²) = 2.85 × 10⁻⁵ W m⁻².

items.stem: How large is the normal reaction from the road at the peak of a circular bridge (radius 22 m) for a 1520 kg car at steady speed 8.08 m s⁻¹? Use g = 9.8 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: At the crest of the road, downward resultant force is mg − N_top = m v² / R, so N_top = m(g − v²/R) = 1520 × (9.8 − (8.08)² / 22) = 1.04 × 10⁴ N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies radial force equation at apex to obtain 1.04 × 10⁴ N.

items.stem: Steady speed in a horizontal circle keeps a light 1.8 m string at 20° to the vertical, while the attached bob has mass 2.2 kg (g = 9.8 m s⁻²).
items.workedSolution: (a) Balancing weight vertically, T cos 20° = (2.2)(9.8) gives T = 22.9 N. (b) Horizontal radius r = 1.8 sin 20° = 0.616 m; horizontal dynamics T sin θ = mv²/r yields v = 1.48 m s⁻¹. (c) Period P = 2πr / v = 2.61 s.

markScheme.criterion: Equates vertical component T cos θ to weight mg.
Obtains tension 22.9 N.
Uses r = L sin θ and equates T sin θ (or mg tan θ) to m v² / r.
Obtains speed 1.48 m s⁻¹.
Applies P = 2π r / v or P = 2π√(L cos θ / g).
Obtains period 2.61 s.

workingSteps: Horizontal radius r = L sin θ = 1.8 sin 20° = 0.616 m.
From T sin θ = m v² / r, v = √(g r tan θ) = 1.48 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Around a planet of radius 7.76 × 10⁶ m and mass 1.47 × 10²⁵ kg, an 803 kg satellite changes from circular orbit r₁ = 1.09 × 10⁷ m to r₂ = 3.05 × 10⁷ m (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²).
items.workedSolution: (a) Inner total energy: E_tot(r₁) = −GMm/(2r₁) = -3.61 × 10¹⁰ J. (b) Final bound energy E_tot(r₂) = -1.29 × 10¹⁰ J, so ΔE_tot = 2.32 × 10¹⁰ J. (c) Outer orbital period T₂ = 2π√(r₂³/GM) = 3.38 × 10⁴ s.

markScheme.criterion: Applies E_tot = −GMm / (2r₁).
Obtains -3.61 × 10¹⁰ J.
Evaluates E_tot(r₂) − E_tot(r₁) = ½GMm(1/r₁ − 1/r₂).
Obtains 2.32 × 10¹⁰ J.
Applies Kepler's third law at outer radius r₂.
Obtains 3.38 × 10⁴ s.

items.stem: Taking g = 9.81 m s⁻², calculate the road's normal reaction at the top of a circular bridge (radius 14 m) as a 1180 kg car passes steadily at 10.1 m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: At the convex crest, downward resultant force is mg − N_top = m v² / R, so N_top = m(g − v²/R) = 1180 × (9.81 − (10.1)² / 14) = 2.98 × 10³ N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies radial force equation at apex to obtain 2.98 × 10³ N.

items.stem: What normal contact force pushes on a small 0.5 kg ball at the top of a smooth vertical circular track (radius 1.2 m)? It passes the base at 8.9 m s⁻¹ with no friction or drag, and g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: Using energy balance to the top, v_top² = v_bot² − 4gR = (8.9)² − 4(9.81)(1.2) = 32.1 m² s⁻². Radial force balance F_top + mg = m v_top² / R gives F_top = 0.5(32.1 / 1.2 − 9.81) = 8.48 N.

markScheme.criterion: Combines v_top² = v_bot² − 4gR with F_top = m(v_top²/R − g) to obtain 8.48 N.

items.stem: In a two-body gravity model, airless spheres Planet Major (mass 1.59 × 10²⁵ kg, 5.41 × 10⁶ m radius) and Planet Minor (mass 1.77 × 10²⁴ kg, 1.57 × 10⁶ m radius) sit 4.06 × 10⁸ m apart, centre to centre. Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻² with V_g = 0 at infinity.
items.workedSolution: (a) Locating the null point gives x₀ = d√M₁/(√M₁ + √M₂) = 3.04 × 10⁸ m. (b) Combined scalar potential V(x₀) = -4.65 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. (c) Potential barrier from x = R₁ to x₀ is ΔV = 1.92 × 10⁸ J kg⁻¹, giving v_min = √(2ΔV) = 1.96 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies x₀ = d√M₁ / (√M₁ + √M₂).
Obtains x₀ = 3.04 × 10⁸ m.
Sums both negative scalar potentials −GM₁/x₀ − GM₂/(d − x₀).
Obtains V(x₀) = -4.65 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹.
Equates ½v_min² to potential barrier V(x₀) − V(R₁).
Obtains v_min = 1.96 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

workingSteps: Equating field magnitudes gives x₀ = [√M₁ / (√M₁ + √M₂)] d = 3.04 × 10⁸ m.

workingSteps: V(x₀) = −G M₁ / x₀ − G M₂ / (d − x₀) = -4.65 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹.

workingSteps: ΔV = V(x₀) − V(R₁) = 1.92 × 10⁸ J kg⁻¹; v_min = √(2ΔV) = 1.96 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A spherical planet of uniform density has mass 5.2 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 5.33 × 10⁶ m. A small probe of mass 134 kg is lowered into a narrow shaft inside the planet to a distance of 2.93 × 10⁶ m from the centre. Taking G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², calculate the gravitational field strength at this point.
items.workedSolution: Inside a uniform sphere (r < R), enclosed mass M_enc = M(r/R)³, so g(r) = G M r / R³ = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.2 × 10²⁴ × 2.93 × 10⁶) / (5.33 × 10⁶)³ = 6.71 N kg⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates gravitational field strength at r = 2.93 × 10⁶ m to obtain 6.71 N kg⁻¹.

items.stem: From the surface of a spherical planet (1.31 × 10²⁵ kg, radius 9.87 × 10⁶ m), what minimum speed reaches infinity? A 620 kg probe lies 3.16 × 10⁷ m from the centre, with G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: For surface escape, ½m v_esc² − G M m / R = 0 gives v_esc = √(2 G M / R) = √(2 × 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 1.31 × 10²⁵ / 9.87 × 10⁶) = 1.33 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates surface escape speed √(2GM / R) = 1.33 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A 1200 kg spacecraft moves along the straight line between Planet Major and Planet Minor, passing 2.86 × 10⁸ m from Planet Major's centre. Their centres stand 4.61 × 10⁸ m apart. Planet Major has mass 7.46 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 5.41 × 10⁶ m, Planet Minor has mass 2.98 × 10²³ kg and radius 1.57 × 10⁶ m, and G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Matching GM₁/x₀² = GM₂/(d − x₀)² yields x₀ = d√M₁/(√M₁ + √M₂) = 3.84 × 10⁸ m. (b) At x = 2.86 × 10⁸ m, |g| = |GM₁/x² − GM₂/(d − x)²| = 0.00543 N kg⁻¹. (c) Net force F = m|g| = 6.52 N.

markScheme.criterion: Equates opposing inverse-square field strengths GM₁/x₀² = GM₂/(d − x₀)².
Takes square root correctly to form x₀ = d√M₁ / (√M₁ + √M₂).
Obtains x₀ = 3.84 × 10⁸ m.
Subtracts opposing field magnitudes at x and (d − x).
Obtains |g| = 0.00543 N kg⁻¹.
Multiplies by spacecraft mass to obtain 6.52 N.

parts.prompt: Calculate the distance from the centre of Planet Major to the point between them where the resultant gravitational field strength is zero.
workingSteps: At the null point, G M₁ / x₀² = G M₂ / (d − x₀)².
Taking square roots gives x₀ = [√M₁ / (√M₁ + √M₂)] d = 3.84 × 10⁸ m.

parts.prompt: Calculate the magnitude of the resultant gravitational field strength when the spacecraft is 2.86 × 10⁸ m from the centre of Planet Major.
workingSteps: |g| = |G M₁ / x² − G M₂ / (d − x)²| = 0.00543 N kg⁻¹.

parts.prompt: State the magnitude of the resultant gravitational force on the 1200 kg spacecraft at this point.

items.stem: With zero sideways friction, a 1950 kg train traces a horizontal circle of radius 120 m on a smooth track sloped at 28°. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Vertical equilibrium N cos 28° = mg gives N = 2.17 × 10⁴ N. (b) Horizontal component F_c = N sin 28° = 1.02 × 10⁴ N. (c) Setting m v² / r = F_c yields v_ideal = 25.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses N cos θ = mg (zero vertical acceleration).
Obtains N = 2.17 × 10⁴ N.
Evaluates F_c = N sin θ or mg tan θ.
Obtains F_c = 1.02 × 10⁴ N.
Equates m v² / r to F_c and solves for v.
Obtains v_ideal = 25.0 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the magnitude of the normal contact force on the train.
workingSteps: Vertical equilibrium gives N cos θ = mg.

parts.prompt: Determine the horizontal centripetal force acting toward the centre of the circle.
workingSteps: Horizontal component of normal reaction provides the centripetal force: F_c = N sin θ = mg tan θ.

parts.prompt: Hence calculate the ideal frictionless speed of the train.
workingSteps: From m v² / r = F_c, v = √(F_c r / m) = √(g r tan θ) = 25.0 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A distant galaxy is 75.57 Mpc from Earth and recedes according to Hubble's law. Taking H₀ = 71.5 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, calculate the observed wavelength in nm of a magnesium absorption line (rest wavelength 517.5 nm).
items.workedSolution: Recession speed v = H₀ d = 71.5 × 75.57 = 5.40 × 10³ km s⁻¹. Redshift z = v / c = 0.0180, so λ_obs = λ₀(1 + z) = 517.5 × (1 + 0.0180) = 527 nm.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates v = H₀d, z = v/c, and λ_obs = λ₀(1 + z) = 527 nm.

items.stem: The AQA Data Sheet gives $H = 65\text{ km s}^{-1}\text{ Mpc}^{-1}$ and $1\text{ Mpc} = 3.08 \times 10^{22}\text{ m}$. Assuming a constant expansion rate, estimate the age of the Universe in seconds.
items.workedSolution: Convert $H$ to SI: $H = \frac{65 \times 10^3}{3.08 \times 10^{22}} = 2.11 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹$. Then $t \approx \frac{1}{H} = 4.74 × 10¹⁷ s$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 4.74 × 10¹⁷ s.

items.stem: A spacecraft of mass 656 kg moves in a circular orbit of radius 1.674 × 10⁷ m around the centre of a spherical planet. The planet has mass 1.07 × 10²⁵ kg and radius 7.97 × 10⁶ m, with G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) With orbital radius r = 1.674 × 10⁷ m, g = GM/r² = 2.55 N kg⁻¹. (b) Orbital speed v = √(GM/r) = 6.53 × 10³ m s⁻¹. (c) Period T = 2πr/v = 1.61 × 10⁴ s.

markScheme.criterion: Uses centre-to-centre orbital radius r in g = GM / r².
Obtains g = 2.55 N kg⁻¹.
Equates v²/r to g (or GM/r²).
Obtains v = 6.53 × 10³ m s⁻¹.
Applies T = 2πr / v or Kepler's third law.
Obtains T = 1.61 × 10⁴ s.

items.stem: With G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², calculate the escape speed from radius 1.71 × 10⁷ m. A 288 kg satellite orbits at r = 1.71 × 10⁷ m around a spherical planet of mass 4.61 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 9.51 × 10⁶ m.
items.workedSolution: Escaping from radial distance r needs ½m v_esc² − GMm/r = 0, so v_esc = √(2GM / r) = √(2 × 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 4.61 × 10²⁴ / 1.71 × 10⁷) = 6.00 × 10³ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates v_esc = √(2GM / r) = 6.00 × 10³ m s⁻¹.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates escape speed from the planet's surface R_p rather than from the satellite's orbital radius r.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies circular orbital speed by 2 instead of √2.

items.stem: A car of mass 1650 kg moves at a constant speed of 13 m s⁻¹ around a flat circular track of radius 52 m. The coefficient of static friction between the tyres and the track is 0.68, and g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) a_c = v² / r = (13)² / 52 = 3.25 m s⁻². (b) Below the slipping limit, f_s = m a_c = 1650 × 3.25 = 5.36 × 10³ N. (c) Maximum speed without slipping v_max = √(μ_s g r) = 18.6 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies a_c = v² / r.
Obtains 3.25 m s⁻².
Multiplies mass by centripetal acceleration (rather than using limiting μ_s mg).
Obtains 5.36 × 10³ N.
Equates m v_max² / r to μ_s mg.
Obtains 18.6 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: An imaging satellite operates in a polar low-Earth orbit rather than a geostationary orbit. What main observation and communication advantages does this give?
items.workedSolution: A polar low-Earth orbit sweeps across the entire Earth surface as Earth rotates beneath it. Its low altitude gives higher image resolution and lower signal delay. Orbiting closer to Earth over the poles lets it scan the whole Earth with higher image resolution and lower signal latency.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct explanation: a polar low-Earth orbit scans the whole Earth as Earth rotates, giving higher image resolution and lower signal latency.

items.stem: A car of mass 1320 kg moves at a constant speed of 19.7 m s⁻¹ around a flat circular track of radius 65 m. The coefficient of static friction between the tyres and the track is 0.82, and g = 9.8 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) a_c = v² / r = (19.7)² / 65 = 5.97 m s⁻². (b) Below the slipping limit, f_s = m a_c = 1320 × 5.97 = 7.88 × 10³ N. (c) Maximum speed without slipping v_max = √(μ_s g r) = 22.9 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies a_c = v² / r.
Obtains 5.97 m s⁻².
Multiplies mass by centripetal acceleration (rather than using limiting μ_s mg).
Obtains 7.88 × 10³ N.
Equates m v_max² / r to μ_s mg.
Obtains 22.9 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: An intermediate-energy X-ray photon (~0.6 MeV) interacts with body tissue by Compton scattering. What happens to the photon and the atomic electron?
items.workedSolution: In Compton scattering, the photon transfers part of its energy and momentum to eject an outer electron and leaves with lower energy (longer λ). Therefore the correct statement is: In Compton scattering an X-ray photon ejects an outer electron and continues as a lower-energy longer-wavelength scattered photon.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: in Compton scattering an X-ray photon ejects an outer electron and continues as a lower-energy longer-wavelength scattered photon.

options.label: C
options.text: The X-ray photon disappears completely and converts into an electron and positron pair near the nucleus.
options.distractorRationale: Describes pair production, which requires at least 1.02 MeV.

options.text: The X-ray photon is absorbed completely by an inner electron so no scattered photon emerges.
options.distractorRationale: Complete photon absorption describes the photoelectric effect, not Compton scattering.

items.stem: A comet orbits the Sun along the elliptical path shown. It sweeps out Area 1 near perihelion and an equal Area 2 near aphelion in equal time intervals $\Delta t$. Which statement correctly explains how its speed changes?
items.workedSolution: By Kepler's 2nd law and conservation of angular momentum (r₁v₁ = r₂v₂), smaller radius r₁ at perihelion means greater speed v₁. A planet therefore moves fastest at perihelion and slowest at aphelion as potential energy converts to kinetic energy.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct explanation: the planet moves fastest at perihelion and slowest at aphelion while conserving energy and angular momentum.

options.text: The comet moves slowest at perihelion because the Sun's stronger gravitational pull acts backwards to brake the comet.
options.distractorRationale: Closer to the Sun gravitational potential energy is lower, so kinetic energy and orbital speed are highest at perihelion.

options.label: B
options.text: A planet moves fastest at perihelion and slowest at aphelion as gravitational potential energy converts into kinetic energy while conserving angular momentum.

options.label: C
options.text: The comet moves at constant orbital speed all around the ellipse because no external work is done over a complete orbit.
options.distractorRationale: Speed is constant only in a circular orbit; in an elliptical orbit r₁v₁ = r₂v₂ requires higher speed at smaller r.

options.label: D
options.text: The comet sweeps out a larger area per second at aphelion because its radial distance r₂ is longer.
options.distractorRationale: Kepler's second law states that equal areas are swept in equal times throughout the orbit.

items.stem: Set g = 9.81 m s⁻² to calculate the circular speed of a 1.8 kg ball on a light 1.25 m cord. The cord makes 38° with the vertical during steady horizontal motion.
items.workedSolution: Circle radius is r = L sin θ = 1.25 sin 38° = 0.770 m. Since T sin θ = mv²/r and T cos θ = mg, v = √(g r tan θ) = √(9.81 × 0.770 × tan 38°) = 2.43 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses r = L sin θ and v = √(g L sin θ tan θ) to obtain 2.43 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: An exoplanet causes its host star to oscillate along our line of sight with a maximum speed of 85.0 m s⁻¹. Calculate the maximum Doppler shift in picometres of a sodium absorption line of rest wavelength 589 nm.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 0.167 pm.

items.stem: Astronomers measure an annual stellar parallax angle of $p = 0.080\text{ arc-second}$ for a nearby star. Use $1\text{ pc} = 3.26\text{ ly} = 3.09 \times 10^{16}\text{ m}$ and $1\text{ AU} = 1.50 \times 10^{11}\text{ m}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $d = 1 / 0.080 = 12.5 pc$. (b) $d = 12.5 \times 3.26 = 40.8 ly$. (c) $d = \frac{12.5 \times 3.09 \times 10^{16}}{1.50 \times 10^{11}} = 2.58 × 10⁶ AU$. (d) Parallax fails at huge distances because $p$ becomes immeasurably small; meanwhile, peak wavelength gives surface temperature while dark absorption lines reveal chemical composition.

Correct distance 2.58 × 10⁶ AU.

Explains peak wavelength gives surface temperature while dark absorption lines reveal chemical composition.

items.stem: According to the Big Bang model, the Universe began from a very hot, dense state. Since then, it has been expanding and cooling.
items.workedSolution: The Big Bang model is supported by the 2.7 K microwave background and the abundance of 75 percent hydrogen and 25 percent helium. Uniform $2.7\text{ K}$ black-body microwaves are high-energy photons from the early Universe that were stretched as space expanded and cooled. In addition, the observed $\approx 75\%$ hydrogen and $\approx 25\%$ helium mass ratio came from brief early fusion halted by rapid cooling. This is far more helium than stars alone could have made.

markScheme.criterion: L1: Identifies Cosmological Microwave Background Radiation (CMBR) as uniform microwave radiation arriving equally from all directions in the sky.
L1: States the observed primordial elemental composition is roughly 75% hydrogen and 25% helium by mass (about 3:1 by mass).
L2: Explains that CMBR corresponds to a ~2.7 K black-body spectrum originating as high-energy short-wavelength radiation in the hot, dense early Universe.
L2: Explains that expansion of space stretched (cosmologically redshifted) the radiation's wavelength into the microwave region as the Universe cooled.
L3: Explains that early nuclear fusion formed helium from protons and neutrons. Rapid expansion then cooled the Universe too much for further fusion.
L3: Links both observations to the Big Bang: stars alone cannot explain the high helium fraction. Uniform CMBR and Hubble expansion confirm a hot, expanding origin.

parts.prompt: Explain how the Cosmological Microwave Background Radiation (CMBR) and the primordial abundance of hydrogen and helium provide evidence for the Big Bang theory.
parts.expectedAnswer: Two independent pillars support the Big Bang model: cosmological microwave background stretched to 2.7 K plus 75 percent hydrogen and 25 percent helium abundance. High-energy short-wavelength gamma radiation filling the hot early Universe has been cosmologically redshifted by the expansion of space into uniform, isotropic 2.7 K black-body microwaves arriving from every direction. Meanwhile, during the brief hot early era, protons and neutrons fused into helium nuclei until expansion cooled the Universe below fusion temperatures, locking in roughly 75% hydrogen and 25% helium by mass (a 3:1 mass ratio) that stellar fusion alone cannot account for.
workingSteps: Identify CMBR as uniform black-body microwave radiation at ~2.7 K arriving equally from all directions in space.
Explain CMBR origin: high-energy short-wavelength radiation from the hot dense early Universe stretched (cosmologically redshifted) to microwaves as space expanded and cooled.
State the observed primordial element abundance: approximately 75% hydrogen and 25% helium by mass (~3:1 mass ratio / ~12:1 nuclear ratio).
Explain why early fusion gave this ratio: temperatures were high enough for hydrogen to fuse into helium. Rapid expansion then cooled the Universe and stopped further fusion.
Note that fusion inside stars cannot make as much helium as observed. This supports Big Bang nucleosynthesis alongside Hubble's recession law.

items.stem: A low-Earth-orbit satellite experiences a small continuous viscous drag force from the tenuous upper atmosphere. How do its total mechanical energy, orbital height, and orbital speed evolve over time?
items.workedSolution: Negative work by drag lowers E_tot = −GMm/(2r), so r decreases. Since v = √(GM/r), orbital speed and E_k increase while 2|ΔE_tot| of E_p is released. Atmospheric drag therefore reduces total mechanical energy, dropping the satellite to a lower height with greater speed.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct explanation: atmospheric drag reduces total mechanical energy, so the satellite drops lower and speeds up.

options.label: A
options.text: Atmospheric drag reduces total energy so the satellite climbs to a higher orbit where its orbital speed decreases.
options.distractorRationale: Lower total energy E_tot = −GMm/(2r) corresponds to a smaller (not larger) orbital radius r.

options.label: B
options.text: Atmospheric drag slows the satellite directly so both its orbital height and its orbital speed decrease continuously.
options.distractorRationale: As the satellite falls to smaller r, half the lost gravitational PE converts into kinetic energy, increasing v = √(GM/r).

options.label: C
options.text: Atmospheric drag leaves total mechanical energy constant while converting orbital kinetic energy into gravitational potential energy.
options.distractorRationale: Drag dissipates mechanical energy as thermal energy, making E_tot more negative while E_k actually rises.

options.label: D
options.text: Atmospheric viscous drag reduces total mechanical energy so the satellite drops to a lower orbital height where its orbital speed increases.

items.stem: Starting at the bottom with speed 10.3 m s⁻¹, a 360 kg roller-coaster car travels around a smooth vertical loop of radius 1.6 m. No friction or drag acts, and g = 9.8 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Equating total energy gives ½mv_bot² = ½mv_top² + mg(2R), v_top = √(v_bot² − 4gR) = 6.59 m s⁻¹. (b) Downward radial balance F_top + mg = mv_top²/R gives F_top = 6.23 × 10³ N. (c) Setting F_top = 0 gives v_top = √(gR) and v_bot,min = √(5gR) = 8.85 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies energy conservation with vertical rise Δh = 2R.
Obtains v_top = 6.59 m s⁻¹.
Uses F_top = m(v_top²/R − g) at the apex.
Obtains F_top = 6.23 × 10³ N.
Combines v_top,min² = gR with v_bot,min² = v_top,min² + 4gR.
Obtains v_bot,min = 8.85 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the speed of the car as it passes the highest point of the circle.
workingSteps: Conservation of mechanical energy with Δh = 2R gives v_top² = v_bot² − 4gR.

parts.prompt: Determine the magnitude of the normal contact force acting on the car at the highest point.
workingSteps: At the apex, F_top + mg = m v_top² / R.

parts.prompt: Calculate the minimum speed at the lowest point needed to complete the loop without losing contact at the top.
workingSteps: At threshold contact, v_top = √(gR), so v_bot,min = √(gR + 4gR) = √(5gR).

items.stem: Set b = 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K and σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴. A spherical black-body star 5.09 × 10¹⁶ m away gives 1.289 × 10⁻⁵ W m⁻² at Earth and peaks at λ_max = 400 nm.
items.workedSolution: (a) Wien's law gives T = 2.90 × 10⁻³ / (400 × 10⁻⁹) = 7.25 × 10³ K. (b) Inverse-square law gives L = 4π d² b_app = 4.20 × 10²⁹ W. (c) Stefan-Boltzmann law gives R = √[L/(4πσT⁴)] = 1.46 × 10¹⁰ m.

markScheme.criterion: Converts nm to m and applies T = b / λ_max.
Obtains T = 7.25 × 10³ K.
Applies L = 4π d² b_app.
Obtains L = 4.20 × 10²⁹ W.
Rearranges L = 4π R² σ T⁴ for R.
Obtains R = 1.46 × 10¹⁰ m.

items.stem: Measured across Earth's 1 AU baseline, a star of luminosity 3.24 × 10²⁹ W has annual parallax 0.326 arcsec. Note d / pc = 1 / (p / arcsec) (1 AU produces 1 arcsecond at 1 pc) and 1 pc = 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m.
items.workedSolution: (a) Using the parsec relation, d = 1 / 0.326 = 3.07 pc. (b) In SI units, d = 9.47 × 10¹⁶ m. (c) Apparent brightness b = L / (4π d²) = 2.88 × 10⁻⁶ W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Applies d(pc) = 1 / p(arcsec).
Obtains 3.07 pc.
Multiplies distance in parsecs by 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m pc⁻¹.
Obtains 9.47 × 10¹⁶ m.
Applies inverse-square law b = L / (4π d²).
Obtains 2.88 × 10⁻⁶ W m⁻².

items.stem: Around the smooth inner wall of a vertical track of radius 0.85 m, a small 1.6 kg ball moves at steady speed 3.87 m s⁻¹. Calculate the upward contact force at the bottom (g = 9.8 m s⁻²).
items.workedSolution: Resolving vertically at the bottom, upward normal contact force opposes downward weight mg to produce upward centripetal acceleration: F_bot − mg = m v² / R, giving F_bot = m(v²/R + g) = 1.6 × ((3.87)² / 0.85 + 9.8) = 43.9 N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses F_bot = m(v²/R + g) to obtain 43.9 N.

items.stem: The figure shows a conical pendulum with a light 1.8 m string tilted at 20° to the vertical. Its 0.75 kg sphere moves at steady speed in a horizontal circle. What is the period? (Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².)
items.workedSolution: Using T cos θ = mg and T sin θ = m ω² (L sin θ), ω = √(g / (L cos θ)). Thus the period is P = 2π√(L cos θ / g) = 2π√((1.8 cos 20°) / 9.8) = 2.61 s.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates 2π√(L cos 20° / g) to obtain 2.61 s.

items.stem: A spherical planet has mass 6.14 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 7.54 × 10⁶ m. A 1500 kg satellite climbs between circular orbits of radii 1.21 × 10⁷ m and 4.84 × 10⁷ m. Given G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², calculate the minimum energy input.

markScheme.criterion: Uses ΔE_tot = ½GMm(1/r₁ − 1/r₂) to obtain 1.90 × 10¹⁰ J.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Reverses initial and final radii, obtaining a negative energy requirement for raising the orbit.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates |E_tot(r₂)| alone instead of subtracting initial total energy E_tot(r₁) from E_tot(r₂).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the gain in gravitational potential energy ΔE_p = GMm(1/r₁ − 1/r₂) and forgets the virial reduction in kinetic energy (factor of 1/2).

items.stem: In a circular-motion experiment, a 0.794 kg mass on a light string traces a vertical circle (radius 2.33 m) at steady speed 7.65 m s⁻¹, with g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) At the top limit, v_min = √(gR) = 4.78 m s⁻¹. (b) At the top, F_top = m(v²/R − g) = 12.2 N. (c) At the bottom, F_bot = m(v²/R + g) = 27.7 N.

markScheme.criterion: Sets support force to zero at apex so mg = m v_min² / R.
Obtains 4.78 m s⁻¹.
Subtracts mg from m v² / R at the top.
Obtains 12.2 N.
Adds mg to m v² / R at the bottom.
Obtains 27.7 N.

items.stem: A light string guides a small 1.2 kg ball in a vertical circle of radius 0.45 m. Its speed at the base is 6.01 m s⁻¹, with zero air resistance and g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Energy conservation gives ½mv_bot² = ½mv_top² + mg(2R), v_top = √(v_bot² − 4gR) = 4.30 m s⁻¹. (b) Downward radial balance F_top + mg = mv_top²/R gives F_top = 37.5 N. (c) Setting F_top = 0 gives v_top = √(gR) and v_bot,min = √(5gR) = 4.70 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies energy conservation with vertical rise Δh = 2R.
Obtains v_top = 4.30 m s⁻¹.
Uses F_top = m(v_top²/R − g) at the apex.
Obtains F_top = 37.5 N.
Combines v_top,min² = gR with v_bot,min² = v_top,min² + 4gR.
Obtains v_bot,min = 4.70 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Refer to the plot for airless spheres Primary (mass 4.18 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 5.41 × 10⁶ m) and Exomoon (mass 4.64 × 10²³ kg, radius 1.57 × 10⁶ m), with centres 3.35 × 10⁸ m apart. Using G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻² and zero potential at infinity, state the total potential at the zero-field peak.
items.workedSolution: At the null point x₀ = d√M₁/(√M₁ + √M₂) = 2.51 × 10⁸ m, scalar potentials add negatively: V_g(x₀) = −GM₁/x₀ − GM₂/(d − x₀) = −(G/d)(√M₁ + √M₂)² = -1.48 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Sums both negative scalar potentials at x₀ to obtain -1.48 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹.

items.stem: A spherical planet of uniform density has mass 3.47 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 9.1 × 10⁶ m. A small probe of mass 508 kg is lowered into a narrow shaft inside the planet to a distance of 2.28 × 10⁶ m from the centre, with G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Surface field g₀ = GM/R² = 2.79 N kg⁻¹. (b) At r = 2.28 × 10⁶ m, uniform-sphere interior scaling g = g₀(r/R) gives 0.700 N kg⁻¹. (c) Force on probe F = mg = 356 N.

items.stem: At distance 2.94 × 10⁷ m from the centre of a non-rotating, airless planet (4.18 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 1.4 × 10⁷ m), a 350 kg spacecraft is at rest. Assume G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) From the surface radius, V_surface = −GM/R = -1.99 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹. (b) Escape speed v_esc = √(−2 V_surface) = √(2GM/R) = 6.31 × 10³ m s⁻¹. (c) At r = 2.94 × 10⁷ m, E_p = −GMm/r = -3.32 × 10⁹ J.

markScheme.criterion: Applies V_g = −GM / R with negative sign.
Obtains -1.99 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹.
Uses v_esc = √(2GM / R) or √(−2 V_surface).
Obtains 6.31 × 10³ m s⁻¹.
Applies E_p = −GMm / r at probe radius.
Obtains -3.32 × 10⁹ J.

items.stem: With 3.66 × 10⁸ m between their centres, Ice Giant has radius 5.41 × 10⁶ m and mass 5.36 × 10²⁴ kg, and Retrograde Moon has radius 1.57 × 10⁶ m and mass 6.62 × 10²² kg. Calculate how far from Ice Giant's centre the net field is zero.
items.workedSolution: Balancing both opposing gravitational fields, G M₁ / x₀² = G M₂ / (d − x₀)² gives (d − x₀)/x₀ = √(M₂/M₁), so x₀ = [√M₁ / (√M₁ + √M₂)] d = 3.29 × 10⁸ m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses x₀ = d √M₁ / (√M₁ + √M₂) to obtain 3.29 × 10⁸ m.

items.stem: A smooth track of radius 145 m slopes at 25° to the horizontal with no sideways friction. Travelling horizontally around it is a 320 kg trolley. Calculate the normal reaction force (g = 9.81 m s⁻²).
items.workedSolution: Since vertical acceleration is zero, N cos θ = mg, so N = (320 × 9.81) / cos 25° = 3.46 × 10³ N.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves vertically N cos 25° = mg to obtain N = 3.46 × 10³ N.

items.stem: Astronomers observe a calcium absorption line in the spectrum of a distant galaxy, where its rest wavelength of 393.4 nm is shifted to 400.76 nm. Take the speed of light as c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and the Hubble constant as H₀ = 73.5 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) z = (λ_obs − λ₀)/λ₀ = 0.0187. (b) Recession speed v ≈ zc = 5.61 × 10³ km s⁻¹. (c) Hubble distance d = v/H₀ = 76.4 Mpc.

markScheme.criterion: Applies z = Δλ / λ₀.
Obtains z = 0.0187.
Multiplies z by c and converts to km s⁻¹.
Obtains v = 5.61 × 10³ km s⁻¹.
Applies d = v / H₀.
Obtains d = 76.4 Mpc.

items.stem: A spacecraft of mass 1490 kg moves in a circular orbit of radius r = 3.186 × 10⁷ m around the centre of a spherical planet. The planet has mass 2.34 × 10²⁵ kg and radius 7.76 × 10⁶ m. Taking G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², calculate the circular orbital speed of the spacecraft.
items.workedSolution: Equating GMm / r² = mv² / r gives v = √(GM / r) = √(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 2.34 × 10²⁵ / 3.186 × 10⁷) = 7.00 × 10³ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses r = 3.186 × 10⁷ m to obtain 7.00 × 10³ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Around a spherical planet (radius 6.74 × 10⁶ m, mass 3.16 × 10²⁴ kg), a 1390 kg spacecraft orbits in a circle of radius 1.01 × 10⁷ m. Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻² and zero potential energy at infinity.
items.workedSolution: (a) E_k = GMm/(2r) = 1.45 × 10¹⁰ J. (b) E_p = −GMm/r = -2.90 × 10¹⁰ J. (c) Total mechanical energy E_tot = E_k + E_p = −GMm/(2r) = -1.45 × 10¹⁰ J.

markScheme.criterion: Applies E_k = GMm / (2r).
Obtains E_k = 1.45 × 10¹⁰ J.
Applies E_p = −GMm / r including negative sign.
Obtains E_p = -2.90 × 10¹⁰ J.
Sums E_k + E_p or applies E_tot = −GMm / (2r).
Obtains E_tot = -1.45 × 10¹⁰ J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the kinetic energy of the spacecraft in this circular orbit.
workingSteps: From m v² / r = G M m / r², E_k = ½ m v² = G M m / (2r).

parts.prompt: Calculate the gravitational potential energy of the spacecraft.
Determine the total mechanical energy of the spacecraft.
workingSteps: E_tot = E_k + E_p = −G M m / (2r) = -1.45 × 10¹⁰ J.

items.stem: A Hertzsprung–Russell diagram shows four stars with region names removed, including Star Delta at surface temperature 4400 K and luminosity 35000 L☉. Use solar values L☉ = 3.83 × 10²⁶ W, R☉ = 6.96 × 10⁸ m, and σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.
items.workedSolution: (a) Star Delta lies in the supergiant region. (b) L = 35000 × 3.83 × 10²⁶ = 1.34 × 10³¹ W. (c) R = √[L/(4πσT⁴)] = 2.24 × 10¹¹ m = 322 R☉.

markScheme.criterion: States supergiant.
Multiplies L / L☉ by 3.83 × 10²⁶ W.
Obtains L = 1.34 × 10³¹ W.
Applies R = √[L / (4π σ T⁴)] and divides by R☉.
Obtains 322 R☉.

items.stem: A single satellite in a polar orbit can photograph every landmass on Earth within a day without firing sideways thrusters. How is this possible?
items.workedSolution: Earth turns beneath the fixed orbital plane of the polar low-Earth satellite. It therefore sweeps the entire Earth surface, giving higher image resolution and lower signal latency.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct explanation: a polar low-Earth orbit scans the whole Earth as Earth rotates, giving higher image resolution and lower signal latency.

items.stem: A car of mass 1650 kg travels at a constant speed of 14.6 m s⁻¹ around a flat circular track of radius 105 m without slipping. The coefficient of static friction is μ_s = 0.36, and g = 9.8 m s⁻². Calculate the sideways static frictional force acting on the tyres.
items.workedSolution: Because 14.6 m s⁻¹ is below the slipping limit v_max = √(μ_s g r) = 19.2 m s⁻¹, static friction self-adjusts to match the required centripetal force: f_s = m v² / r = 1650 × (14.6)² / 105 = 3.35 × 10³ N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses f_s = m v² / r (not μ_s mg) to obtain 3.35 × 10³ N.

items.stem: Patients having diagnostic X-ray imaging of the digestive tract often swallow a barium sulfate meal ($Z = 56$). Why does barium greatly improve soft-tissue image contrast at diagnostic energies (~50 keV)?
items.workedSolution: At diagnostic energies (~20–100 keV), photoelectric absorption dominates with μ ∝ Z³. High-Z barium or iodine therefore absorbs strongly and casts a sharp X-ray shadow, outlining soft-tissue structures.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct explanation: barium and iodine have high atomic numbers, so photoelectric attenuation scales as Z cubed and gives sharp contrast.

options.distractorRationale: Barium (Z = 56) has a far higher atomic number than soft tissue (Z ≈ 7) and absorbs strongly.

options.text: At 50 keV barium triggers intense electron-positron pair production which blocks the X-ray beam.
options.distractorRationale: Pair production requires photon energy at least 1.02 MeV and cannot occur at 50 keV.

options.label: D
options.text: Barium and iodine contrast media have high atomic numbers so photoelectric attenuation scales as Z cubed and sharply outlines soft-tissue structures.

items.stem: Modern Big Bang cosmology builds upon the Cosmological Principle. Which statement accurately defines the Cosmological Principle?
items.workedSolution: Homogeneous means the same large-scale average density everywhere, and isotropic means it looks the same in every direction, with universal physical laws. The Cosmological Principle applies on sufficiently large scales.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct definition: on large scales, the universe is homogeneous and isotropic with universal physical laws.

options.label: A
options.text: The universe has a unique central galaxy from which matter density drops smoothly to zero at a physical boundary edge.
options.distractorRationale: Homogeneity and isotropy imply no privileged centre and no physical edge.

options.label: B
options.text: Homogeneous means looking identical in all directions while isotropic means having the same chemical elements in every planet.
options.distractorRationale: Swaps homogeneous (uniform average density everywhere) and isotropic (same in all viewing directions).

options.label: C
options.text: On sufficiently large scales the universe is homogeneous with uniform average density everywhere and isotropic looking the same in all directions with universal physical laws.

options.label: D
options.text: The universe is strictly static in time so the average distance between galaxy clusters never changes.
options.distractorRationale: The Cosmological Principle applies spatially at a given cosmic epoch; it does not forbid cosmic expansion.

items.stem: A student sets a 0.45 kg bob moving in a horizontal circle on a light 3.2 m string. At constant speed, the string holds 42° to the vertical, with g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Balancing weight vertically, T cos 42° = (0.45)(9.81) gives T = 5.94 N. (b) Horizontal radius r = 3.2 sin 42° = 2.14 m; horizontal dynamics T sin θ = mv²/r yields v = 4.35 m s⁻¹. (c) Period P = 2πr / v = 3.09 s.

markScheme.criterion: Equates vertical component T cos θ to weight mg.
Obtains tension 5.94 N.
Uses r = L sin θ and equates T sin θ (or mg tan θ) to m v² / r.
Obtains speed 4.35 m s⁻¹.
Applies P = 2π r / v or P = 2π√(L cos θ / g).
Obtains period 3.09 s.

items.stem: Quasars were first detected as star-like radio sources in the mid-twentieth century. Their optical spectra puzzled astronomers until hydrogen lines were recognised at very large redshifts.
items.workedSolution: Level 3 synthesis: a large cosmological redshift shows a huge distance, and the inverse-square law then proves vast power output. Rapid brightness variations limit the source size via $c\Delta t$ to roughly the size of the Solar System. Matter accreting onto a supermassive black hole in an active galactic nucleus powers this emission.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies large cosmological redshift of quasar spectral lines and links this via Hubble's law to immense distance.
Deduces extreme luminosity / power output (exceeding entire galaxies) using observed brightness and the inverse-square law.
Explains that rapid intensity variations imply a compact emitting region roughly the size of the Solar System (limited by speed $c$).
Identifies the central engine as a supermassive black hole at the centre of an active galaxy.
Explains that infalling matter forms a hot accretion disc converting gravitational potential energy into radiation across the EM spectrum.
Links quasar abundance at high redshift to early-Universe galaxy interactions supplying ample gas to the central black hole.

parts.prompt: Describe the key observed properties of quasars and explain how astronomers find their distances, power outputs, and compact sizes. Outline the mechanism thought to power them.
parts.expectedAnswer: Astronomers deduce that large cosmological redshift implies immense distance and vast luminosity from a compact solar system sized active galactic nucleus. First, optical spectra show enormous cosmological redshifts ($z$ often exceeding $1$), which via Hubble's law indicate distances of billions of light-years—meaning we observe quasars in the early Universe. Second, despite these immense distances, quasars are easily detectable across radio to X-ray bands; applying the inverse-square law reveals luminosities thousands of times greater than an entire normal galaxy. Third, their brightness fluctuates noticeably over days or weeks; since no causal signal can cross a source faster than $c$, the emitting region must be no larger than a few light-days across (comparable to the Solar System). The only mechanism capable of producing such huge power in such a compact volume is gravitational energy released as gas spirals into an accretion disc around a supermassive black hole at the core of a young, often merging active galaxy, driving intense thermal radiation and relativistic bipolar jets.
workingSteps: State quasars appear point-like with strong broad-spectrum emission and very large cosmological redshifts.
Link huge redshift via Hubble's law to immense cosmological distances and early cosmic epochs.
Apply inverse-square law to deduce extreme power output surpassing entire galaxies.
Use rapid variability timescales and finite speed of light $c$ to infer solar-system-scale compact emitting size.
Identify supermassive black hole accretion disc as the gravitational energy source.
Note feeding via abundant gas in early-Universe galaxy collisions and relativistic jets.

items.stem: A spectroscopic binary star system is viewed edge-on in its orbital plane. The $\text{H}\alpha$ line (rest wavelength $656.3\text{ nm}$) shifts periodically by up to $\pm 0.220\text{ nm}$ about its mean position. Calculate the orbital speed of the star in $\text{km s}^{-1}$.
items.workedSolution: From $\frac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda} = \frac{v}{c}$, $v = \frac{0.220}{656.3} \times 3.00 \times 10^8 = 1.01 \times 10^5\text{ m s}^{-1} = 101 km s⁻¹$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 101 km s⁻¹.

items.stem: A $600\text{ kg}$ probe is launched from rest on a non-rotating planet of mass $M = 4.87 \times 10^{24}\text{ kg}$ and radius $R = 6050\text{ km}$. It enters a circular orbit at altitude $h = 950\text{ km}$ ($r = 7000\text{ km}$, $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\text{ N m}^2\text{ kg}^{-2}$).
items.workedSolution: (a) $E_{\text{surface}} = −32.2 GJ$. (b) $E_{\text{orbit}} = −13.9 GJ$. (c) $\Delta E_{\text{launch}} = 18.3 GJ$. (d) Escape from orbit requires $13.9 GJ$. Launching from rest on a non-rotating planet into circular orbit must supply both the gain in gravitational potential energy and the orbital kinetic energy.

markScheme.criterion: Applies E_p = −GMm/R with negative sign.
Obtains E_surface = −32.2 GJ.
Applies circular orbit total energy E_orbit = −GMm/(2r) with r = R + h = 7000 km.
Obtains E_orbit = −13.9 GJ.
Computes ΔE = E_orbit − E_surface.
Obtains minimum launch energy 18.3 GJ.
Sets total energy at infinity to zero: ΔE_esc = 0 − E_orbit.
Obtains escape energy from orbit 13.9 GJ.
Explains that launch supplies ΔE_p plus orbital E_k: both the gain in gravitational potential energy and the orbital kinetic energy.

parts.expectedAnswer: Extra energy to escape is 13.9 GJ; launching from rest on a non-rotating planet surface into circular orbit requires supplying both the gain in gravitational potential energy and the orbital kinetic energy.

items.stem: In a loop-the-loop trial on a smooth vertical track of radius 6.5 m with no friction or drag, a small 0.8 kg ball enters at 21.8 m s⁻¹. Using g = 9.8 m s⁻², find the minimum base speed to keep contact at the top.
items.workedSolution: At the top contact limit, v_top ≥ √(gR). Conservation of energy from bottom to top (Δh = 2R) gives ½m v_bot,min² = ½m(gR) + mg(2R) => v_bot,min = √(5gR) = √(5 × 9.8 × 6.5) = 17.8 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates v_bot,min = √(5gR) = 17.8 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A black-body sphere of temperature 9600 K and radius 3.83 × 10⁹ m sits 2.41 × 10¹⁶ m from Earth. Taking σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴, work out its apparent brightness at Earth.
items.workedSolution: By the Stefan-Boltzmann law, L = 4π R² σ T⁴ = 4π(3.83 × 10⁹)²(5.67 × 10⁻⁸)(9600)⁴ = 8.88 × 10²⁸ W. Apparent brightness b = L / (4π d²) = σ T⁴ (R / d)² = 1.22 × 10⁻⁵ W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses L = 4πR²σT⁴ and b = L / (4πd²) to obtain 1.22 × 10⁻⁵ W m⁻².

items.stem: Use 1 pc = 3.26 ly and d / pc = 1 / (p / arcsec), as a 1 AU baseline produces 1 arcsecond at 1 pc. Over Earth's 1 AU orbit, a 9.96 × 10²⁹ W star has parallax angle 0.38 arcsec. Calculate its distance in light-years.
items.workedSolution: In parsecs, d = 1 / p = 1 / 0.38 = 2.63 pc. Converting to light-years gives d = 2.63 × 3.26 = 8.58 ly.

items.stem: Star A has surface temperature $9000\text{ K}$ and radius $2.00 R_{\odot}$, whereas Star B has surface temperature $4500\text{ K}$ and radius $1.00 R_{\odot}$. Treating both stars as spherical black bodies ($P = \sigma A T^4$), calculate the power output ratio $P_{\text{A}} / P_{\text{B}}$.
items.workedSolution: From $P = 4\pi R^2 \sigma T^4$, $\frac{P_{\text{A}}}{P_{\text{B}}} = \left(\frac{2.00}{1.00}\right)^2 \left(\frac{9000}{4500}\right)^4 = 4 \times 16 = 64.0$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 64.0.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses linear radius ratio $R_{\text{A}}/R_{\text{B}}$ instead of surface-area ratio $(R_{\text{A}}/R_{\text{B}})^2$.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits the fourth power on the temperature ratio.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Accounts for $T^4$ but neglects the difference in stellar radii.

items.stem: In the loop diagram, a small ball of mass 3.5 kg glides at steady speed 3.38 m s⁻¹ inside a smooth vertical track (radius 0.65 m). With g = 9.8 m s⁻², what upward normal force acts at the base?
items.workedSolution: Resolving vertically at the bottom, upward normal contact force opposes downward weight mg to produce upward centripetal acceleration: F_bot − mg = m v² / R, giving F_bot = m(v²/R + g) = 3.5 × ((3.38)² / 0.65 + 9.8) = 95.8 N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses F_bot = m(v²/R + g) to obtain 95.8 N.

items.stem: Suspended from a light 0.95 m cord, a 0.75 kg sphere traces a horizontal circle at steady speed. The cord makes 24° with the vertical, and g = 9.8 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Vertical force balance gives T cos 24° = (0.75)(9.8) gives T = 8.05 N. (b) Horizontal radius r = 0.95 sin 24° = 0.386 m; horizontal dynamics T sin θ = mv²/r yields v = 1.30 m s⁻¹. (c) Period P = 2πr / v = 1.87 s.

markScheme.criterion: Equates vertical component T cos θ to weight mg.
Obtains tension 8.05 N.
Uses r = L sin θ and equates T sin θ (or mg tan θ) to m v² / r.
Obtains speed 1.30 m s⁻¹.
Applies P = 2π r / v or P = 2π√(L cos θ / g).
Obtains period 1.87 s.

parts.prompt: Calculate the tension in the cord supporting the sphere.
workingSteps: Vertical force balance gives T cos θ = mg.

parts.prompt: Determine the linear speed of the sphere along its horizontal circular path.
workingSteps: Horizontal radius r = L sin θ = 0.95 sin 24° = 0.386 m.
From T sin θ = m v² / r, v = √(g r tan θ) = 1.30 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the time period for one complete revolution of the sphere.

items.stem: Consider an 8.53 × 10²⁴ kg spherical planet of radius 9.0 × 10⁶ m. Mission control shifts a 1540 kg spacecraft from circular orbit r₁ = 1.98 × 10⁷ m to r₂ = 7.92 × 10⁷ m. Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Inner total energy: E_tot(r₁) = −GMm/(2r₁) = -2.21 × 10¹⁰ J. (b) Final bound energy E_tot(r₂) = -5.53 × 10⁹ J, so ΔE_tot = 1.66 × 10¹⁰ J. (c) Outer orbital period T₂ = 2π√(r₂³/GM) = 1.86 × 10⁵ s.

markScheme.criterion: Applies E_tot = −GMm / (2r₁).
Obtains -2.21 × 10¹⁰ J.
Evaluates E_tot(r₂) − E_tot(r₁) = ½GMm(1/r₁ − 1/r₂).
Obtains 1.66 × 10¹⁰ J.
Applies Kepler's third law at outer radius r₂.
Obtains 1.86 × 10⁵ s.

items.stem: Over a curved bridge of radius 44 m, a 1350 kg car travels at steady speed 17.9 m s⁻¹. What normal contact force acts on the car at the highest point? (Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².)
items.workedSolution: Over the top of the bridge, downward resultant force is mg − N_top = m v² / R, so N_top = m(g − v²/R) = 1350 × (9.81 − (17.9)² / 44) = 3.41 × 10³ N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies radial force equation at apex to obtain 3.41 × 10³ N.

items.stem: Tied to a light string of length 9 m, a small 0.2 kg ball swings through the lowest point at 25.6 m s⁻¹. Ignore air resistance. Using g = 9.81 m s⁻², work out its speed at the highest point.
items.workedSolution: From bottom to top, height rises by Δh = 2R. By conservation of energy, ½m v_top² + mg(2R) = ½m v_bot², so v_top = √(v_bot² − 4gR) = √((25.6)² − 4 × 9.81 × 9) = 17.4 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses Δh = 2R in v_top = √(v_bot² − 4gR) to obtain 17.4 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Two airless worlds, Body Alpha and Body Beta, are 3.95 × 10⁸ m apart centre to centre. Their masses are 5.83 × 10²⁴ kg and 3.64 × 10²³ kg, with radii 6.37 × 10⁶ m and 1.83 × 10⁶ m. Take zero potential at infinity (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²).
items.workedSolution: (a) Null point distance x₀ = d√M₁/(√M₁ + √M₂) = 3.16 × 10⁸ m. (b) Combined scalar potential V(x₀) = -1.54 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. (c) Potential barrier from x = R₁ to x₀ is ΔV = 5.96 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹, giving v_min = √(2ΔV) = 1.09 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies x₀ = d√M₁ / (√M₁ + √M₂).
Obtains x₀ = 3.16 × 10⁸ m.
Sums both negative scalar potentials −GM₁/x₀ − GM₂/(d − x₀).
Obtains V(x₀) = -1.54 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹.
Equates ½v_min² to potential barrier V(x₀) − V(R₁).
Obtains v_min = 1.09 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A spherical planet of uniform density has mass 7.58 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 1.08 × 10⁷ m. A small probe of mass 1010 kg is lowered into a narrow shaft inside the planet to r = 7.02 × 10⁶ m from the centre. Taking G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², determine the gravitational field strength g(r) at this point.
items.workedSolution: Inside a uniform sphere (r < R), enclosed mass M_enc = M(r/R)³, so g(r) = G M r / R³ = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 7.58 × 10²⁴ × 7.02 × 10⁶) / (1.08 × 10⁷)³ = 2.82 N kg⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates gravitational field strength at r = 7.02 × 10⁶ m to obtain 2.82 N kg⁻¹.

items.stem: Consider a 360 kg probe held 1.51 × 10⁷ m from the centre of a 2.77 × 10²⁴ kg planet (radius 7.21 × 10⁶ m). Set zero potential at infinity, with G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². What is the potential V_g at the probe's location?
items.workedSolution: Using the radial potential formula, V_g = −G M / r = −(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 2.77 × 10²⁴) / 1.51 × 10⁷ = -1.22 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Computes V_g = −GM / r = -1.22 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹ including the negative sign.

items.stem: The diagram shows Primary Asteroid (mass 3.58 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 5.41 × 10⁶ m) and Secondary Moonlet (mass 5.03 × 10²³ kg, radius 1.57 × 10⁶ m) with centres 7.1 × 10⁸ m apart. Along the line between them, a 412 kg spacecraft passes 3.91 × 10⁸ m from Primary Asteroid's centre. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Balancing GM₁/x₀² = GM₂/(d − x₀)² yields x₀ = d√M₁/(√M₁ + √M₂) = 5.16 × 10⁸ m. (b) At x = 3.91 × 10⁸ m, |g| = |GM₁/x² − GM₂/(d − x)²| = 0.00123 N kg⁻¹. (c) Net force F = m|g| = 0.508 N.

markScheme.criterion: Equates opposing inverse-square field strengths GM₁/x₀² = GM₂/(d − x₀)².
Takes square root correctly to form x₀ = d√M₁ / (√M₁ + √M₂).
Obtains x₀ = 5.16 × 10⁸ m.
Subtracts opposing field magnitudes at x and (d − x).
Obtains |g| = 0.00123 N kg⁻¹.
Multiplies by spacecraft mass to obtain 0.508 N.

items.stem: In a circular-motion study, a 1750 kg car moves horizontally around a smooth road of radius 58 m banked at 25° with zero sideways friction (g = 9.81 m s⁻²).
items.workedSolution: (a) Balancing vertical forces gives N cos 25° = mg gives N = 1.89 × 10⁴ N. (b) Horizontal component F_c = N sin 25° = 8.01 × 10³ N. (c) Setting m v² / r = F_c yields v_ideal = 16.3 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses N cos θ = mg (zero vertical acceleration).
Obtains N = 1.89 × 10⁴ N.
Evaluates F_c = N sin θ or mg tan θ.
Obtains F_c = 8.01 × 10³ N.
Equates m v² / r to F_c and solves for v.
Obtains v_ideal = 16.3 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the magnitude of the normal contact force on the car.
workingSteps: Vertical equilibrium gives N cos θ = mg.

parts.prompt: Determine the horizontal centripetal force acting toward the centre of the circle.
workingSteps: Horizontal component of normal reaction provides the centripetal force: F_c = N sin θ = mg tan θ.

parts.prompt: Hence calculate the ideal frictionless speed of the car.
workingSteps: From m v² / r = F_c, v = √(F_c r / m) = √(g r tan θ) = 16.3 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: In the spectrum of a distant galaxy, a helium spectral line (rest wavelength 587.6 nm) is observed at 598.18 nm. Taking c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and H₀ = 72 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹, calculate the distance to the galaxy in Mpc.
items.workedSolution: Redshift z = (λ_obs − λ₀) / λ₀ = (598.18 − 587.6) / 587.6 = 0.0180. Recession speed v ≈ z c = 5.40 × 10³ km s⁻¹. From Hubble's law v = H₀ d, d = v / H₀ = 5.40 × 10³ / 72 = 75.0 Mpc.

markScheme.criterion: Finds z = 0.0180, v = 5.40 × 10³ km s⁻¹, and d = v / H₀ = 75.0 Mpc.

items.stem: What unexpected observational discovery from high-redshift Type Ia supernovae led cosmologists to propose the existence of dark energy?
items.workedSolution: Comparing Type Ia luminosity distances with redshifts showed that distant type Ia supernovae are dimmer than predicted indicating accelerating expansion driven by dark energy.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that distant type Ia supernovae are dimmer than predicted indicating accelerating expansion driven by dark energy.

items.stem: A spacecraft of mass 226 kg orbits a spherical planet in a circular path at altitude h = 1.84 × 10⁶ m above the surface. The planet has mass 3.68 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 5.25 × 10⁶ m, with G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) With orbital radius r = 7.09 × 10⁶ m, g = GM/r² = 4.88 N kg⁻¹. (b) Orbital speed v = √(GM/r) = 5.88 × 10³ m s⁻¹. (c) Period T = 2πr/v = 7.57 × 10³ s.

markScheme.criterion: Uses centre-to-centre orbital radius r in g = GM / r².
Obtains g = 4.88 N kg⁻¹.
Equates v²/r to g (or GM/r²).
Obtains v = 5.88 × 10³ m s⁻¹.
Applies T = 2πr / v or Kepler's third law.
Obtains T = 7.57 × 10³ s.

Determine the circular orbital speed of the spacecraft.
workingSteps: Setting centripetal acceleration v² / r = g gives v = √(g r) = √(G M / r).

items.stem: At orbital radius 1.77 × 10⁷ m around a planet of mass 1.49 × 10²⁵ kg and radius 4.92 × 10⁶ m, a 1100 kg spacecraft circles steadily. What is the escape speed from this orbit? Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: Escaping from radial distance r needs ½m v_esc² − GMm/r = 0, so v_esc = √(2GM / r) = √(2 × 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 1.49 × 10²⁵ / 1.77 × 10⁷) = 1.06 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates v_esc = √(2GM / r) = 1.06 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates circular orbital speed √(GM / r) and omits the √2 factor needed to escape from orbit.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies circular orbital speed by 2 instead of √2.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates escape speed from the planet's surface R_p rather than from the satellite's orbital radius r.

items.stem: On a Hertzsprung–Russell diagram, Star Kappa has surface temperature 3600 K and luminosity 320 L☉. Taking L☉ = 3.83 × 10²⁶ W, R☉ = 6.96 × 10⁸ m, and σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴, determine the radius of the star in solar radii (R☉).
items.workedSolution: Luminosity L = 320 × 3.83 × 10²⁶ = 1.23 × 10²⁹ W. From L = 4π R² σ T⁴, R = √[L / (4π σ T⁴)] = 3.20 × 10¹⁰ m, so R / R☉ = R / (6.96 × 10⁸) = 46.0 R☉.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Stefan-Boltzmann scaling to obtain 46.0 R☉.

items.stem: A cart of mass 140 kg moves at a constant speed of 6.23 m s⁻¹ around a flat circular track of radius 28 m. The coefficient of static friction between the tyres and the track is 0.42, and g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) a_c = v² / r = (6.23)² / 28 = 1.39 m s⁻². (b) Below the slipping limit, f_s = m a_c = 140 × 1.39 = 194 N. (c) Maximum speed without slipping v_max = √(μ_s g r) = 10.7 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies a_c = v² / r.
Obtains 1.39 m s⁻².
Multiplies mass by centripetal acceleration (rather than using limiting μ_s mg).
Obtains 194 N.
Equates m v_max² / r to μ_s mg.
Obtains 10.7 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A car of mass 480 kg moves at a constant speed of 22.9 m s⁻¹ around a flat circular track of radius 125 m. The coefficient of static friction between the tyres and the track is 0.74, and g = 9.8 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) a_c = v² / r = (22.9)² / 125 = 4.20 m s⁻². (b) Below the slipping limit, f_s = m a_c = 480 × 4.20 = 2.01 × 10³ N. (c) Maximum speed without slipping v_max = √(μ_s g r) = 30.1 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies a_c = v² / r.
Obtains 4.20 m s⁻².
Multiplies mass by centripetal acceleration (rather than using limiting μ_s mg).
Obtains 2.01 × 10³ N.
Equates m v_max² / r to μ_s mg.
Obtains 30.1 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: What centripetal acceleration acts on a 0.85 kg bob tracing a steady horizontal circle on a light 2.4 m cord at 42° from vertical? Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: Dividing horizontal Newton's second law T sin θ = m a_c by vertical equilibrium T cos θ = mg gives a_c = g tan θ = 9.81 × tan 42° = 8.83 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Applies a_c = g tan 42° to obtain 8.83 m s⁻².

items.stem: What astrophysical engine is widely accepted as powering the immense electromagnetic output of a quasar?
items.workedSolution: Quasars are powered by gravitational energy released by a supermassive black hole accreting matter at the centre of a distant active galaxy.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that supermassive black hole accreting matter at the centre of a distant active galaxy.

items.stem: A Sun-like star ($1\,M_{\odot}$) leaves the main sequence and becomes a red giant. Its surface temperature falls to $3500\text{ K}$ while its luminosity rises to $160\,L_{\odot}$ ($6.13 \times 10^{28}\text{ W}$).
items.workedSolution: (a) $\lambda_{\max} = \frac{2.90 \times 10^{-3}}{3500} = 829 nm$. (b) $R / R_{\odot} = 34.4 R⊙$. (c) A Sun-like star moves up-right from the main sequence to the red giant region as its outer layers expand and cool. It later sheds a planetary nebula, leaving a hot, tiny white dwarf.

markScheme.criterion: Applies $\lambda_{\max} = 2.90 \times 10^{-3} / 3500$.
Correct peak wavelength 829 nm.
Computes $R$ from $L = 4\pi R^2 \sigma T^4$ and divides by $R_{\odot}$.
Correct radius ratio 34.4 R⊙.
Describes sequence: main sequence to red giant then planetary nebula leaving a white dwarf.
Links core contraction and envelope expansion to movement up-right on HR diagram.
Identifies exposed hot dense white dwarf in the bottom-left region.

parts.prompt: Calculate the peak black-body emission wavelength $\lambda_{\max}$ of the star during its red giant phase.
Calculate the radius of the star in this red giant phase as a multiple of $R_{\odot} = 6.96 \times 10^8\text{ m}$.
workingSteps: Divide by $6.96 \times 10^8\text{ m}$ to obtain 34.4 R⊙.

parts.prompt: Describe the complete post-main-sequence evolutionary path of this low-mass star on the HR diagram, including its final remnant.
parts.expectedAnswer: The star evolves from the main sequence to red giant then planetary nebula leaving a white dwarf. As core hydrogen is exhausted, the core contracts while outer layers expand and cool (moving up and right); after helium burning ends, outer layers are ejected as a planetary nebula exposing the hot, small, dense white dwarf in the bottom-left.
workingSteps: State the full sequence: main sequence to red giant then planetary nebula leaving a white dwarf.
Explain expansion and cooling into upper-right red giant region.
Explain ejection of planetary nebula leaving a hot, low-luminosity white dwarf cooling slowly.

items.stem: A radio telescope monitors the $1420\text{ MHz}$ neutral-hydrogen emission line from a gas cloud moving radially at $180\text{ km s}^{-1}$ relative to Earth. Using $\frac{\Delta f}{f} = \frac{v}{c}$, calculate the magnitude of the frequency shift $\Delta f$ in kHz.
items.workedSolution: $\Delta f = \frac{v}{c} f = \frac{1.80 \times 10^5}{3.00 \times 10^8} \times 1420 \times 10^3\text{ kHz} = 852 kHz$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 852 kHz.

items.stem: An asteroid orbits the Sun in an ellipse with perihelion distance $r_{\text{p}} = 0.600\text{ AU}$ and aphelion distance $r_{\text{a}} = 1.80\text{ AU}$. Using Kepler's second law, calculate the speed ratio $v_{\text{p}} / v_{\text{a}}$ between perihelion and aphelion.
items.workedSolution: Equal areas in small time $\Delta t$ give $\frac{1}{2}r_{\text{p}}(v_{\text{p}}\Delta t) = \frac{1}{2}r_{\text{a}}(v_{\text{a}}\Delta t)$, so $\frac{v_{\text{p}}}{v_{\text{a}}} = \frac{r_{\text{a}}}{r_{\text{p}}} = \frac{1.80}{0.600} = 3.00$.

markScheme.criterion: Applies $v_{\text{p}}/v_{\text{a}} = r_{\text{a}}/r_{\text{p}} = 3.00$.

items.stem: Arriving at the base of a smooth vertical loop (radius 1.6 m) at 10.3 m s⁻¹, a roller-coaster car of mass 240 kg climbs the inside of the track. Friction and air resistance are negligible, and g = 9.8 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) By energy conservation, ½mv_bot² = ½mv_top² + mg(2R), v_top = √(v_bot² − 4gR) = 6.59 m s⁻¹. (b) Downward radial balance F_top + mg = mv_top²/R gives F_top = 4.15 × 10³ N. (c) Setting F_top = 0 gives v_top = √(gR) and v_bot,min = √(5gR) = 8.85 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies energy conservation with vertical rise Δh = 2R.
Obtains v_top = 6.59 m s⁻¹.
Uses F_top = m(v_top²/R − g) at the apex.
Obtains F_top = 4.15 × 10³ N.
Combines v_top,min² = gR with v_bot,min² = v_top,min² + 4gR.
Obtains v_bot,min = 8.85 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the speed of the car as it passes the highest point of the circle.
workingSteps: Conservation of mechanical energy with Δh = 2R gives v_top² = v_bot² − 4gR.

parts.prompt: Determine the magnitude of the normal contact force acting on the car at the highest point.
workingSteps: At the apex, F_top + mg = m v_top² / R.

parts.prompt: Calculate the minimum speed at the lowest point needed to complete the loop without losing contact at the top.
workingSteps: At threshold contact, v_top = √(gR), so v_bot,min = √(gR + 4gR) = √(5gR).

items.stem: At 11900 K, a spherical black-body star of radius 4.07 × 10⁹ m shines from 1.14 × 10¹⁶ m away from Earth. Use σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴ and b = 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K.
items.workedSolution: (a) By Wien's law, λ_max = b/T = 244 nm. (b) L = 4πR²σT⁴ = 2.37 × 10²⁹ W. (c) Apparent brightness b_app = L/(4πd²) = 1.45 × 10⁻⁴ W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses λ_max = 2.90 × 10⁻³ / T.
Obtains 244 nm.
Applies L = 4π R² σ T⁴.
Obtains 2.37 × 10²⁹ W.
Applies b_app = L / (4π d²).
Obtains 1.45 × 10⁻⁴ W m⁻².

items.stem: Convert distances via 1 pc = 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m. A star radiating 6.89 × 10²⁹ W has parallax 0.68 arcsec across Earth's 1 AU orbital radius. Here d / pc = 1 / (p / arcsec), as 1 pc gives 1 arcsecond over 1 AU.
items.workedSolution: (a) By parallax, d = 1 / 0.68 = 1.47 pc. (b) In SI units, d = 4.54 × 10¹⁶ m. (c) Apparent brightness b = L / (4π d²) = 2.66 × 10⁻⁵ W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Applies d(pc) = 1 / p(arcsec).
Obtains 1.47 pc.
Multiplies distance in parsecs by 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m pc⁻¹.
Obtains 4.54 × 10¹⁶ m.
Applies inverse-square law b = L / (4π d²).
Obtains 2.66 × 10⁻⁵ W m⁻².

items.stem: A red giant star on the HR diagram has a surface temperature of $3800\text{ K}$ and a radius equal to $40.0$ solar radii ($R_{\odot} = 6.96 \times 10^8\text{ m}$). Taking $\sigma = 5.67 \times 10^{-8}\text{ W m}^{-2}\text{ K}^{-4}$, calculate its total radiated power output $P$.
items.workedSolution: Radius $R = 40.0 \times 6.96 \times 10^8 = 2.78 \times 10^{10}\text{ m}$. Then $P = \sigma (4\pi R^2) T^4 = 1.15 × 10²⁹ W$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 1.15 × 10²⁹ W.

items.stem: Taking g = 9.8 m s⁻², consider a 1.6 kg ball tracing a vertical circle (radius 0.85 m) on a light string at constant speed 5.34 m s⁻¹. Work out the minimum top speed so the string does not go slack.
items.workedSolution: At the top limit, tension = 0 so weight alone provides centripetal force: mg = m v_min² / R => v_min = √(g R) = √(9.8 × 0.85) = 2.89 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Sets top support force to zero to obtain v_min = √(gR) = 2.89 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Suppose a 0.35 kg bob circles horizontally at constant speed on a light 0.8 m cord held at 24° from vertical. Find the cord tension with g = 9.8 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: Vertical force balance gives T cos θ = mg, so T = (0.35 × 9.8) / cos 24° = 3.75 N.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves T cos 24° = mg to obtain T = 3.75 N.

items.stem: What is the signed change in kinetic energy of a 1270 kg spacecraft moving from r₁ = 1.78 × 10⁷ m to r₂ = 6.41 × 10⁷ m around a planet of mass 6.49 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 7.11 × 10⁶ m? Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: Given that E_k(r) = +GMm/(2r) decreases as r increases, ΔE_k = ½GMm(1/r₂ − 1/r₁) = -1.12 × 10¹⁰ J.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ΔE_k = ½GMm(1/r₂ − 1/r₁) = -1.12 × 10¹⁰ J (negative).

items.stem: Shown in the diagram is a 1.29 kg mass tied to a light string, circling vertically with radius 2.68 m at steady speed 7.69 m s⁻¹. Use g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Critical apex speed v_min = √(gR) = 5.13 m s⁻¹. (b) At the top, F_top = m(v²/R − g) = 15.8 N. (c) At the bottom, F_bot = m(v²/R + g) = 41.1 N.

markScheme.criterion: Sets support force to zero at apex so mg = m v_min² / R.
Obtains 5.13 m s⁻¹.
Subtracts mg from m v² / R at the top.
Obtains 15.8 N.
Adds mg to m v² / R at the bottom.
Obtains 41.1 N.

items.stem: Where g = 9.81 m s⁻², a small 0.206 kg ball enters a smooth vertical circular track (radius 9.26 m) at the base at 30.7 m s⁻¹ with zero drag or friction.
items.workedSolution: (a) Using ½mv_bot² = ½mv_top² + mg(2R), v_top = √(v_bot² − 4gR) = 24.1 m s⁻¹. (b) Downward radial balance F_top + mg = mv_top²/R gives F_top = 10.9 N. (c) Setting F_top = 0 gives v_top = √(gR) and v_bot,min = √(5gR) = 21.3 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies energy conservation with vertical rise Δh = 2R.
Obtains v_top = 24.1 m s⁻¹.
Uses F_top = m(v_top²/R − g) at the apex.
Obtains F_top = 10.9 N.
Combines v_top,min² = gR with v_bot,min² = v_top,min² + 4gR.
Obtains v_bot,min = 21.3 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Find the minimum launch speed from Primary Asteroid's surface to clear the null point and reach Secondary Moonlet. Both airless spheres have centres 6.05 × 10⁸ m apart, with mass 1.32 × 10²⁵ kg (radius 6.37 × 10⁶ m) for Primary Asteroid and mass 8.25 × 10²³ kg (radius 1.83 × 10⁶ m) for Secondary Moonlet. Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: Surface potential at x = R₁ is V(R₁) = −GM₁/R₁ − GM₂/(d − R₁) = -1.38 × 10⁸ J kg⁻¹. Null-point potential at x₀ = 4.84 × 10⁸ m is V(x₀) = -2.27 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. Potential barrier ΔV = V(x₀) − V(R₁) = 1.36 × 10⁸ J kg⁻¹, so v_min = √(2ΔV) = 1.65 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ΔV = V(x₀) − V(R₁) and v_min = √(2ΔV) = 1.65 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A spherical planet of uniform density has mass 2.77 × 10²⁵ kg and radius 7.76 × 10⁶ m. A small probe of mass 190 kg is lowered into a narrow shaft inside the planet to r = 4.27 × 10⁶ m from the centre, with G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Surface field g₀ = GM/R² = 30.7 N kg⁻¹. (b) At r = 4.27 × 10⁶ m, uniform-sphere interior scaling g = g₀(r/R) gives 16.9 N kg⁻¹. (c) Force on probe F = mg = 3.21 × 10³ N.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes M and R into g₀ = GM / R².
Obtains g₀ = 30.7 N kg⁻¹.
Applies linear interior field law g(r) = GMr/R³.
Obtains g = 16.9 N kg⁻¹.
Multiplies probe mass by field strength at r.
Obtains F = 3.21 × 10³ N.

items.stem: The graph plots the field of an airless, non-rotating planet (mass 2.71 × 10²⁵ kg, radius 1.18 × 10⁷ m). A 254 kg spacecraft lies 2.07 × 10⁷ m from its centre. Set potential to zero at infinity, with G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) At the planet's surface, V_surface = −GM/R = -1.53 × 10⁸ J kg⁻¹. (b) Escape speed v_esc = √(−2 V_surface) = √(2GM/R) = 1.75 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹. (c) At r = 2.07 × 10⁷ m, E_p = −GMm/r = -2.22 × 10¹⁰ J.

Obtains -2.22 × 10¹⁰ J.

items.stem: What is the magnitude of the resultant gravitational field acting on a 900 kg probe between World P and World Q? It lies 2.22 × 10⁸ m from World P's centre, with 4.03 × 10⁸ m between centres. Take mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg (radius 7.33 × 10⁶ m) for World P, mass 9.55 × 10²³ kg (radius 2.09 × 10⁶ m) for World Q, and G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: Subtracting the opposing field magnitudes gives |g_net| = |G M₁ / x² − G M₂ / (d − x)²| = |0.00808 − 0.00194| = 0.00614 N kg⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts opposing inverse-square field magnitudes to obtain 0.00614 N kg⁻¹.

items.stem: With μ_s = 0.25 and bank angle 28°, a 1050 kg train travels at 26.9 m s⁻¹ around a curved track of radius 105 m. Given g = 9.81 m s⁻², determine the limiting speed before outward slip.
items.workedSolution: At maximum speed, limiting friction μ_s N acts down the slope: N(cos θ − μ_s sin θ) = mg and N(sin θ + μ_s cos θ) = m v_max² / r. Dividing yields v_max = √[g r (sin 28° + 0.25 cos 28°) / (cos 28° − 0.25 sin 28°)] = 30.5 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves N and down-slope μ_s N horizontally and vertically to obtain v_max = 30.5 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Cosmologists observe Type Ia supernovae in distant galaxies. They use these measurements to determine the Hubble constant and study the expansion history of the Universe.
items.workedSolution: Level 3 synthesis: distance modulus from Type Ia peak absolute magnitude gives distance, and spectral redshift gives recession velocity. The graph gradient gives $H$ in $\text{km s}^{-1}\text{ Mpc}^{-1}$, and $t \approx 1/H$ assumes a constant expansion rate. Fainter high-$z$ supernovae show accelerating expansion, pointing to dark energy.

markScheme.criterion: Explains Type Ia supernovae act as standard candles with known peak absolute magnitude due to the Chandrasekhar mass limit.
States how measuring peak apparent magnitude $m$ yields distance $d$ via $m - M = 5\lg(d/10)$ (with conversion from pc to Mpc).
Explains how measuring fractional wavelength shift of host galaxy spectral lines gives recession velocity $v = |z|c$.
Explains plotting recession speed $v$ against distance $d$ so the straight-line gradient equals $H$ (in $\text{km s}^{-1}\text{ Mpc}^{-1}$).
Evaluates limitations of $t \approx 1/H$ (assumes constant expansion rate, dust absorption, or local galaxy motions).
Explains that distant supernovae appeared dimmer than expected, showing accelerating expansion driven by dark energy.
