parts.prompt: Explain how astronomers use Type Ia supernovae and spectral measurements to determine the Hubble constant. Discuss uncertainties in estimating the age of the Universe from $H$, and explain why very distant supernovae led to the dark-energy hypothesis.
parts.expectedAnswer: In this method, distance modulus from type Ia peak absolute magnitude and recession velocity from spectral redshift determine the Hubble constant. A Type Ia supernova occurs when a white dwarf accretes matter up to the Chandrasekhar limit, producing a predictable peak absolute magnitude ($M \approx -19.3$). Measuring peak apparent magnitude $m$ gives distance $d$ in parsecs from $m - M = 5\lg(d/10)$, which is converted into megaparsecs. At the same time, comparing shifted absorption lines in the host galaxy's spectrum against laboratory wavelengths yields redshift $|z| = \Delta\lambda / \lambda$ and recession velocity $v = |z|c$ in $\text{km s}^{-1}$. Plotting $v$ against $d$ yields a straight line through the origin whose gradient is $H$ in $\text{km s}^{-1}\text{ Mpc}^{-1}$. Estimating age via $t \approx 1/H$ assumes a constant expansion rate and is limited by distance-calibration uncertainties, interstellar dust dimming, and local peculiar galaxy velocities. For very high-redshift supernovae, objects appeared dimmer than predicted by steady or decelerating expansion, indicating that cosmic expansion is accelerating under dark energy.
workingSteps: Explain why Type Ia supernovae have known peak absolute magnitude (Chandrasekhar limit).
Show how $m - M = 5\lg(d/10)$ gives distance in pc and converts to Mpc.
Explain how spectral redshift gives recession speed $v = |z|c$.
Explain plotting $v$ against $d$ and taking gradient $H$ with units $\text{km s}^{-1}\text{ Mpc}^{-1}$.

items.stem: Mission records describe a 432 kg spacecraft in a circular orbit (radius 1.44 × 10⁷ m) around a spherical planet (mass 8.6 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 6.55 × 10⁶ m). Set potential energy to zero at infinity, with G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) From circular orbit dynamics, E_k = GMm/(2r) = 8.60 × 10⁹ J. (b) E_p = −GMm/r = -1.72 × 10¹⁰ J. (c) Total mechanical energy E_tot = E_k + E_p = −GMm/(2r) = -8.60 × 10⁹ J.

markScheme.criterion: Applies E_k = GMm / (2r).
Obtains E_k = 8.60 × 10⁹ J.
Applies E_p = −GMm / r including negative sign.
Obtains E_p = -1.72 × 10¹⁰ J.
Sums E_k + E_p or applies E_tot = −GMm / (2r).
Obtains E_tot = -8.60 × 10⁹ J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the kinetic energy of the spacecraft in this circular orbit.
workingSteps: From m v² / r = G M m / r², E_k = ½ m v² = G M m / (2r).

parts.prompt: Calculate the gravitational potential energy of the spacecraft.
Determine the total mechanical energy of the spacecraft.
workingSteps: E_tot = E_k + E_p = −G M m / (2r) = -8.60 × 10⁹ J.

items.stem: A Hertzsprung–Russell diagram shows four stars with region names removed, including Star Beta at surface temperature 15000 K and luminosity 0.004 L☉. Use solar values L☉ = 3.83 × 10²⁶ W, R☉ = 6.96 × 10⁸ m, and σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.
items.workedSolution: (a) Star Beta lies in the white-dwarf region. (b) L = 0.004 × 3.83 × 10²⁶ = 1.53 × 10²⁴ W. (c) R = √[L/(4πσT⁴)] = 6.52 × 10⁶ m = 0.00936 R☉.

markScheme.criterion: States white-dwarf.
Multiplies L / L☉ by 3.83 × 10²⁶ W.
Obtains L = 1.53 × 10²⁴ W.
Applies R = √[L / (4π σ T⁴)] and divides by R☉.
Obtains 0.00936 R☉.

items.stem: A car of mass 920 kg travels at 11.8 m s⁻¹ around a flat circular track of radius 44 m. Taking μ_s = 0.48 and g = 9.81 m s⁻², calculate the maximum speed of the car before it starts to slip.
items.workedSolution: Just before slipping, m v_max² / r = μ_s m g, independent of mass: v_max = √(μ_s g r) = √(0.48 × 9.81 × 44) = 14.4 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates v_max = √(μ_s g r) = 14.4 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: In a lab demonstration, a 1.2 kg bob hangs on a light 2.4 m cord and circles horizontally at constant speed. The cord stays at 42° to the vertical (g = 9.81 m s⁻²).
items.workedSolution: (a) Vertical equilibrium T cos 42° = (1.2)(9.81) gives T = 15.8 N. (b) Horizontal radius r = 2.4 sin 42° = 1.61 m; horizontal dynamics T sin θ = mv²/r yields v = 3.77 m s⁻¹. (c) Period P = 2πr / v = 2.68 s.

markScheme.criterion: Equates vertical component T cos θ to weight mg.
Obtains tension 15.8 N.
Uses r = L sin θ and equates T sin θ (or mg tan θ) to m v² / r.
Obtains speed 3.77 m s⁻¹.
Applies P = 2π r / v or P = 2π√(L cos θ / g).
Obtains period 2.68 s.

parts.prompt: Calculate the tension in the cord supporting the bob.
workingSteps: Vertical force balance gives T cos θ = mg.

parts.prompt: Determine the linear speed of the bob along its horizontal circular path.
workingSteps: Horizontal radius r = L sin θ = 2.4 sin 42° = 1.61 m.
From T sin θ = m v² / r, v = √(g r tan θ) = 3.77 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the time period for one complete revolution of the bob.

items.stem: An exoplanet of radius 5.00 × 10⁷ m orbits a star of radius 7.50 × 10⁸ m. It causes a maximum star speed of 42.0 m s⁻¹ along our line of sight, measured using the H-alpha line at 656 nm.
items.workedSolution: (a) $\Delta\lambda = 0.0918 pm$. (b) Dip $= 0.444\%$. (c) periodic Doppler shift of stellar absorption lines caused by orbit around the common centre of mass.

markScheme.criterion: Applies $\Delta\lambda / \lambda = v / c$.
Correct shift 0.0918 pm.
Computes $(r_p / R_s)^2 \times 100$.
Correct transit dip 0.444%.
States star and planet orbit their common centre of mass.
Links line-of-sight wobble to periodic Doppler shift of stellar absorption lines.

Calculate the expected percentage transit dip if the orbit is viewed edge-on.

workingSteps: Star and planet both orbit their shared centre of mass.
Periodic motion toward and away from Earth causes alternating blueshifts and redshifts.

items.stem: Star X lies in the bottom-left region of the IB Hertzsprung–Russell diagram (near the $0.01\,R_{\odot}$ constant-radius line). Which set of physical properties describes Star X?
items.workedSolution: Because $L = 4\pi R^2 \sigma T^4$ and temperature decreases to the right, a star in the bottom-left has a high surface temperature. It also has low luminosity and a very small stellar radius.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that high surface temperature low luminosity and very small stellar radius in the bottom-left region.

options.distractorRationale: High-luminosity stars sit near the top of the HR diagram, far above $0.01\,R_{\odot}$.

options.label: C
options.text: It is a white dwarf with high surface temperature low luminosity and very small stellar radius in the bottom-left region.

options.label: D
options.text: It is a cool red dwarf with very low surface temperature and low luminosity on the lower-right main sequence.
options.distractorRationale: Since temperature decreases from left to right on an HR diagram, the bottom-left region is hot, not cool.

items.stem: How do the design and siting of infrared (I-R) and X-ray telescopes differ from ground-based visible reflectors?
items.workedSolution: Observing outside the visible band needs special telescope designs. Infrared telescopes must be cooled to very low temperatures, while X-ray telescopes use grazing-incidence mirrors in space.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that infrared telescopes need cooling to very low temperatures, while X-ray telescopes use grazing-incidence mirrors in space.

options.label: A
options.text: Infrared telescopes use wide wire-mesh dishes at sea level while X-ray telescopes use thick glass refracting lenses.
options.distractorRationale: Wire mesh is for radio wavelengths, and thick glass absorbs X-rays completely.

options.label: B
options.text: Astronomical infrared telescopes need cryogenic cooling while X-ray telescopes use grazing-incidence mirrors in space because Earth's atmosphere absorbs X-rays and water vapour absorbs I-R.

options.label: C
options.text: X-ray telescopes work best on low humid plains using parabolic silver mirrors at normal incidence.
options.distractorRationale: High-energy X-rays penetrate normal-incidence mirrors and are completely absorbed by the atmosphere.

options.label: D
options.text: Infrared telescopes must be heated above 1000 K to emit reference radiation while X-ray scopes use plastic lenses.
options.distractorRationale: Infrared telescopes must be cooled to very low temperatures so their own thermal infrared emission does not swamp faint targets.

items.stem: Newton's universal law of gravitation $F = G m_1 m_2 / r^2$ is applied to a satellite orbiting outside a planet. Under what physical condition can the planet be treated as a point mass?
items.workedSolution: A uniform-density (or spherically symmetric) sphere produces an external radial field identical to a point mass at its centre. Therefore, outside its surface, it acts gravitationally as if all its mass were concentrated at its centre.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct explanation: outside its surface, a uniform spherical body acts as if all its mass were at its centre.

options.label: B
options.text: A spherical body of uniform density acts gravitationally outside its surface as if all its mass were concentrated at its centre.

options.label: C
options.text: Only when the satellite mass equals the planet mass so their mutual gravitational forces cancel.
options.distractorRationale: The point-mass approximation depends on the spherical symmetry of the attracting body, not equal masses.

options.label: D
options.text: Only when the planet stops rotating and carries zero atmosphere.
options.distractorRationale: The shell theorem requires spherical symmetry of mass distribution, regardless of atmosphere.

items.stem: The diagram shows a smooth vertical circular track of radius 1.2 m. A small ball of mass 1.2 kg enters at the bottom at 10.4 m s⁻¹. Ignore friction and air drag. With g = 9.8 m s⁻², what normal force acts on the ball at the top?
items.workedSolution: At the top of the loop, v_top² = v_bot² − 4gR = (10.4)² − 4(9.8)(1.2) = 61.1 m² s⁻². Radial force balance F_top + mg = m v_top² / R gives F_top = 1.2(61.1 / 1.2 − 9.8) = 49.4 N.

markScheme.criterion: Combines v_top² = v_bot² − 4gR with F_top = m(v_top²/R − g) to obtain 49.4 N.

items.stem: Find the peak wavelength in nm for a spherical black-body star at 14800 K. Its radius is 1.55 × 10¹⁰ m and distance from Earth is 1.56 × 10¹⁶ m. Use b = 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K.
items.workedSolution: From Wien's law, λ_max = b / T = 2.90 × 10⁻³ / 14800 = 1.96 × 10⁻⁷ m = 196 nm.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates λ_max = 2.90 × 10⁻³ / 14800 = 196 nm.

items.stem: Find the apparent brightness b = L / (4πd²) at Earth of a 1.03 × 10³⁰ W star with parallax 0.387 arcsec across Earth's 1 AU baseline. At 1 pc, 1 AU gives 1 arcsecond, so d / pc = 1 / (p / arcsec). Take 1 pc = 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m.
items.workedSolution: Converting parallax to metres gives d = (1 / 0.387) pc = 2.58 pc = 7.97 × 10¹⁶ m. Apparent brightness b = L / (4π d²) = 1.03 × 10³⁰ / (4π × (7.97 × 10¹⁶)²) = 1.29 × 10⁻⁵ W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Converts d = (1/p) pc to metres and evaluates b = L/(4πd²) = 1.29 × 10⁻⁵ W m⁻².

items.stem: The AQA Hertzsprung–Russell diagram plots absolute magnitude $M$ from $-10$ to $+15$ against temperature decreasing from $50\,000\text{ K}$ to $2500\text{ K}$. What evolutionary path does a Sun-like star follow after leaving the main sequence?
items.workedSolution: A $1 M_{\odot}$ star starts on the main sequence ($M \approx +4.8, T \approx 5800\text{ K}$) and evolves along the path main sequence to red giant then white dwarf.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that main sequence to red giant then white dwarf.

options.label: A
options.text: It cools straight down the main sequence to become a red dwarf and eventually explodes as a Type Ia supernova.
options.distractorRationale: Single Sun-like stars expand into red giants before shedding a planetary nebula to leave a white dwarf.

options.label: B
options.text: After spending billions of years fusing hydrogen, it moves from the main sequence to red giant then white dwarf at the bottom left.

options.label: C
options.text: It moves straight up to blue supergiants and collapses directly into a stellar-mass black hole.
options.distractorRationale: Only very massive stars ($> 8 M_{\odot}$) become supergiants and end as neutron stars or black holes.

options.label: D
options.text: It moves left to hotter main-sequence class O stars before shrinking back to its starting point.
options.distractorRationale: Core hydrogen exhaustion causes the outer envelope to expand and cool into the red giant region.

items.stem: What upward tension pulls on a 0.9 kg ball at the base of a vertical circle (radius 1.35 m)? A light string keeps its speed steady at 4.87 m s⁻¹; take g = 9.8 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: At the base of the circle, upward tension opposes downward weight mg to produce upward centripetal acceleration: F_bot − mg = m v² / R, giving F_bot = m(v²/R + g) = 0.9 × ((4.87)² / 1.35 + 9.8) = 24.6 N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses F_bot = m(v²/R + g) to obtain 24.6 N.

options.distractorRationale: Quotes net centripetal force m v² / R alone without adding mg to overcome downward weight.

items.stem: Held at 24° to the vertical, a light 1.65 m string swings a 2.5 kg bob at constant speed in a horizontal circle. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Vertical force balance gives T cos 24° = (2.5)(9.8) gives T = 26.8 N. (b) Horizontal radius r = 1.65 sin 24° = 0.671 m; horizontal dynamics T sin θ = mv²/r yields v = 1.71 m s⁻¹. (c) Period P = 2πr / v = 2.46 s.

markScheme.criterion: Equates vertical component T cos θ to weight mg.
Obtains tension 26.8 N.
Uses r = L sin θ and equates T sin θ (or mg tan θ) to m v² / r.
Obtains speed 1.71 m s⁻¹.
Applies P = 2π r / v or P = 2π√(L cos θ / g).
Obtains period 2.46 s.

workingSteps: Vertical force balance gives T cos θ = mg.

parts.prompt: Determine the linear speed of the bob along its horizontal circular path.
workingSteps: Horizontal radius r = L sin θ = 1.65 sin 24° = 0.671 m.
From T sin θ = m v² / r, v = √(g r tan θ) = 1.71 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the time period for one complete revolution of the bob.

items.stem: Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². Around a spherical planet (1.07 × 10²⁵ kg, radius 7.33 × 10⁶ m), a 600 kg spacecraft moves from inner circle r₁ = 1.39 × 10⁷ m to outer circle r₂ = 3.34 × 10⁷ m.
items.workedSolution: (a) At the inner orbit, E_tot(r₁) = −GMm/(2r₁) = -1.54 × 10¹⁰ J. (b) Final bound energy E_tot(r₂) = -6.41 × 10⁹ J, so ΔE_tot = 8.99 × 10⁹ J. (c) Outer orbital period T₂ = 2π√(r₂³/GM) = 4.54 × 10⁴ s.

markScheme.criterion: Applies E_tot = −GMm / (2r₁).
Obtains -1.54 × 10¹⁰ J.
Evaluates E_tot(r₂) − E_tot(r₁) = ½GMm(1/r₁ − 1/r₂).
Obtains 8.99 × 10⁹ J.
Applies Kepler's third law at outer radius r₂.
Obtains 4.54 × 10⁴ s.

parts.prompt: Calculate the initial total mechanical energy of the spacecraft in the orbit of radius r₁.
Determine the minimum energy that must be supplied to transfer the spacecraft to the circular orbit of radius r₂.
Calculate the orbital period of the spacecraft in the outer circular orbit of radius r₂.

items.stem: At steady speed 11.4 m s⁻¹, a 960 kg car passes over the crest of a circular road bridge of radius 18 m. Given g = 9.81 m s⁻², determine the normal force from the road.
items.workedSolution: At the crest of the road, downward resultant force is mg − N_top = m v² / R, so N_top = m(g − v²/R) = 960 × (9.81 − (11.4)² / 18) = 2.49 × 10³ N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies radial force equation at apex to obtain 2.49 × 10³ N.

items.stem: Passing the bottom of a smooth vertical circular track (radius 0.6 m) at 5.97 m s⁻¹, a 240 kg roller-coaster car reaches the top. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect friction and drag to find the normal force.
items.workedSolution: At the top, v_top² = v_bot² − 4gR = (5.97)² − 4(9.81)(0.6) = 12.1 m² s⁻². Radial force balance F_top + mg = m v_top² / R gives F_top = 240(12.1 / 0.6 − 9.81) = 2.48 × 10³ N.

markScheme.criterion: Combines v_top² = v_bot² − 4gR with F_top = m(v_top²/R − g) to obtain 2.48 × 10³ N.

items.stem: Both Ice Giant (radius 7.33 × 10⁶ m, mass 1.64 × 10²⁵ kg) and Retrograde Moon (radius 1.57 × 10⁶ m, mass 6.56 × 10²³ kg) are airless spheres lying 3.0 × 10⁸ m apart centre to centre. Set potential to zero at infinity, with G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Null point distance x₀ = d√M₁/(√M₁ + √M₂) = 2.50 × 10⁸ m. (b) Combined scalar potential V(x₀) = -5.25 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. (c) Potential barrier from x = R₁ to x₀ is ΔV = 1.44 × 10⁸ J kg⁻¹, giving v_min = √(2ΔV) = 1.70 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies x₀ = d√M₁ / (√M₁ + √M₂).
Obtains x₀ = 2.50 × 10⁸ m.
Sums both negative scalar potentials −GM₁/x₀ − GM₂/(d − x₀).
Obtains V(x₀) = -5.25 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹.
Equates ½v_min² to potential barrier V(x₀) − V(R₁).
Obtains v_min = 1.70 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A spherical planet of uniform density has mass 2.69 × 10²⁵ kg and radius 4.92 × 10⁶ m. A small probe of mass 123 kg is lowered into a narrow shaft inside the planet to r = 3.2 × 10⁶ m from the centre. Taking G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², determine the gravitational field strength g(r) at this point.
items.workedSolution: Inside a uniform sphere (r < R), enclosed mass M_enc = M(r/R)³, so g(r) = G M r / R³ = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 2.69 × 10²⁵ × 3.2 × 10⁶) / (4.92 × 10⁶)³ = 48.2 N kg⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates gravitational field strength at r = 3.2 × 10⁶ m to obtain 48.2 N kg⁻¹.

items.stem: Consider a 620 kg spacecraft positioned 2.65 × 10⁷ m from the centre of a spherical planet (8.95 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 8.28 × 10⁶ m). Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². Determine the planet's surface escape speed.
items.workedSolution: From energy conservation, ½m v_esc² − G M m / R = 0 gives v_esc = √(2 G M / R) = √(2 × 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 8.95 × 10²⁴ / 8.28 × 10⁶) = 1.20 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates surface escape speed √(2GM / R) = 1.20 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: The centres of Body Alpha and Body Beta are 3.56 × 10⁸ m apart. Body Alpha has mass 6.14 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 7.33 × 10⁶ m, while Body Beta has mass 6.82 × 10²³ kg and radius 2.09 × 10⁶ m. A 926 kg probe travels along the line between their centres and passes 1.25 × 10⁸ m from Body Alpha's centre. Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Matching GM₁/x₀² = GM₂/(d − x₀)² yields x₀ = d√M₁/(√M₁ + √M₂) = 2.67 × 10⁸ m. (b) At x = 1.25 × 10⁸ m, |g| = |GM₁/x² − GM₂/(d − x)²| = 0.0254 N kg⁻¹. (c) Net force F = m|g| = 23.5 N.

markScheme.criterion: Equates opposing inverse-square field strengths GM₁/x₀² = GM₂/(d − x₀)².
Takes square root correctly to form x₀ = d√M₁ / (√M₁ + √M₂).
Obtains x₀ = 2.67 × 10⁸ m.
Subtracts opposing field magnitudes at x and (d − x).
Obtains |g| = 0.0254 N kg⁻¹.
Multiplies by spacecraft mass to obtain 23.5 N.

parts.prompt: Calculate the distance from the centre of Body Alpha to the point between them where the resultant gravitational field strength is zero.
workingSteps: At the null point, G M₁ / x₀² = G M₂ / (d − x₀)².
Taking square roots gives x₀ = [√M₁ / (√M₁ + √M₂)] d = 2.67 × 10⁸ m.

parts.prompt: Calculate the magnitude of the resultant gravitational field strength when the probe is 1.25 × 10⁸ m from the centre of Body Alpha.
workingSteps: |g| = |G M₁ / x² − G M₂ / (d − x)²| = 0.0254 N kg⁻¹.

parts.prompt: State the magnitude of the resultant gravitational force on the 926 kg probe at this point.

items.stem: Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² to model a 160 kg trolley on a smooth banked track (radius 85 m, angle 28°, no sideways friction) in horizontal circular motion.
items.workedSolution: (a) Zero vertical acceleration gives N cos 28° = mg gives N = 1.78 × 10³ N. (b) Horizontal component F_c = N sin 28° = 835 N. (c) Setting m v² / r = F_c yields v_ideal = 21.1 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses N cos θ = mg (zero vertical acceleration).
Obtains N = 1.78 × 10³ N.
Evaluates F_c = N sin θ or mg tan θ.
Obtains F_c = 835 N.
Equates m v² / r to F_c and solves for v.
Obtains v_ideal = 21.1 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the magnitude of the normal contact force on the trolley.
workingSteps: Vertical equilibrium gives N cos θ = mg.

parts.prompt: Determine the horizontal centripetal force acting toward the centre of the circle.
workingSteps: Horizontal component of normal reaction provides the centripetal force: F_c = N sin θ = mg tan θ.

parts.prompt: Hence calculate the ideal frictionless speed of the trolley.
workingSteps: From m v² / r = F_c, v = √(F_c r / m) = √(g r tan θ) = 21.1 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: In the spectrum of a distant galaxy, the hydrogen-beta line shifts from a rest wavelength of 486.1 nm to 494.85 nm. Taking c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and H₀ = 67.4 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹, calculate the recession speed of the galaxy in km s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses v ≈ (Δλ / λ₀) c to obtain 5.40 × 10³ km s⁻¹.

items.stem: A satellite of mass 638 kg moves in a circular orbit of radius 1.583 × 10⁷ m around the centre of a spherical planet. The planet has mass 7.99 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 7.54 × 10⁶ m, with G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) With orbital radius r = 1.583 × 10⁷ m, g = GM/r² = 2.13 N kg⁻¹. (b) Orbital speed v = √(GM/r) = 5.80 × 10³ m s⁻¹. (c) Period T = 2πr/v = 1.71 × 10⁴ s.

markScheme.criterion: Uses centre-to-centre orbital radius r in g = GM / r².
Obtains g = 2.13 N kg⁻¹.
Equates v²/r to g (or GM/r²).
Obtains v = 5.80 × 10³ m s⁻¹.
Applies T = 2πr / v or Kepler's third law.
Obtains T = 1.71 × 10⁴ s.

items.stem: Find the total energy of a 280 kg spacecraft circling a spherical planet at radius 7.17 × 10⁶ m. The planet has mass 2.99 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 4.78 × 10⁶ m. Set E_p = 0 at infinity and G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: For a circular orbit, E_k = +GMm/(2r) and E_p = −GMm/r, so E_tot = E_k + E_p = −GMm/(2r) = −(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 2.99 × 10²⁴ × 280) / (2 × 7.17 × 10⁶) = -3.89 × 10⁹ J.

markScheme.criterion: Applies E_tot = −GMm / (2r) with negative sign to obtain -3.89 × 10⁹ J.

options.label: A

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits the negative bound-state sign, reporting +GMm/(2r) instead of −GMm/(2r).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omits both the negative sign and the virial factor of 1/2, reporting +GMm/r.

items.stem: On a Hertzsprung–Russell diagram, Star Iota has surface temperature 7600 K and luminosity 14 L☉. Taking L☉ = 3.83 × 10²⁶ W, R☉ = 6.96 × 10⁸ m, and σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴, determine the radius of Star Iota in solar radii (R☉).
items.workedSolution: Luminosity L = 14 × 3.83 × 10²⁶ = 5.36 × 10²⁷ W. From L = 4π R² σ T⁴, R = √[L / (4π σ T⁴)] = 1.50 × 10⁹ m, so R / R☉ = R / (6.96 × 10⁸) = 2.16 R☉.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Stefan-Boltzmann scaling to obtain 2.16 R☉.

items.stem: A car of mass 1320 kg travels at a constant speed of 13.8 m s⁻¹ around a flat circular track of radius 105 m without slipping. The coefficient of static friction between the tyres and the track is 0.55, and g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the sideways static frictional force acting on the tyres.
items.workedSolution: Because 13.8 m s⁻¹ is below the slipping limit v_max = √(μ_s g r) = 23.8 m s⁻¹, static friction self-adjusts to match the required centripetal force: f_s = m v² / r = 1320 × (13.8)² / 105 = 2.39 × 10³ N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses f_s = m v² / r (not μ_s mg) to obtain 2.39 × 10³ N.

items.stem: Why are polar low-Earth orbits chosen instead of geostationary orbits for weather monitoring, environmental mapping, and detailed Earth imaging?
items.workedSolution: A polar low-Earth orbit sweeps the entire Earth surface as Earth rotates beneath it. Its lower altitude also gives higher image resolution and lower signal latency.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct explanation: a polar low-Earth orbit scans the whole Earth as Earth rotates, giving higher image resolution and lower signal latency.

items.stem: A car of mass 480 kg travels at 12.4 m s⁻¹ around a flat circular track of radius 52 m. Taking μ_s = 0.74 and g = 9.8 m s⁻², calculate the maximum speed of the car before it starts to slip.
items.workedSolution: Just before slipping, m v_max² / r = μ_s m g, independent of mass: v_max = √(μ_s g r) = √(0.74 × 9.8 × 52) = 19.4 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates v_max = √(μ_s g r) = 19.4 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: In a class demo, a 0.35 kg sphere traces a horizontal circle on a light 1.1 m string held at 42° to the vertical. Taking g = 9.81 m s⁻², determine the speed along the path.
items.workedSolution: From geometry, r = L sin θ = 1.1 sin 42° = 0.736 m. Since T sin θ = mv²/r and T cos θ = mg, v = √(g r tan θ) = √(9.81 × 0.736 × tan 42°) = 2.55 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses r = L sin θ and v = √(g L sin θ tan θ) to obtain 2.55 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Sustained hydrogen nuclear fusion occurs in the core of a main-sequence star, but not in its cooler outer layers. Why does this happen?
items.workedSolution: Positively charged nuclei repel electrostatically; sustained stellar fusion therefore demands extremely high temperature to overcome electrostatic Coulomb repulsion and high density for frequent collisions.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that extremely high temperature to overcome electrostatic Coulomb repulsion and high density for frequent collisions.

options.label: A
options.text: Fusion requires low core temperature and very low density so protons avoid colliding with electrons.
options.distractorRationale: Low temperature and low density prevent nuclei from overcoming Coulomb repulsion or colliding frequently.

options.label: B
options.text: Fusion requires extremely high temperature to overcome electrostatic Coulomb repulsion and high density for frequent collisions so nuclei approach close enough for the strong nuclear force to bind them.

options.label: C
options.text: Fusion requires extreme temperature solely to break gravitational bonds while density has no effect on reaction rate.
options.distractorRationale: Both high temperature (to overcome electrostatic repulsion) and high density (for frequent collisions) are essential.

options.label: D
options.text: Fusion occurs only where neutral hydrogen atoms remain un-ionized at low kinetic energy.
options.distractorRationale: Stellar cores are completely ionized hot plasma where bare nuclei collide at high kinetic energy.

items.stem: Two stars orbit their common centre of mass so closely that a telescope cannot resolve them spatially. How does spectroscopy reveal they are a binary system when viewed edge-on?
items.workedSolution: When viewed edge-on in its orbital plane, a spectroscopic binary produces periodic alternating blue and red Doppler shifts. These shifts allow astronomers to measure the orbital speed and radius.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that spectroscopic binary viewed in its orbital plane produces periodic alternating blue and red Doppler shifts.

options.label: A
options.text: A spectroscopic binary viewed in its orbital plane produces periodic alternating blue and red Doppler shifts as each star alternately moves toward and away from Earth.

options.label: B
options.text: Both stars remain permanently blue-shifted by the same constant wavelength regardless of orbital phase.
options.distractorRationale: Circular orbital motion reverses each star's radial velocity every half period.

options.label: C
options.text: Their spectral classes cycle continuously from O to M every few hours.
options.distractorRationale: Surface temperature does not cycle across all spectral classes during an orbit; Doppler shifts move line wavelengths.

options.label: D
options.text: No Doppler shift occurs edge-on because orbital velocity is strictly perpendicular to the line of sight.
options.distractorRationale: Edge-on (in the orbital plane) gives the MAXIMUM radial velocity component along the line of sight.

items.stem: Atmospheric viscous drag causes an $800\text{ kg}$ Earth satellite ($M = 5.97 \times 10^{24}\text{ kg}$) to spiral slowly from a circular orbit of radius $r_1 = 7000\text{ km}$ down to a circular orbit of radius $r_2 = 6600\text{ km}$. How much mechanical energy is dissipated as thermal energy during this decay?
items.workedSolution: Thermal energy dissipated equals the decrease in total mechanical energy: $Q = E_{\text{tot},1} - E_{\text{tot},2} = \frac{GMm}{2}\left(\frac{1}{r_2} - \frac{1}{r_1}\right) = 1.38 GJ$.

items.stem: Consider a roller-coaster car of mass 123 kg arriving at the base of a smooth vertical loop (radius 12.9 m) at 30.7 m s⁻¹. Friction and air resistance are negligible; use g = 9.8 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) By energy conservation, ½mv_bot² = ½mv_top² + mg(2R), v_top = √(v_bot² − 4gR) = 20.9 m s⁻¹. (b) Downward radial balance F_top + mg = mv_top²/R gives F_top = 2.96 × 10³ N. (c) Setting F_top = 0 gives v_top = √(gR) and v_bot,min = √(5gR) = 25.1 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies energy conservation with vertical rise Δh = 2R.
Obtains v_top = 20.9 m s⁻¹.
Uses F_top = m(v_top²/R − g) at the apex.
Obtains F_top = 2.96 × 10³ N.
Combines v_top,min² = gR with v_bot,min² = v_top,min² + 4gR.
Obtains v_bot,min = 25.1 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the speed of the car as it passes the highest point of the circle.
workingSteps: Conservation of mechanical energy with Δh = 2R gives v_top² = v_bot² − 4gR.

parts.prompt: Determine the magnitude of the normal contact force acting on the car at the highest point.
workingSteps: At the apex, F_top + mg = m v_top² / R.

parts.prompt: Calculate the minimum speed at the lowest point needed to complete the loop without losing contact at the top.
workingSteps: At threshold contact, v_top = √(gR), so v_bot,min = √(gR + 4gR) = √(5gR).

items.stem: With radius 1.46 × 10¹⁰ m and distance 2.96 × 10¹⁶ m from Earth, a spherical star radiates as a black body at 11600 K. Use σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴ and b = 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K.
items.workedSolution: (a) By Wien's law, λ_max = b/T = 250 nm. (b) L = 4πR²σT⁴ = 2.75 × 10³⁰ W. (c) Apparent brightness b_app = L/(4πd²) = 2.50 × 10⁻⁴ W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses λ_max = 2.90 × 10⁻³ / T.
Obtains 250 nm.
Applies L = 4π R² σ T⁴.
Obtains 2.75 × 10³⁰ W.
Applies b_app = L / (4π d²).
Obtains 2.50 × 10⁻⁴ W m⁻².

items.stem: Astronomers observe a star of luminosity 9.96 × 10²⁸ W with annual parallax 0.26 arcsec across Earth's 1 AU baseline. Take 1 pc = 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m, where 1 pc is the distance giving 1 arcsecond over 1 AU so d / pc = 1 / (p / arcsec).
items.workedSolution: (a) Using the parsec relation, d = 1 / 0.26 = 3.85 pc. (b) In SI units, d = 1.19 × 10¹⁷ m. (c) Apparent brightness b = L / (4π d²) = 5.63 × 10⁻⁷ W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Applies d(pc) = 1 / p(arcsec).
Obtains 3.85 pc.
Multiplies distance in parsecs by 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m pc⁻¹.
Obtains 1.19 × 10¹⁷ m.
Applies inverse-square law b = L / (4π d²).
Obtains 5.63 × 10⁻⁷ W m⁻².

items.stem: What normal force does a smooth vertical track (radius 1.1 m) exert at the highest point on a small ball of mass 1.25 kg moving steadily at 5.19 m s⁻¹? Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: Resolving towards the centre at the top, both normal contact force and weight mg act downward toward the centre: F_top + mg = m v² / R, so F_top = m(v²/R − g) = 1.25 × ((5.19)² / 1.1 − 9.8) = 18.4 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies radial force equation at apex to obtain 18.4 N.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Equates the support force directly to net centripetal force m v² / R, ignoring gravity mg.

options.distractorRationale: Adds weight mg to m v² / R instead of subtracting mg, confusing the top of a vertical circle with the bottom.

items.stem: A light 2.1 m cord hangs at 24° to the vertical as its 1.8 kg bob moves steadily in a horizontal circle. Find the period of the motion (g = 9.8 m s⁻²).
items.workedSolution: By vertical and radial balance, T cos θ = mg and T sin θ = m ω² (L sin θ), ω = √(g / (L cos θ)). Thus the period is P = 2π√(L cos θ / g) = 2π√((2.1 cos 24°) / 9.8) = 2.78 s.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates 2π√(L cos 24° / g) to obtain 2.78 s.

options.distractorRationale: Substitutes L sin θ instead of vertical height L cos θ under the square root in T = 2π√(L cos θ / g).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Applies the simple pendulum formula 2π√(L/g), omitting the cos θ vertical-projection factor.

options.label: D

items.stem: Find the Hohmann transfer time from r₁ = 8.67 × 10⁶ m to r₂ = 3.47 × 10⁷ m for a 1590 kg satellite. Its spherical planet has mass 8.76 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 6.19 × 10⁶ m. Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: The elliptical path has semi-major axis a = ½(r₁ + r₂) = 2.17 × 10⁷ m. Moving from the inner orbit to the outer orbit takes half an orbital period: t_H = π√(a³ / GM) = 1.31 × 10⁴ s.

markScheme.criterion: Uses a = ½(r₁ + r₂) and t_H = π√(a³ / GM) to obtain 1.31 × 10⁴ s.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Averages the inner and outer half-periods linearly rather than applying T ∝ a^(3/2).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the full elliptical period 2π√(a³ / GM) instead of the half-orbit Hohmann coast time π√(a³ / GM).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses major axis (r₁ + r₂) instead of semi-major axis a = (r₁ + r₂)/2 in Kepler's third law.

items.stem: A light string guides a 0.772 kg mass around a vertical circle (radius 1.8 m) at constant speed 5.46 m s⁻¹. Take gravitational field strength g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Critical top speed v_min = √(gR) = 4.20 m s⁻¹. (b) At the top, F_top = m(v²/R − g) = 5.21 N. (c) At the bottom, F_bot = m(v²/R + g) = 20.4 N.

markScheme.criterion: Sets support force to zero at apex so mg = m v_min² / R.
Obtains 4.20 m s⁻¹.
Subtracts mg from m v² / R at the top.
Obtains 5.21 N.
Adds mg to m v² / R at the bottom.
Obtains 20.4 N.

parts.prompt: Calculate the minimum speed at the highest point needed for the string to remain taut.
workingSteps: Setting support force at the top to zero gives m v_min² / R = mg.

parts.prompt: Calculate the tension in the string when the mass passes the highest point at 5.46 m s⁻¹.
workingSteps: At the top, F_top + mg = m v² / R.

parts.prompt: Determine the tension in the string when the mass passes the lowest point at 5.46 m s⁻¹.
workingSteps: At the bottom, F_bot − mg = m v² / R.

items.stem: Zero friction and air drag act as a 370 kg roller-coaster car enters the lowest point of a smooth vertical loop (radius 6.69 m) at 26.1 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) From energy balance, ½mv_bot² = ½mv_top² + mg(2R), v_top = √(v_bot² − 4gR) = 20.5 m s⁻¹. (b) Downward radial balance F_top + mg = mv_top²/R gives F_top = 1.95 × 10⁴ N. (c) Setting F_top = 0 gives v_top = √(gR) and v_bot,min = √(5gR) = 18.1 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies energy conservation with vertical rise Δh = 2R.
Obtains v_top = 20.5 m s⁻¹.
Uses F_top = m(v_top²/R − g) at the apex.
Obtains F_top = 1.95 × 10⁴ N.
Combines v_top,min² = gR with v_bot,min² = v_top,min² + 4gR.
Obtains v_bot,min = 18.1 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the minimum speed at the lowest point needed to complete the loop without losing contact at the top.
workingSteps: At threshold contact, v_top = √(gR), so v_bot,min = √(gR + 4gR) = √(5gR).

items.stem: Set zero potential at infinity and G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². Planet Major (mass 6.87 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 7.33 × 10⁶ m) and Planet Minor (mass 2.75 × 10²³ kg, radius 1.57 × 10⁶ m) are airless spheres with centres 3.84 × 10⁸ m apart. Calculate the total potential at the null point.
items.workedSolution: Where the fields cancel, x₀ = d√M₁/(√M₁ + √M₂) = 3.20 × 10⁸ m, scalar potentials add negatively: V_g(x₀) = −GM₁/x₀ − GM₂/(d − x₀) = −(G/d)(√M₁ + √M₂)² = -1.72 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Sums both negative scalar potentials at x₀ to obtain -1.72 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹.

items.stem: A spherical planet of uniform density has mass 1.29 × 10²⁵ kg and radius 5.9 × 10⁶ m. A probe of mass 844 kg is lowered into a narrow shaft inside the planet to a distance of 4.43 × 10⁶ m from the centre, with G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Surface field g₀ = GM/R² = 24.7 N kg⁻¹. (b) At r = 4.43 × 10⁶ m, uniform-sphere interior scaling g = g₀(r/R) gives 18.6 N kg⁻¹. (c) Force on probe F = mg = 1.57 × 10⁴ N.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes M and R into g₀ = GM / R².
Obtains g₀ = 24.7 N kg⁻¹.
Applies linear interior field law g(r) = GMr/R³.
Obtains g = 18.6 N kg⁻¹.
Multiplies probe mass by field strength at r.
Obtains F = 1.57 × 10⁴ N.

Determine the gravitational field strength at r = 4.43 × 10⁶ m from the centre.
workingSteps: For a uniform sphere with r < R, g(r) = g₀ (r / R) = G M r / R³.

parts.prompt: Calculate the magnitude of the gravitational force on the 844 kg probe at this position.

items.stem: A non-rotating airless planet has radius 1.22 × 10⁷ m and mass 2.85 × 10²⁴ kg. Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². A 656 kg probe lies 3.9 × 10⁷ m from its centre.
items.workedSolution: (a) At the planet's surface, V_surface = −GM/R = -1.56 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹. (b) Escape speed v_esc = √(−2 V_surface) = √(2GM/R) = 5.58 × 10³ m s⁻¹. (c) At r = 3.9 × 10⁷ m, E_p = −GMm/r = -3.20 × 10⁹ J.

markScheme.criterion: Applies V_g = −GM / R with negative sign.
Obtains -1.56 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹.
Uses v_esc = √(2GM / R) or √(−2 V_surface).
Obtains 5.58 × 10³ m s⁻¹.
Applies E_p = −GMm / r at probe radius.
Obtains -3.20 × 10⁹ J.

items.stem: In the diagram, Companion Moon (mass 3.86 × 10²³ kg, radius 2.09 × 10⁶ m) is 7.51 × 10⁸ m centre-to-centre from Primary Planet (mass 1.39 × 10²⁵ kg, radius 7.33 × 10⁶ m). A 978 kg spacecraft lies between them, 2.63 × 10⁸ m from Primary Planet's centre. Calculate the magnitude of the resultant field strength at the spacecraft (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²).
items.workedSolution: Since the two pulls oppose on the line between them, |g_net| = |G M₁ / x² − G M₂ / (d − x)²| = |0.0134 − 1.08 × 10⁻⁴| = 0.0133 N kg⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts opposing inverse-square field magnitudes to obtain 0.0133 N kg⁻¹.

items.stem: Suppose a 320 kg trolley follows a horizontal circle along a smooth track tilted at 28° (radius 145 m, no sideways friction). Work out the normal reaction using g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: Since vertical acceleration is zero, N cos θ = mg, so N = (320 × 9.81) / cos 28° = 3.56 × 10³ N.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves vertically N cos 28° = mg to obtain N = 3.56 × 10³ N.

items.stem: Astronomers observe the hydrogen-gamma line in the spectrum of a distant galaxy. Its wavelength shifts from rest wavelength λ₀ = 434 nm to λ_obs = 441.81 nm, with c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and H₀ = 68 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) z = (λ_obs − λ₀)/λ₀ = 0.0180. (b) Recession speed v ≈ zc = 5.40 × 10³ km s⁻¹. (c) Hubble distance d = v/H₀ = 79.4 Mpc.

markScheme.criterion: Applies z = Δλ / λ₀.
Obtains z = 0.0180.
Multiplies z by c and converts to km s⁻¹.
Obtains v = 5.40 × 10³ km s⁻¹.
Applies d = v / H₀.
Obtains d = 79.4 Mpc.

Determine the recession speed of the galaxy in km s⁻¹.
Estimate the distance from Earth to the galaxy in Mpc.

items.stem: A spectral line in a distant galaxy has a fractional wavelength shift of $+0.0172$. Take $c = 3.00 \times 10^8\text{ m s}^{-1}$, $H = 65\text{ km s}^{-1}\text{ Mpc}^{-1}$, and $1\text{ Mpc} = 3.08 \times 10^{22}\text{ m}$.

markScheme.criterion: Applies $v = |z| c$ and converts to km s⁻¹.
Correct recession speed 5.16 × 10³ km s⁻¹.
Divides recession speed by $H = 65\text{ km s}^{-1}\text{ Mpc}^{-1}$.
Correct distance 79.4 Mpc.
Converts $H$ to $\text{s}^{-1}$ and evaluates $1/H$.
Correct age estimate 15.0 Gyr.

items.stem: A satellite of mass 750 kg orbits a spherical planet in a circular path at an altitude of 7.65 × 10⁶ m above the surface. The planet has mass 1.01 × 10²⁵ kg and radius 5.1 × 10⁶ m. Taking G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², calculate the orbital period of the satellite.
items.workedSolution: Orbital radius from planet centre r = R_p + h = 5.1 × 10⁶ + 7.65 × 10⁶ = 1.275 × 10⁷ m. By Kepler's third law, T = 2π√(r³ / GM) = 2π√((1.275 × 10⁷)³ / (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 1.01 × 10²⁵)) = 1.10 × 10⁴ s.

markScheme.criterion: Uses r = 1.275 × 10⁷ m to obtain 1.10 × 10⁴ s.

items.stem: At orbital radius 2.18 × 10⁷ m, a 906 kg satellite circles a planet of mass 1.53 × 10²⁵ kg and radius 6.06 × 10⁶ m. Take E_p = 0 at infinity (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²).
items.workedSolution: (a) Using standard orbit relations, E_k = GMm/(2r) = 2.12 × 10¹⁰ J. (b) E_p = −GMm/r = -4.24 × 10¹⁰ J. (c) Total mechanical energy E_tot = E_k + E_p = −GMm/(2r) = -2.12 × 10¹⁰ J.

markScheme.criterion: Applies E_k = GMm / (2r).
Obtains E_k = 2.12 × 10¹⁰ J.
Applies E_p = −GMm / r including negative sign.
Obtains E_p = -4.24 × 10¹⁰ J.
Sums E_k + E_p or applies E_tot = −GMm / (2r).
Obtains E_tot = -2.12 × 10¹⁰ J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the kinetic energy of the satellite in this circular orbit.
workingSteps: From m v² / r = G M m / r², E_k = ½ m v² = G M m / (2r).

parts.prompt: Calculate the gravitational potential energy of the satellite.
Determine the total mechanical energy of the satellite.
workingSteps: E_tot = E_k + E_p = −G M m / (2r) = -2.12 × 10¹⁰ J.

items.stem: A Hertzsprung–Russell diagram shows four stars with region names removed, including Star Mu at surface temperature 5400 K and luminosity 22000 L☉. Use solar values L☉ = 3.83 × 10²⁶ W, R☉ = 6.96 × 10⁸ m, and σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.
items.workedSolution: (a) Star Mu lies in the supergiant region. (b) L = 22000 × 3.83 × 10²⁶ = 8.43 × 10³⁰ W. (c) R = √[L/(4πσT⁴)] = 1.18 × 10¹¹ m = 169 R☉.

markScheme.criterion: States supergiant.
Multiplies L / L☉ by 3.83 × 10²⁶ W.
Obtains L = 8.43 × 10³⁰ W.
Applies R = √[L / (4π σ T⁴)] and divides by R☉.
Obtains 169 R☉.

items.stem: A car of mass 1820 kg travels at a constant speed of 7.12 m s⁻¹ around a flat circular track of radius 22 m. Taking g = 9.81 m s⁻², calculate the minimum coefficient of static friction needed so the car does not slip.
items.workedSolution: Cornering without slipping requires μ_s m g ≥ m v² / r, so μ_min = v² / (g r) = (7.12)² / (9.81 × 22) = 0.235.

markScheme.criterion: Computes μ_min = v² / (g r) = 0.235.

items.stem: Taking G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², Earth mass M = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg, Earth radius R_E = 6.37 × 10⁶ m (giving surface g = 9.81 m s⁻²), and T = 86400 s, calculate the altitude above Earth's surface of a geostationary satellite.
items.workedSolution: r = (G M T² / 4π²)^(1/3) = 4.22 × 10⁷ m. Subtracting Earth's radius: h = r − R_E = 3.59 × 10⁷ m.

markScheme.criterion: Computes r and subtracts R_E to obtain altitude 3.59 × 10⁷ m.

items.stem: A car of mass 920 kg travels at a constant speed of 16.5 m s⁻¹ around a flat circular track of radius 78 m without slipping. The coefficient of static friction is μ_s = 0.62, and g = 9.8 m s⁻². Calculate the sideways static frictional force acting on the tyres.
items.workedSolution: Because 16.5 m s⁻¹ is below the slipping limit v_max = √(μ_s g r) = 21.8 m s⁻¹, static friction self-adjusts to match the required centripetal force: f_s = m v² / r = 920 × (16.5)² / 78 = 3.21 × 10³ N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses f_s = m v² / r (not μ_s mg) to obtain 3.21 × 10³ N.

items.stem: In a conical pendulum, a 0.75 kg sphere orbits steadily in a horizontal circle on a light 2.75 m string tilted at 38° to vertical. Calculate its centripetal acceleration using g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: Combining radial and vertical equations by dividing T sin θ = m a_c by vertical equilibrium T cos θ = mg gives a_c = g tan θ = 9.81 × tan 38° = 7.66 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Applies a_c = g tan 38° to obtain 7.66 m s⁻².

items.stem: What physical balance maintains the stable radius of a main-sequence star over billions of years?

options.text: Hydrostatic equilibrium, in which outward radiation pressure balances inward gravitational force in a stable star.

options.label: B
options.text: Outward gravitational repulsion balances inward radiation pressure from the star's corona.
options.distractorRationale: Gravity always acts inward toward the centre of mass, while radiation pressure acts outward.

options.label: C
options.text: Electrostatic repulsion between protons in the photosphere balances the strong nuclear force across the star.
options.distractorRationale: The strong nuclear force is very short-range inside nuclei and cannot act across a whole star.

options.label: D
options.text: Magnetic field lines generated by sunspots hold up the entire stellar mass against nuclear fission.
options.distractorRationale: Main-sequence stars are powered by nuclear fusion and supported by outward thermal/radiation pressure against gravity.

items.stem: Planet P orbits a star in a circular orbit of radius $1.00\text{ AU}$ with orbital period $1.00\text{ yr}$. A second planet Q orbits the same star at orbital radius $4.00\text{ AU}$. Using Kepler's third law, what is the orbital period of planet Q?
items.workedSolution: By Kepler's third law, $\left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{r_2}{r_1}\right)^3 = 4.00^3 = 64.0 \Rightarrow T_2 = 1.00 \times \sqrt{64.0} = 8.00 yr$.

items.stem: Swinging vertically in a vertical circle (radius 6.69 m) on a light string, a small ball of mass 0.823 kg moves at 26.1 m s⁻¹ at the base. Neglect air drag; what is the ball's speed at the top? (g = 9.8 m s⁻²)
items.workedSolution: Climbing one diameter raises height by Δh = 2R. By conservation of energy, ½m v_top² + mg(2R) = ½m v_bot², so v_top = √(v_bot² − 4gR) = √((26.1)² − 4 × 9.8 × 6.69) = 20.5 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses Δh = 2R in v_top = √(v_bot² − 4gR) to obtain 20.5 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: The spectrum graph shows a black-body star peaking at 195.9 nm with luminosity 2.059 × 10³⁰ W. Given σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴ and b = 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K, what is its radius?
items.workedSolution: By Wien's law, T = b / λ_max = 2.90 × 10⁻³ / (195.9 × 10⁻⁹) = 1.48 × 10⁴ K. From L = 4π R² σ T⁴, R = √[L / (4π σ T⁴)] = 7.76 × 10⁹ m.

markScheme.criterion: Finds T = 1.48 × 10⁴ K via Wien's law and R = √[L/(4πσT⁴)] = 7.76 × 10⁹ m.

items.stem: An observation records annual parallax 0.127 arcsec over Earth's 1 AU orbit for a star of luminosity 4.74 × 10²⁸ W. Convert via 1 pc = 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m and recall d / pc = 1 / (p / arcsec) (1 AU gives 1 arcsecond at 1 pc). Determine its apparent brightness b = L / (4πd²) at Earth.
items.workedSolution: Converting parallax to metres gives d = (1 / 0.127) pc = 7.87 pc = 2.43 × 10¹⁷ m. Apparent brightness b = L / (4π d²) = 4.74 × 10²⁸ / (4π × (2.43 × 10¹⁷)²) = 6.39 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Converts d = (1/p) pc to metres and evaluates b = L/(4πd²) = 6.39 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻².

items.stem: Star X plotted on the AQA Hertzsprung–Russell diagram has a high surface temperature of $14\,000\text{ K}$ yet a very faint absolute magnitude of $M = +11.8$. To which stellar region does Star X belong?
items.workedSolution: High $T$ combined with very large positive (dim) $M = +11.8$ places Star X in the bottom-left white dwarf region.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that white dwarf.

items.stem: Find the minimum speed at the top before a small 0.9 kg ball loses contact inside a smooth vertical loop (radius 1.6 m) while moving steadily at 7.33 m s⁻¹. Use g = 9.8 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: At the top limit, normal contact force = 0 so weight alone provides centripetal force: mg = m v_min² / R => v_min = √(g R) = √(9.8 × 1.6) = 3.96 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Sets top support force to zero to obtain v_min = √(gR) = 3.96 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: How large is the tension in the light 0.95 m cord shown if its 0.75 kg sphere orbits steadily in a horizontal circle at 20° to the vertical? Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: Vertical equilibrium requires T cos θ = mg, so T = (0.75 × 9.8) / cos 20° = 7.82 N.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves T cos 20° = mg to obtain T = 7.82 N.

items.stem: A spherical planet of mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 8.28 × 10⁶ m has a 450 kg satellite shifting from radius 1.32 × 10⁷ m to radius 2.64 × 10⁷ m (both circular). With G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², what is the signed change in kinetic energy ΔE_k?
items.workedSolution: As E_k(r) = +GMm/(2r) decreases as r increases, ΔE_k = ½GMm(1/r₂ − 1/r₁) = -3.39 × 10⁹ J.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ΔE_k = ½GMm(1/r₂ − 1/r₁) = -3.39 × 10⁹ J (negative).

items.stem: Moving steadily at 4.97 m s⁻¹ on a light string, a 0.75 kg ball follows a vertical circle (radius 0.85 m). Given g = 9.81 m s⁻², determine the bottom tension.
items.workedSolution: At the bottom, upward tension opposes downward weight mg to produce upward centripetal acceleration: F_bot − mg = m v² / R, giving F_bot = m(v²/R + g) = 0.75 × ((4.97)² / 0.85 + 9.81) = 29.2 N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses F_bot = m(v²/R + g) to obtain 29.2 N.

items.stem: The diagram shows a roller-coaster car of mass 123 kg entering a smooth vertical circular track (radius 0.617 m) at 7.04 m s⁻¹. Neglect friction and air resistance. With g = 9.81 m s⁻², what minimum base speed keeps contact at the top?
items.workedSolution: Maintaining contact at the apex requires v_top ≥ √(gR). Conservation of energy from bottom to top (Δh = 2R) gives ½m v_bot,min² = ½m(gR) + mg(2R) => v_bot,min = √(5gR) = √(5 × 9.81 × 0.617) = 5.50 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates v_bot,min = √(5gR) = 5.50 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: The potential curve links airless spheres Primary Planet (mass 7.27 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 5.41 × 10⁶ m) and Companion Moon (mass 2.02 × 10²³ kg, radius 1.83 × 10⁶ m), 2.92 × 10⁸ m apart centre to centre. A probe launches from Primary Planet towards Companion Moon. With G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², work out the minimum launch speed to pass the null point.
items.workedSolution: At launch (x = R₁), the potential is V(R₁) = −GM₁/R₁ − GM₂/(d − R₁) = -8.97 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹. Null-point potential at x₀ = 2.50 × 10⁸ m is V(x₀) = -2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. Potential barrier ΔV = V(x₀) − V(R₁) = 8.74 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹, so v_min = √(2ΔV) = 1.32 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ΔV = V(x₀) − V(R₁) and v_min = √(2ΔV) = 1.32 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A spherical planet of uniform density has mass 4.92 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 4.92 × 10⁶ m. A probe of mass 370 kg is lowered into a narrow shaft inside the planet to a distance of 1.97 × 10⁶ m from the centre. Taking G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², calculate the gravitational field strength at this point.
items.workedSolution: Inside a uniform sphere (r < R), enclosed mass M_enc = M(r/R)³, so g(r) = G M r / R³ = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 4.92 × 10²⁴ × 1.97 × 10⁶) / (4.92 × 10⁶)³ = 5.43 N kg⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates gravitational field strength at r = 1.97 × 10⁶ m to obtain 5.43 N kg⁻¹.

items.stem: An 825 kg spacecraft is at distance 2.17 × 10⁷ m from a 4.42 × 10²⁴ kg planet of radius 5.72 × 10⁶ m. Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². State the escape speed at the planet's surface.
items.workedSolution: For surface escape, ½m v_esc² − G M m / R = 0 gives v_esc = √(2 G M / R) = √(2 × 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 4.42 × 10²⁴ / 5.72 × 10⁶) = 1.02 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates surface escape speed √(2GM / R) = 1.02 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: The zero-field point lies on the line joining Ice Giant (mass 6.32 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 5.41 × 10⁶ m) and Retrograde Moon (mass 7.8 × 10²² kg, radius 1.57 × 10⁶ m). Their centres are 3.66 × 10⁸ m apart. How far is this point from Ice Giant's centre?
items.workedSolution: For zero net field, equate the opposing pulls: G M₁ / x₀² = G M₂ / (d − x₀)² gives (d − x₀)/x₀ = √(M₂/M₁), so x₀ = [√M₁ / (√M₁ + √M₂)] d = 3.29 × 10⁸ m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses x₀ = d √M₁ / (√M₁ + √M₂) to obtain 3.29 × 10⁸ m.

items.stem: Zero sideways friction acts on a 640 kg car tracing a horizontal circle of radius 215 m along a 25° banked road. Use g = 9.81 m s⁻² to determine the normal reaction force.
items.workedSolution: With zero vertical acceleration in a horizontal circle, N cos θ = mg, so N = (640 × 9.81) / cos 25° = 6.93 × 10³ N.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves vertically N cos 25° = mg to obtain N = 6.93 × 10³ N.

items.stem: A distant galaxy is 80.96 Mpc from Earth and recedes according to Hubble's law. Taking H₀ = 71.5 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, calculate the observed wavelength in nm of the hydrogen-beta line (λ₀ = 486.1 nm).
items.workedSolution: Recession speed v = H₀ d = 71.5 × 80.96 = 5.79 × 10³ km s⁻¹. Redshift z = v / c = 0.0193, so λ_obs = λ₀(1 + z) = 486.1 × (1 + 0.0193) = 495 nm.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates v = H₀d, z = v/c, and λ_obs = λ₀(1 + z) = 495 nm.

items.stem: Hydrogen absorption lines from a receding galaxy show a cosmological redshift magnitude $|z| = 0.0390$. Taking $c = 3.00 \times 10^8\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and the Hubble constant $H = 65\text{ km s}^{-1}\text{ Mpc}^{-1}$, estimate the distance to the galaxy.
items.workedSolution: The recession speed is $v = |z|c = 0.0390 \times 3.00 \times 10^{5}\text{ km s}^{-1} = 1.17 × 10⁴ km s⁻¹$. By Hubble's law, $d = \frac{v}{H} = \frac{11700}{65} = 180 Mpc$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 180 Mpc.

items.stem: Consider a 4.61 × 10²⁴ kg spherical planet of radius 5.9 × 10⁶ m with a 1650 kg satellite circling at radius 8.85 × 10⁶ m. Work out the satellite's orbital kinetic energy (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²).
items.workedSolution: Using m v² / r = G M m / r² gives orbital kinetic energy E_k = ½ m v² = G M m / (2r) = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 4.61 × 10²⁴ × 1650) / (2 × 8.85 × 10⁶) = 2.87 × 10¹⁰ J.

markScheme.criterion: Computes E_k = GMm / (2r) = 2.87 × 10¹⁰ J.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Assigns a negative sign to kinetic energy by confusing E_k with total orbital energy E_tot.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 1/2 in E_k = ½mv² = GMm/(2r), computing GMm/r instead.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses surface altitude (r − R_p) instead of orbital radius r.

items.stem: On a Hertzsprung–Russell diagram with region labels hidden, Star Delta-2 has surface temperature 4460 K and luminosity 36600 L☉. In which region of the diagram does Star Delta-2 lie?
items.workedSolution: With T = 4460 K and L = 36600 L☉ (note temperature increases from right to left on an HR diagram), Star Delta-2 lies in the supergiant region (supergiant).

markScheme.criterion: Identifies the supergiant region from T = 4460 K and L = 36600 L☉.

items.stem: A car of mass 920 kg travels at a constant speed of 12.2 m s⁻¹ around a flat circular track of radius 35 m. Taking g = 9.81 m s⁻², calculate the minimum coefficient of static friction needed so the car does not slip.
items.workedSolution: Cornering without slipping requires μ_s m g ≥ m v² / r, so μ_min = v² / (g r) = (12.2)² / (9.81 × 35) = 0.433.

markScheme.criterion: Computes μ_min = v² / (g r) = 0.433.

items.stem: A communications satellite must stay fixed above one point on Earth's surface. Which complete set of orbital conditions must it satisfy?
items.workedSolution: All three AQA requirements are needed: a twenty-four hour orbital period matching Earth's rotation, directly above the equator, and orbiting west-to-east. Therefore the correct statement is: It must have a twenty-four hour orbital period matching Earth's rotation, directly above the equator, and orbiting west-to-east.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: twenty-four hour orbital period matching Earth rotation, directly above the equator, and orbiting west-to-east.

options.distractorRationale: Orbiting east-to-west opposes Earth's west-to-east rotation.

items.stem: Examine the sketch of a light 1.25 m cord tilted 42° from vertical while carrying a 0.45 kg sphere in a horizontal circle. Calculate the steady speed using g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: Orbit radius r = L sin θ = 1.25 sin 42° = 0.836 m. Since T sin θ = mv²/r and T cos θ = mg, v = √(g r tan θ) = √(9.81 × 0.836 × tan 42°) = 2.72 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses r = L sin θ and v = √(g L sin θ tan θ) to obtain 2.72 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A gas-giant exoplanet of radius 6.40 × 10⁷ m transits directly across the face of a host star of radius 8.00 × 10⁸ m. What percentage dip in the star's observed intensity occurs during full transit?
items.workedSolution: The fractional intensity dip equals the cross-sectional area ratio $\frac{\Delta I}{I} = \left(\frac{r_p}{R_s}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{6.40 \times 10^7}{8.00 \times 10^8}\right)^2 = 0.080^2 = 0.00640 = 0.640\%$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 0.640%.

items.stem: Astronomers analyse the light spectrum emitted by a star. How do they use it to determine both its surface temperature and the elements in its outer atmosphere?
items.workedSolution: In stellar spectroscopy, the peak wavelength gives surface temperature while dark absorption lines reveal chemical composition.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that peak wavelength gives surface temperature while dark absorption lines reveal chemical composition.

options.text: Dark absorption lines measure the star's distance in parsecs while the overall brightness alone gives its exact chemical composition.
options.distractorRationale: Distance is found via parallax (for nearby stars), and overall brightness does not identify elements.

options.label: B
options.text: Surface temperature is determined purely from the number of dark absorption lines while peak wavelength identifies individual elements.
options.distractorRationale: Peak wavelength gives surface temperature through Wien's law, whereas specific absorption wavelengths identify elements.

options.label: C
options.text: Stellar spectra show only bright emission lines from the fusion core without any continuous radiation.
options.distractorRationale: Stars produce a continuous surface spectrum crossed by dark absorption lines from the cooler outer atmosphere.

options.label: D
options.text: The continuous black-body peak wavelength gives surface temperature while dark absorption lines reveal chemical composition via characteristic wavelengths matching laboratory reference lines.

items.stem: What is the defining physical property of a black hole's event horizon (at the Schwarzschild radius $R_{\text{s}} \approx 2GM / c^2$)?
items.workedSolution: Setting $\frac{1}{2}mv_{\text{esc}}^2 = \frac{GMm}{R_{\text{s}}}$ with $v_{\text{esc}} = c$ yields $R_{\text{s}} \approx 2GM/c^2$: the escape velocity at the event horizon equals or exceeds the speed of light.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that escape velocity at the event horizon equals or exceeds the speed of light.

options.text: Gravitational field strength drops to zero inside the event horizon so photons drift freely away.
options.distractorRationale: Gravity grows even stronger inside the event horizon.

options.label: B
options.text: A black hole has zero mass and reflects all incident visible light with 100 percent efficiency.
options.distractorRationale: Black holes possess huge mass and trap all incoming radiation.

options.label: C
options.text: The escape velocity equals the speed of sound in interstellar hydrogen gas.
options.distractorRationale: The defining boundary is where escape velocity reaches the speed of light $c$.

options.label: D
options.text: The escape velocity at the event horizon equals or exceeds the speed of light, so no matter or electromagnetic radiation can escape from inside it.

items.stem: A $500\text{ kg}$ satellite is launched from rest on the surface of a non-rotating planet of mass $M = 5.97 \times 10^{24}\text{ kg}$ and radius $R = 6370\text{ km}$ into a circular orbit at altitude $h = 630\text{ km}$ ($G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\text{ N m}^2\text{ kg}^{-2}$). What is the minimum energy required to place the satellite into this orbit?
items.workedSolution: Surface energy $E_{\text{s}} = -\frac{GMm}{R} = −31.3 GJ$. Circular orbit ($r = 7000\text{ km}$) total energy $E_{\text{o}} = -\frac{GMm}{2r} = −14.2 GJ$. Minimum energy $\Delta E = E_{\text{o}} - E_{\text{s}} = 17.0 GJ$.

markScheme.criterion: Applies $\Delta E = GMm\left(\frac{1}{R} - \frac{1}{2r}\right) = 17.0 GJ$.

items.stem: Suppose an object of mass 247 kg on a light string passes the base of a vertical circle (radius 1.65 m) at 12.1 m s⁻¹ with zero air drag. Using g = 9.8 m s⁻², find the object's top speed.
items.workedSolution: The height gain to the peak is Δh = 2R. By conservation of energy, ½m v_top² + mg(2R) = ½m v_bot², so v_top = √(v_bot² − 4gR) = √((12.1)² − 4 × 9.8 × 1.65) = 9.04 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses Δh = 2R in v_top = √(v_bot² − 4gR) to obtain 9.04 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: From 3.04 × 10¹⁶ m away, a spherical black-body star of radius 1.51 × 10¹⁰ m glows at 9820 K. Find its peak wavelength in nm (b = 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K).
items.workedSolution: Wien's law yields λ_max = b / T = 2.90 × 10⁻³ / 9820 = 2.95 × 10⁻⁷ m = 295 nm.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates λ_max = 2.90 × 10⁻³ / 9820 = 295 nm.

items.stem: Receiving 2.954 × 10⁻⁷ W m⁻² at Earth (1 AU baseline) from a 1.51 × 10²⁹ W star, astronomers determine its parallax in arcsec. Recall that d / pc = 1 / (p / arcsec) (1 pc gives 1 arcsecond for 1 AU), with 1 pc = 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m.
items.workedSolution: From b = L / (4π d²), d = √[L / (4π b)] = 2.02 × 10¹⁷ m = 6.54 pc. Hence p = 1 / d_pc = 0.153 arcsec.

markScheme.criterion: Solves d = √[L/(4πb)] in parsecs and p = 1/d = 0.153 arcsec.

items.stem: How strong is the upward normal contact force at the lowest point for a small 0.9 kg ball moving steadily at 4.4 m s⁻¹ inside a smooth vertical loop (radius 1.1 m)? Use g = 9.8 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: At the base of the circle, upward normal contact force opposes downward weight mg to produce upward centripetal acceleration: F_bot − mg = m v² / R, giving F_bot = m(v²/R + g) = 0.9 × ((4.4)² / 1.1 + 9.8) = 24.7 N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses F_bot = m(v²/R + g) to obtain 24.7 N.

items.stem: A conical pendulum runs steadily in a horizontal circle with a light 1.65 m string at 20° from the vertical and a 2.2 kg sphere. State its period using g = 9.8 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: Resolving forces gives T cos θ = mg and T sin θ = m ω² (L sin θ), ω = √(g / (L cos θ)). Thus the period is P = 2π√(L cos θ / g) = 2π√((1.65 cos 20°) / 9.8) = 2.50 s.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates 2π√(L cos 20° / g) to obtain 2.50 s.

items.stem: Moving along a Hohmann ellipse from r₁ = 8.67 × 10⁶ m to r₂ = 3.47 × 10⁷ m, a 1590 kg spacecraft orbits a 1.16 × 10²⁵ kg planet (radius 6.19 × 10⁶ m). What is the transfer time? (Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².)
items.workedSolution: For the transfer ellipse, semi-major axis a = ½(r₁ + r₂) = 2.17 × 10⁷ m. Moving from the inner orbit to the outer orbit takes half an orbital period: t_H = π√(a³ / GM) = 1.14 × 10⁴ s.

markScheme.criterion: Uses a = ½(r₁ + r₂) and t_H = π√(a³ / GM) to obtain 1.14 × 10⁴ s.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Averages the inner and outer half-periods linearly rather than applying T ∝ a^(3/2).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the full elliptical period 2π√(a³ / GM) instead of the half-orbit Hohmann coast time π√(a³ / GM).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses major axis (r₁ + r₂) instead of semi-major axis a = (r₁ + r₂)/2 in Kepler's third law.

items.stem: Crossing the top of a circular bridge (radius 18 m) at constant speed 11.4 m s⁻¹, a 1180 kg car presses on the road. Calculate the normal reaction force using g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: At the crest of the road, downward resultant force is mg − N_top = m v² / R, so N_top = m(g − v²/R) = 1180 × (9.81 − (11.4)² / 18) = 3.06 × 10³ N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies radial force equation at apex to obtain 3.06 × 10³ N.

items.stem: Ignoring air resistance, calculate the top-of-loop speed for a 46.3 kg object moving in a vertical circle (radius 4.32 m) on a light string. Its speed at the base is 16.9 m s⁻¹, with g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: Rising from bottom to top increases height by Δh = 2R. By conservation of energy, ½m v_top² + mg(2R) = ½m v_bot², so v_top = √(v_bot² − 4gR) = √((16.9)² − 4 × 9.81 × 4.32) = 10.8 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses Δh = 2R in v_top = √(v_bot² − 4gR) to obtain 10.8 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Measured at the zero-field null point between Dwarf Planet A and Companion B, what is the total gravitational potential? The airless spheres are 5.01 × 10⁸ m apart centre to centre, with mass 1.1 × 10²⁵ kg (radius 5.41 × 10⁶ m) for Dwarf Planet A and mass 1.22 × 10²⁴ kg (radius 1.57 × 10⁶ m) for Companion B. Take zero potential at infinity and G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: At the null point x₀ = d√M₁/(√M₁ + √M₂) = 3.76 × 10⁸ m, scalar potentials add negatively: V_g(x₀) = −GM₁/x₀ − GM₂/(d − x₀) = −(G/d)(√M₁ + √M₂)² = -2.60 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Sums both negative scalar potentials at x₀ to obtain -2.60 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹.

items.stem: A spherical planet of uniform density has mass 4.78 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 1.18 × 10⁷ m. A probe of mass 250 kg is lowered into a narrow shaft inside the planet to r = 6.49 × 10⁶ m from the centre. Taking G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², determine the gravitational field strength g(r) at this point.
items.workedSolution: Inside a uniform sphere (r < R), enclosed mass M_enc = M(r/R)³, so g(r) = G M r / R³ = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 4.78 × 10²⁴ × 6.49 × 10⁶) / (1.18 × 10⁷)³ = 1.26 N kg⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates gravitational field strength at r = 6.49 × 10⁶ m to obtain 1.26 N kg⁻¹.

items.stem: Set zero potential at infinity, with G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². An 803 kg probe is 3.24 × 10⁷ m from the centre of a planet (mass 6.76 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 8.52 × 10⁶ m). Calculate the gravitational potential at that point.
items.workedSolution: Using the radial potential formula, V_g = −G M / r = −(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 6.76 × 10²⁴) / 3.24 × 10⁷ = -1.39 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Computes V_g = −GM / r = -1.39 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹ including the negative sign.

items.stem: Measured from the centre of Body Alpha, where between Body Alpha and Body Beta do their gravitational fields cancel? Body Alpha has mass 9.47 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 5.41 × 10⁶ m, Body Beta has mass 1.52 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 1.57 × 10⁶ m, and their centres are 5.69 × 10⁸ m apart.
items.workedSolution: Equating opposing field magnitudes G M₁ / x₀² = G M₂ / (d − x₀)² gives (d − x₀)/x₀ = √(M₂/M₁), so x₀ = [√M₁ / (√M₁ + √M₂)] d = 4.06 × 10⁸ m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses x₀ = d √M₁ / (√M₁ + √M₂) to obtain 4.06 × 10⁸ m.

items.stem: The diagram shows a smooth track banked at 25° to the horizontal, with radius 120 m and zero sideways friction. A 320 kg trolley moves round it horizontally. Using g = 9.81 m s⁻², what normal force acts on the trolley?
items.workedSolution: Vertical force balance for horizontal circular motion gives N cos θ = mg, so N = (320 × 9.81) / cos 25° = 3.46 × 10³ N.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves vertically N cos 25° = mg to obtain N = 3.46 × 10³ N.

items.stem: In the spectrum of a distant galaxy, a calcium absorption line (rest wavelength 396.8 nm) is observed at 422.2 nm. Using v ≈ zc with c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and H₀ = 66 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹, calculate the distance to the galaxy in megaparsecs.
items.workedSolution: Redshift z = (λ_obs − λ₀) / λ₀ = (422.2 − 396.8) / 396.8 = 0.0640. Recession speed v ≈ z c = 1.92 × 10⁴ km s⁻¹. From Hubble's law v = H₀ d, d = v / H₀ = 1.92 × 10⁴ / 66 = 291 Mpc.

markScheme.criterion: Finds z = 0.0640, v = 1.92 × 10⁴ km s⁻¹, and d = v / H₀ = 291 Mpc.

items.stem: A satellite of mass 508 kg orbits a spherical planet in a circular path at altitude h = 4.16 × 10⁶ m above the surface. The planet has mass 8.21 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 5.54 × 10⁶ m. Taking G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², calculate the circular orbital speed of the satellite.
items.workedSolution: Orbital radius from planet centre r = R_p + h = 5.54 × 10⁶ + 4.16 × 10⁶ = 9.7 × 10⁶ m. Equating GMm / r² = mv² / r gives v = √(GM / r) = √(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 8.21 × 10²⁴ / 9.7 × 10⁶) = 7.51 × 10³ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses r = 9.7 × 10⁶ m to obtain 7.51 × 10³ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: The energy graph tracks a 296 kg satellite orbiting at radius 1.83 × 10⁷ m around a 6.32 × 10²⁴ kg spherical planet of radius 8.3 × 10⁶ m. Work out its orbital kinetic energy using G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: From m v² / r = G M m / r², the kinetic energy is E_k = ½ m v² = G M m / (2r) = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 6.32 × 10²⁴ × 296) / (2 × 1.83 × 10⁷) = 3.41 × 10⁹ J.

markScheme.criterion: Computes E_k = GMm / (2r) = 3.41 × 10⁹ J.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses surface altitude (r − R_p) instead of orbital radius r.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 1/2 in E_k = ½mv² = GMm/(2r), computing GMm/r instead.

items.stem: On a Hertzsprung–Russell diagram, Star Zeta-2 has surface temperature 4160 K and luminosity 272 L☉. Taking L☉ = 3.83 × 10²⁶ W, R☉ = 6.96 × 10⁸ m, and σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴, calculate the radius of Star Zeta-2 as a multiple of R☉.
items.workedSolution: Luminosity L = 272 × 3.83 × 10²⁶ = 1.04 × 10²⁹ W. From L = 4π R² σ T⁴, R = √[L / (4π σ T⁴)] = 2.21 × 10¹⁰ m, so R / R☉ = R / (6.96 × 10⁸) = 31.7 R☉.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Stefan-Boltzmann scaling to obtain 31.7 R☉.

options.distractorRationale: Uses first power (T☉ / T) instead of squared (T☉ / T)² after taking the square root of T⁴.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes (R / R☉)² = L / (4π R☉² σ T⁴) and forgets to take the square root.
